Champion–challenger requires the same population, mature outcomes and pre-specified promotion criteria
Fairness definitions conflict mathematically; the institution must choose and justify one
Test error rates across groups, not only approval rates
Reject inference is assumption-heavy; TTC and PIT serve different purposes and must not be confused

quiz.q: Why do many institutions retain interpretable models for IFRS 9 expected credit loss while using machine learning for early warning?
opts: Regulators prohibit ML in accounting
Machine learning cannot model credit
ECL is audited and enters the financial statements, so calibration and explainability are non-negotiable
Interpretable models are always more accurate
quiz.fb: This is a defensible architecture: the audited provision requires numerically correct, explainable output, while early warning tolerates more complexity.

quiz.q: A team reports their credit model is 'fair'. The correct challenge is:
opts: Accept the finding and move on
Demand demographic parity always
Ask for the model's AUC
Ask which fairness definition was used and why, since demographic parity, equalised odds and within-group calibration cannot generally all hold
quiz.fb: The impossibility of simultaneously satisfying these definitions when base rates differ is a proven result. An unqualified fairness claim means the trade-off was never confronted.

quiz.q: Reject inference addresses which problem?
opts: Origination models are trained only on approved applicants, a systematically biased sample
Customers rejecting marketing offers
Regulators rejecting model submissions
Servers rejecting API calls
quiz.fb: Performance is observed only for those approved. Reject inference attempts to correct this, but it is assumption-heavy and must be documented as inferred.

quiz.q: Confusing through-the-cycle and point-in-time estimates typically produces:
opts: Improved fairness
Either volatile capital or unresponsive provisions, depending on which is misapplied
Faster model training
No material effect
quiz.fb: TTC suits capital because it is stable across the cycle; PIT suits IFRS 9 and pricing because it reflects current conditions.

quiz.q: In a champion–challenger programme, promotion criteria should be:
opts: Left to the vendor
Based on discrimination alone
Pre-specified — what improvement, on which metrics, sustained over what period
Decided after reviewing the results
quiz.fb: Agreeing criteria after seeing results invites motivated reasoning. Pre-specification is also the strongest evidence to a supervisor that change is controlled.

quiz.q: A model trained entirely on benign economic conditions is used for stress testing. The principal concern is:
opts: It cannot handle missing data
It will be too conservative
It will run too slowly
It has never observed the scenario it is being asked to predict, and complex models extrapolate unreliably
quiz.fb: Extrapolation beyond the training range is unreliable. Test that sensitivities are economically plausible and document judgemental overlays.

finance-advanced.title: Financial Crime at Scale: Graph & Network Intelligence
finance-advanced.summary: Entity resolution, network analytics and privacy-preserving collaboration
objectives: Apply graph analytics to financial crime beyond transaction-level monitoring
Understand entity resolution and why it determines detection capability
Understand typology discovery and unsupervised detection of unknown patterns
Evaluate privacy-enhancing technologies for cross-institution collaboration
Design a target financial crime architecture appropriate to a Nepali institution
Understand model risk considerations specific to financial crime systems

sections.h: Why the network is the unit of analysis
sections.html:
The foundational programme introduced graph analytics for mule networks and layering. At an advanced level, the shift is conceptual: in sophisticated financial crime, the network is the criminal artefact. Individual transactions are deliberately unremarkable — that is the design intent of structuring.

Formally, accounts and parties become nodes and transfers become edges, with attributes on both. Detection then draws on established network measures:

  • Centrality — accounts through which disproportionate flow passes, characteristic of collectors and hubs.
  • Community detection — densely connected clusters transacting far more with each other than with the wider network.
  • Path and cycle analysis — funds returning to origin through intermediaries, or moving through a chain within a compressed timeframe.
  • Temporal patterns — synchronised behaviour across nominally unrelated accounts, a strong signal of coordination.
  • Shared attributes — device identifiers, phone numbers, addresses, beneficiaries or employers linking supposedly independent customers.

Given the scale of remittance flows and the rapid growth of digital wallets in Nepal, shared-attribute and temporal analysis are particularly productive: mule recruitment concentrates where accounts are numerous, newly opened and individually low-value.

Network analytics is worthless if the same person appears as four unconnected nodes. Entity resolution — determining which records refer to the same real-world person or business — is the prerequisite capability, and it is genuinely hard in the Nepali context:

  • Transliteration variance between Devanagari and Roman script, with multiple valid romanisations of the same name.
  • Name ordering and patronymics applied inconsistently across systems.
  • Address formats that are descriptive rather than standardised.
  • Identifier gaps where citizenship number, PAN and national ID are captured inconsistently across products and vintages.

Machine learning contributes through probabilistic matching — phonetic similarity, edit distance, contextual signals such as shared addresses or devices — producing a match confidence rather than a binary answer. Institutions should hold two thresholds: a high one for automatic linkage and a lower one routing candidate matches to human review.

Entity resolution improvement typically delivers more detection uplift per rupee than any new detection model. It is unglamorous and it is where the leverage sits.

sections.h: Finding typologies nobody has written a rule for
sections.html:
Supervised models learn known patterns from labelled cases. Their structural limitation is that they cannot detect a typology absent from the training data — and novel typologies are precisely what causes losses.

Unsupervised and semi-supervised methods address this gap:

  • Anomaly detection — flagging behaviour that does not resemble any established pattern, whether or not it resembles known crime.
  • Peer-group analysis — comparing a customer against genuinely similar customers rather than a portfolio average. A cash pattern normal for a retail merchant is abnormal for a salaried professional.
  • Behavioural change detection — a dormant account suddenly transacting actively, or a stable pattern shifting abruptly, is often more informative than any absolute threshold.
  • Graph embeddings — representing each node's network position numerically so that structurally similar accounts can be identified even when their transactions differ.

These methods generate hypotheses rather than conclusions. Their proper output is a prioritised queue for skilled investigators, and their value depends entirely on investigator capacity to work it.

Financial crime crosses institutional boundaries; detection data does not. A mule network spanning five banks is visible to none of them individually. Several technologies address this without pooling raw customer data:

  • Federated learning — institutions jointly train a model while data remains local; only model updates are shared.
  • Secure multi-party computation — parties jointly compute a result without revealing their inputs.
  • Homomorphic encryption — computation performed directly on encrypted data. Powerful, still computationally expensive.
  • Privacy-preserving record linkage — determining whether two institutions hold records for the same entity without disclosing the underlying identifiers.

These are technically mature enough to matter and, in most markets, blocked by legal and governance questions rather than by engineering. For Nepal, this is properly a sector-level conversation involving NRB and the Financial Information Unit rather than something an individual bank can resolve alone. It is worth raising precisely because the coordination barrier, not the technology, is the obstacle.

A defensible financial crime architecture layers capabilities so that each does what it is best at:

  1. Deterministic rules for regulatory thresholds and mandatory reporting — transparent, auditable, non-negotiable.
  2. Entity resolution beneath everything, continuously improved.
  3. Supervised models scoring and prioritising alerts against known typologies.
  4. Unsupervised detection surfacing novel behaviour the rules and supervised models would miss.
  5. Network analytics assessing structure across linked entities.
  6. Investigator workbench — enriched, assembled cases with the context already gathered (a strong agentic use case, per Module 6).
  7. Governed feedback — investigation outcomes returning as training data, with controls against reinforcing existing blind spots.

sections.h: Model risk in financial crime systems
sections.html:
Financial crime models carry risk characteristics that differ from credit models and deserve explicit treatment:

  • The label is unreliable. "Not reported" does not mean "not criminal" — it may mean not detected. Models trained on historical dispositions learn to reproduce past detection capability, including its blind spots.
  • Adversarial drift. Unlike credit risk, the population actively adapts to evade detection. A model's performance decays because criminals learn it, not merely because conditions change.
  • Feedback loops. If the model directs attention to certain profiles, cases will be found there, confirming the model — while other typologies remain unexamined. Deliberate random sampling outside the model's priorities is a necessary counterweight.
  • Suppression risk. Alert suppression reduces workload but, if wrongly calibrated, systematically hides a category of activity. Suppression rules require the same governance as detection rules, and periodic review of what they excluded.

Filing decisions and customer exit remain human, accountable determinations. AI's role is directing scarce investigative capacity — which, given the false-positive burden documented in the foundational programme, is transformative enough.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: fix entity resolution first
practitioner.text: Before commissioning any new detection model, measure your entity resolution quality: take 200 customers known to hold multiple relationships and check how many are correctly linked across core, cards, digital and loans. Institutions are routinely shocked by the result. Improving entity resolution typically lifts detection more than a new model would, costs less, and simultaneously improves credit, marketing and customer service.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Design a network-analytics pilot for your institution. Specify: which entities and relationships form the graph; which shared attributes you can actually link on today; which network measure you would start with and why; how a flagged network would reach an investigator; and what deliberate random sampling you would run outside the model's priorities to detect its blind spots. Note explicitly which data you would need but do not currently hold reliably.

takeaways: In sophisticated financial crime the network is the criminal artefact; individual transactions are designed to look ordinary
Entity resolution is the prerequisite capability and usually the highest-return investment
Transliteration, name ordering and inconsistent identifiers make entity resolution genuinely hard in Nepal
Unsupervised methods detect typologies no rule anticipated, but produce hypotheses requiring investigator capacity
Privacy-enhancing technologies enable cross-institution detection; the barrier is legal and coordinative, not technical
Financial crime labels are unreliable, populations adapt adversarially, and feedback loops entrench blind spots
Random sampling outside model priorities is a necessary counterweight to feedback loops

quiz.q: Before commissioning a new financial crime detection model, the highest-return investment is usually:
opts: Improving entity resolution so the same person is correctly linked across systems
A larger model
More alert rules
Additional cloud capacity
quiz.fb: Network analytics is worthless if one person appears as four unconnected nodes. Entity resolution also improves credit, marketing and service simultaneously.

quiz.q: Why can supervised models alone not address novel money-laundering typologies?
opts: They run too slowly
They learn only patterns present in labelled training data, so they cannot detect a typology never previously observed
They require cloud infrastructure
They are prohibited by regulators
quiz.fb: Novel typologies are precisely what causes losses. Unsupervised and anomaly methods surface behaviour that fits no established pattern.

quiz.q: A distinctive model risk in financial crime, compared with credit risk, is:
opts: Outcomes are observed immediately
Models are easier to explain
Adversarial drift — the population actively adapts to evade detection, so performance decays because criminals learn the model
Data volumes are smaller
quiz.fb: Credit populations change with conditions; criminal populations change deliberately in response to your controls.

quiz.q: Federated learning allows institutions to:
opts: Eliminate the need for investigators
Avoid all regulatory obligations
Pool all raw customer data centrally
Jointly train a model while data remains local, sharing only model updates
quiz.fb: Privacy-enhancing technologies enable collaboration without pooling raw data. In most markets the barrier is legal and coordinative rather than technical.

quiz.q: 'Feedback loops' in financial crime models create the risk that:
opts: Attention concentrates where the model already looks, confirming itself while other typologies go unexamined
Investigators become too skilled
Models become too conservative
Alerts arrive too quickly
quiz.fb: Cases are found where you look. Deliberate random sampling outside the model's priorities is the counterweight that reveals blind spots.

quiz.q: In an AML context, a historical label of 'not reported' means:
opts: The alert was a false positive
Possibly not detected — labels reflect past detection capability including its blind spots
The customer was exited
Definitively not criminal
quiz.fb: Training on historical dispositions teaches the model to reproduce previous detection capability, blind spots included.

finance-advanced.title: Enterprise Governance & the Target Operating Model
finance-advanced.summary: Structures, decision rights and the organisation AI requires
objectives: Design an AI governance structure with unambiguous decision rights
Apply the three lines of defence to AI without duplicating existing risk functions
Choose between centralised, federated and hub-and-spoke operating models
Build the policy stack a supervisor would expect to see
Understand talent composition, capability building and the Centre of Excellence
Address the cultural barriers that defeat well-designed frameworks

sections.h: Governance as an enabler, not a brake
sections.html:
The evidence is unambiguous that governance accelerates rather than impedes scaling. EY's research found that more than 70% of large global banks have integrated AI governance into their group-wide risk management frameworks, and that among banks deploying generative AI at scale, more than 80% have established cross-functional AI governance committees or "control towers". Most tellingly, one global commercial bank tripled its number of AI applications without a proportional increase in model-related compliance incidents after implementing a group-level framework.

The Cambridge study reinforces the demand side: clearer regulatory guidance is ranked a top priority by 69% of industry, 67% of vendors and 79% of regulators. Institutions are not resisting governance; they are asking for clarity.

sections.h: Decision rights — the part most frameworks omit
sections.html:
Most AI policies describe principles. Few specify who may decide what. A workable scheme states, for each decision, the accountable role and the evidence required:

  • Approve AI strategy and risk appetite — Board, on recommendation of the executive committee.
  • Approve a Tier 1 model into production — AI or model risk committee, on evidence of independent validation.
  • Approve a Tier 2 model — delegated to the business owner with risk sign-off.
  • Approve a generative AI use case involving customer data — joint approval of information governance and the business owner.
  • Approve an agentic deployment above Level 1 autonomy — AI committee, with documented tool list and limits.
  • Suspend a model in production — named individual, unilaterally, without waiting for a committee.
  • Accept a validation finding as remediated — validation function, not the model owner.

That last item prevents the most common governance failure: the team that built the model deciding its own findings have been addressed.

sections.h: Three lines of defence, applied to AI
sections.html:
AI risk should sit inside existing enterprise risk management rather than beside it. Oxford's research is explicit that AI risk management should not be separate from enterprise risk management, and that the last line of defence will remain human.

  • First line — business and development. Owns the model, its appropriate use, its performance and its customer outcomes. Runs day-to-day monitoring.
  • Second line — risk and compliance. Owns the framework, tiering, independent validation, challenge and aggregate reporting. Must be resourced with people who genuinely understand the models; a second line that cannot challenge technically is ceremonial.
  • Third line — internal audit. Assures that the framework operates as documented. Audits the process, not the mathematics.

Deeper dive: the second-line capability problem

The binding constraint in most institutions is second-line technical capability. If validation cannot interrogate a gradient-boosted model, examine a calibration curve or evaluate an explanation's adequacy, then validation becomes documentation review and the control is nominal. Options are to recruit, to build through structured development, or to buy independent validation — but pretending the capability exists when it does not is the single most dangerous position an institution can hold.

Three operating models, each with a defensible use:

  • Centralised. A single team builds all AI. Strong consistency and control; becomes a bottleneck and drifts from business context. Appropriate at low maturity, where scarce expertise must be concentrated.
  • Federated. Business units build their own with central standards. Fast and contextual; risks duplication, inconsistency and uneven quality. Appropriate at high maturity with strong standards.
  • Hub-and-spoke. A central Centre of Excellence owns platforms, standards, tooling, validation and scarce specialists, while embedded practitioners sit in business units. Most institutions converge here.

Oxford's research adds a caution that matters: introducing central coordination after a period of free experimentation risks "frustrating key individuals", and notes that firms report retention of talent, not just attraction, becoming front of mind. Centralise the standards and the platform; avoid centralising all the interesting work.

EY's finding on composition remains the practical benchmark: in high-return banks, 40–50% of AI team members come from business rather than purely technical backgrounds, and institutions with mature AI talent systems cut the cycle from project approval to launch by 30–50%.

A supervisor examining your institution will expect a coherent documentary hierarchy:

  1. AI policy — board-approved. Scope, principles, risk appetite, accountability, prohibited uses.
  2. Model risk management standard — inventory, tiering, development, validation, monitoring, retirement.
  3. Acceptable use policy for generative AI — what staff may and may not do, and with which approved tools. This is the cheapest and most urgent document most institutions lack.
  4. Data and privacy standards — consent, purpose limitation, retention, cross-border transfer, aligned to the Privacy Act (2075) and NRB requirements.
  5. Third-party and outsourcing standard — due diligence, contractual minimums, exit, concentration limits.
  6. Agentic AI standard — autonomy levels, tool approval, limits, logging, kill-switch authority.
  7. Procedures and templates — validation report format, model documentation template, monitoring pack, incident process.

Templates matter more than they appear to. A standard validation report format makes quality visible and comparable across models, and makes gaps obvious rather than negotiable.

Capability is built through structure rather than enthusiasm:

  • Segment the audience. Board and executive need enough to govern; business leaders need enough to specify and challenge; practitioners need working fluency; specialists need depth. A single training programme serves none of them well.
  • Make AI literacy part of professional development rather than a one-off event — BCG's guidance is explicit that organisations should embed AI literacy in professional development as roles evolve.
  • Train challenge, not just use. Staff must be able to recognise when output is wrong and be genuinely empowered to override it. This is the operational antidote to automation bias.
  • Rotate people through the CoE so capability diffuses into the business rather than concentrating permanently.
  • Retain deliberately. The people you train become externally marketable. Career path, interesting work and recognition matter more than incremental salary.

sections.h: The cultural barriers that defeat good frameworks
sections.html:
The XAI literature review identified organisational and cultural barriers as more fundamental than technical ones. The same applies to governance generally. The recurring failures:

  • Governance experienced as an obstacle rather than a condition of deployment. Countered by making approval paths fast, predictable and proportionate — a Tier 3 tool should not face Tier 1 process.
  • Business–technical misalignment — models built to technical specifications that satisfy no business need. Countered by joint accountability and the 40–50% business composition benchmark.
  • Deployment as the only rewarded outcome. If nobody is ever thanked for stopping a project, unsafe projects proceed. Celebrate a well-reasoned stop publicly at least once.
  • Silence on employment. The Cambridge data offers a usefully balanced position: around two-thirds of industry respondents expect a net increase in jobs, roughly 25% expect significant reskilling, and 24% expect a net reduction. Saying this plainly is better than allowing rumour to fill the vacuum.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: publish the decision-rights table
practitioner.text: Produce a single page listing every AI-related decision, the accountable role, and the evidence required — then circulate it. Most governance failures are not disagreements about principle; they are ambiguity about who decides. A published decision-rights table resolves more disputes than a fifty-page policy, and it is the first artefact a supervisor can use to test whether your framework is real.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft the decision-rights table for your institution covering the seven decisions listed in this module. For each, name the accountable role, the required evidence, and the escalation path. Identify which of the seven currently has no clear owner — that gap is your most urgent governance action, and it costs nothing to close.

takeaways: Governance accelerates scaling: over 70% of large global banks embed AI governance in group risk frameworks
One bank tripled AI applications without proportional increase in compliance incidents after establishing group-level governance
Most frameworks describe principles but omit decision rights — publish who decides what, on what evidence
AI risk belongs inside enterprise risk management; second-line technical capability is the binding constraint
Hub-and-spoke suits most institutions; centralise standards and platforms, not all the interesting work
High-return banks have 40–50% business people on AI teams; mature talent systems cut approval-to-launch by 30–50%
Address employment openly: roughly two-thirds expect net job increases, 24% expect net reduction

quiz.q: Which decision should explicitly NOT rest with the team that built a model?
opts: Choosing the programming language
Selecting training data
Accepting that a validation finding has been remediated
Scheduling the project
quiz.fb: Allowing the builder to close their own validation findings is the most common governance failure and defeats independence entirely.

quiz.q: The binding constraint on effective second-line AI oversight in most institutions is:
opts: Insufficient policy documents
Lack of committee meetings
Too few vendors
Technical capability — if validation cannot interrogate the model, the control is nominal
quiz.fb: A second line that cannot examine a calibration curve or challenge an explanation performs documentation review, not validation.

quiz.q: EY's evidence on governance and scaling shows that a bank implementing a group-level AI governance framework:
opts: Tripled its AI applications without a proportional rise in model-related compliance incidents
Exited AI entirely
Slowed deployment substantially
Reduced its model count
quiz.fb: Governance is what enabled the institution to go faster safely — it is an enabler of scale, not a brake on it.

quiz.q: Oxford's research warns that introducing central coordination after free experimentation risks:
opts: Regulatory breach
Frustrating key individuals, with talent retention becoming front of mind
Higher licence costs
Model drift
quiz.fb: Centralise standards and platforms, but avoid centralising all the interesting work — the people you trained are externally marketable.

quiz.q: Which policy document is typically the cheapest and most urgent for institutions that lack it?
opts: A board-approved AI strategy
An agentic AI standard
An acceptable use policy for generative AI tools
A third-party outsourcing standard
quiz.fb: It addresses shadow AI immediately, costs nothing to produce, and closes the most common real-world exposure.

quiz.q: On employment effects, the Cambridge study found that:
opts: Job numbers are unaffected
No institution has considered the question
All respondents expect mass redundancy
Around two-thirds expect a net increase in jobs, while 24% expect a net reduction and roughly 25% expect significant reskilling
quiz.fb: Stating this balanced position openly is better than allowing rumour to fill the vacuum and generate resistance.

finance-advanced.title: Systemic Risk, Financial Stability & the Regulatory Frontier
finance-advanced.summary: What AI means for the financial system, and how regulation is responding
objectives: Understand AI's implications for financial stability at system rather than firm level
Explain model herding, uniformity and network connectedness as stability risks
Understand third-party and foundation-model concentration as a systemic exposure
Compare emerging regulatory models internationally
Understand how supervisors themselves are adopting AI, and what that implies
Apply this system-level perspective to Nepal's context and NRB's framework

sections.h: From firm risk to system risk
sections.html:
Every preceding module has considered risk to your institution. This module considers risk to the financial system — the perspective a central bank takes, and one that senior bankers are expected to understand.

The Bank for International Settlements working paper Intelligent financial system: how AI is transforming finance (Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Korinek, Shreeti and Stein, 2024) provides the most rigorous available treatment. Its framing is elegant: the financial system exists to process dispersed information and aggregate it into price signals that coordinate the economy. Advances in information processing have repeatedly transformed finance; AI is the latest and possibly the most consequential.

The paper examines four functions — financial intermediation, insurance, asset management and payments — and assesses implications for financial stability and prudential policy.

The BIS analysis identifies the core stability concern directly. Even early rule-based computer trading systems produced cascade effects and herding — the 1987 US stock market crash being the canonical example. With machine learning, the paper argues, the risks of uniformity, model herding and network connectedness have only compounded.

The mechanism is straightforward and worth stating precisely:

  • Institutions increasingly use similar models, often built on the same foundation models, trained on overlapping data, procured from the same small set of vendors.
  • Similar models reach similar conclusions from similar inputs.
  • Similar conclusions produce correlated actions — tightening credit to the same segments, selling the same assets, restricting the same customers — at the same moment.
  • Correlated actions amplify whatever movement triggered them.

The paper adds a specific generative-AI dimension: co-pilots and robo-advising can make decisions more homogeneous, potentially adding to systemic risk. If every credit analyst in a market is assisted by the same model, drafting from the same reasoning patterns, the diversity of judgement that historically dampened cycles is quietly reduced.

A second concern in the BIS paper deserves particular attention from anyone who will interact with a supervisor: the proliferation of complex interactions and the inherent lack of explainability makes it difficult to spot market manipulation or financial stability risks in time.

This inverts the usual framing of explainability. It is normally discussed as a consumer-protection and conduct issue — can you explain a decline to an applicant? The BIS point is that opacity is also a macroprudential problem. A supervisor cannot detect emerging systemic patterns if the decisions producing them cannot be interpreted, and the speed of automated decisioning removes the friction that historically gave authorities time to intervene.

Module 5 discussed vendor concentration as an institutional risk. At system level it becomes something more serious. Recall the Cambridge findings: OpenAI used by 76% of industry respondents, Google by 57%, with AWS leading cloud at 46%, and 63% of industry building internal workflows on external foundation models.

Concentration of this degree creates exposures that no individual institution can diversify away:

  • Correlated operational failure. A single provider outage simultaneously degrades many institutions.
  • Correlated model failure. A flaw or behavioural change in a widely used model propagates across the sector at once.
  • Cross-border dependency. Critical financial infrastructure depending on providers outside the jurisdiction, beyond the supervisor's reach.
  • Substitutability limits. The concentration exists partly because genuine alternatives are few.

For a small market such as Nepal this is sharper still: the entire banking sector could plausibly depend on two or three foreign providers, with no domestic alternative and limited negotiating power.

sections.h: Two scenarios for the real economy
sections.html:
The BIS paper also examines spillovers from the real economy, presenting two scenarios:

  • The benign scenario. Widespread AI adoption produces broad productivity gains with largely manageable effects — higher output, gradual labour reallocation, improved credit quality as firms become more productive.
  • The disruptive scenario. Significant labour-market displacement occurs faster than reallocation, with consequences for household income, consumer credit performance and demand.

For a bank, the second scenario is a credit risk question, not a technology one: which segments of your portfolio are exposed to occupations most susceptible to displacement? Very few institutions have examined their portfolio through this lens, and it is a legitimate and forward-looking stress scenario to propose.

The BIS paper proposes general principles for AI regulation built on social well-being, transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy protection, safety, human oversight and robustness, and compares regulatory models across the United States, the European Union and China — concluding with an urgent call for international coordination on integrating AI into the global financial system.

The broad picture practitioners should carry:

  • European Union. Comprehensive, risk-tiered legislation with heightened obligations for high-risk uses including credit scoring for individuals.
  • United States. Supervisory guidance and existing law applied to AI — model risk management, fair lending, consumer protection — rather than a single AI statute.
  • China. Directive, application-specific rules issued rapidly alongside active state promotion of adoption.
  • Convergence. Despite differing instruments, supervisors everywhere ask the same four questions: who is accountable, can you explain it, is it fair, and are you monitoring it.

Nepal Rastra Bank's Artificial Intelligence Guidelines sit recognisably within this convergence — board accountability, risk classification, explainability, fairness, privacy aligned to the Privacy Act (2075), consent and opt-out, and embedded ongoing monitoring. An institution that builds to the four convergent questions will be well positioned as NRB's expectations develop. As always, work from the current published text and confirm with your compliance function.

The Cambridge study surveyed 130 central banks and financial regulators, and the findings shape what supervision will look like:

  • 48% remain in the Exploring stage or are not engaged with AI at all; 33% are piloting and 18% scaling.
  • Only 20% report advanced adoption, against 40% of industry.
  • 24% of regulators use no foundation models, and 46% report using no cloud infrastructure at all.
  • 79% rank clearer regulatory guidance as a top priority — the highest of any group.

Two implications follow. First, supervisory capability will lag industry capability for some years, which places more weight on institutions' own governance rather than less. Second, the gap is closing — and supervisory technology will eventually allow authorities to analyse far more than they can today. Institutions whose documentation is genuinely in order will find this unremarkable; others will not.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask the herding question
practitioner.text: At your next risk committee, ask one question: "If every bank in Nepal used a model similar to ours, trained on similar data, what would happen in a downturn?" The answer is that they would tighten simultaneously, on the same segments, at the same moment — amplifying the contraction. It is not your institution's job to solve systemic risk, but it is your job to understand that your model's behaviour is correlated with your competitors', and to say so when the board asks whether AI has made the bank safer.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Conduct a concentration assessment for your institution: list every external AI dependency — foundation model providers, cloud, vendor models embedded in core systems — and for each record what happens to which business process if it becomes unavailable for 48 hours, whether a tested alternative exists, and where processing occurs geographically. Then answer the BIS displacement question: which segments of your loan portfolio are concentrated in occupations most exposed to automation?

takeaways: BIS analyses AI across intermediation, insurance, asset management and payments, and its stability implications
Model uniformity, herding and network connectedness have compounded with machine learning; 1987 is the precedent
Co-pilots and robo-advising can homogenise decisions, reducing the diversity of judgement that dampens cycles
Opacity is a macroprudential problem, not only a conduct one — supervisors cannot spot risks they cannot interpret
Foundation model and cloud concentration is a systemic exposure no single institution can diversify away
The disruptive labour-displacement scenario is a credit risk question for your portfolio
Regulatory models differ but converge on accountability, explainability, fairness and monitoring — as NRB's framework does
48% of surveyed regulators are still exploring AI; 79% want clearer guidance

quiz.q: The BIS working paper identifies which mechanism as a principal AI-related financial stability risk?
opts: Model uniformity and herding producing correlated actions that amplify market movements
Slower transaction processing
Excessive documentation
Rising software licence costs
quiz.fb: Similar models trained on similar data from the same vendors reach similar conclusions and act simultaneously — amplifying whatever triggered them.

quiz.q: Why does BIS treat lack of explainability as a macroprudential issue and not only a conduct issue?
opts: It is not — explainability is purely a consumer matter
Supervisors cannot detect market manipulation or emerging stability risks in time if decisions cannot be interpreted
It affects only retail lending
Explanations slow down trading
quiz.fb: Opacity plus the speed of automated decisioning removes the friction that historically gave authorities time to intervene.

quiz.q: Foundation model concentration — with OpenAI used by 76% of industry respondents — represents a systemic risk mainly because:
opts: The models are poorly built
It increases licence costs
No individual institution can diversify away correlated operational or model failure across the sector
It slows innovation
quiz.fb: Concentration creates sector-wide correlated exposure and, for small markets, cross-border dependency beyond the supervisor's reach.

quiz.q: BIS's 'disruptive scenario' of significant labour-market displacement should be treated by a bank primarily as:
opts: A technology question for IT
A marketing opportunity
An HR matter only
A credit risk question — which portfolio segments are concentrated in exposed occupations
quiz.fb: Household income shocks flow directly into consumer credit performance. Very few institutions have examined their portfolio through this lens.

quiz.q: Despite different regulatory instruments across the EU, US and China, supervisors converge on asking:
opts: Who is accountable, can you explain it, is it fair, and are you monitoring it
Which vendor was selected
What the licence cost was
How many models are deployed
quiz.fb: Building to these four convergent questions positions an institution well as NRB's expectations continue to develop.

quiz.q: The Cambridge survey found that among 130 regulators, the proportion still in the Exploring stage or not engaged with AI is:
opts: None — all are advanced
quiz.fb: Supervisory capability will lag industry for some years, which places more weight on institutions' own governance rather than less.

finance-advanced.title: Value Realisation: From Pilots to P&L
finance-advanced.summary: Measuring, capturing and defending the economics of AI
objectives: Understand why most institutions struggle to evidence AI value
Build a value measurement framework linking AI activity to financial outcomes
Use the efficiency ratio as a forward-looking indicator of AI maturity
Understand the investment threshold effect and what it implies for budgeting
Manage AI as a portfolio rather than a set of projects
Avoid the efficiency trap and the double-counting of benefits

sections.h: The measurement problem is real and widespread
sections.html:
The Cambridge data is candid about this. 55% of industry respondents and 63% of surveyed regulators find it difficult to measure the value of AI deployment — rising to 76% among large financial institutions.

Note the direction: the largest institutions find it hardest. Complexity, attribution across many contributing factors, and long chains between an AI intervention and a financial outcome all work against clean measurement. This is not incompetence; it is a genuinely difficult attribution problem that must nevertheless be solved, because unmeasured value cannot be defended at budget time.

Work through four levels, each closer to the P&L:

  1. Activity. Models deployed, users onboarded, queries handled. Necessary for management, worthless as value evidence. Most reporting stops here.
  2. Operational outcome. Time to decision, cost per file, alert precision, straight-through processing rate, error rate. Measurable and directly attributable, provided a baseline exists.
  3. Business outcome. Approval rates at constant risk, loss rates at constant approval, cross-sell conversion, attrition, cases investigated per analyst. Requires controlling for confounds.
  4. Financial outcome. Revenue, cost, impairment, capital, efficiency ratio. The only level a board ultimately accepts — and reachable only if the preceding levels are instrumented.

The practical discipline is to define, before deployment, one metric at each level and the mechanism linking them. A project that cannot articulate that chain has not been thought through, whatever its technical merit.

sections.h: The efficiency ratio as an AI maturity indicator
sections.html:
PwC makes an argument worth adopting: the efficiency ratio — cost as a proportion of income — is evolving from a backward-looking performance measure into "the most telling forward-looking indicator of your bank's ability to leverage AI innovation to compete, grow and endure."

Their Strategy& analysis concludes that institutions fully embracing AI could achieve up to a 15-percentage-point improvement in their efficiency ratio, through dual effects: revenue growth from better targeting, and cost transformation through intelligent automation.

Its value as a management metric is that it is unavoidably honest. It cannot be improved by activity, pilots or announcements. It moves only if income rises or cost falls, and it captures both sides of the AI thesis simultaneously. An institution claiming AI transformation whose efficiency ratio has not moved over three years has a claim worth examining.

One of the more actionable findings in the Cambridge study concerns the relationship between spend and outcome:

  • 62% of organisations spending more than USD 100,000 annually on AI have reached advanced maturity, and 62% of that group report increased profitability — compared with 39% among lower-spending organisations.
  • Overall, 40% of respondents report increased profitability from AI while 43% report no change.
  • Fintechs again outperform: 56% report higher profitability versus 34% of traditional financial institutions.

Read alongside the earlier finding that 53% of respondents spend under USD 100,000 yet report high GenAI and agentic maturity, a nuanced picture emerges. Modest spend can buy capability; sustained spend above a threshold is associated with profitability. The gap between the two is the cost of scaling — integration, change management, governance and monitoring — which is precisely what Oxford's practitioner observed when noting that 60–70% of use-case spend has nothing to do with AI itself but with foundational integration.

For a Nepali institution the practical implication is encouraging: the entry threshold is low, but budget honestly for the integration layer or capability will not convert into profit.

sections.h: Two traps that destroy business cases
sections.html:
The efficiency trap

Oxford's research records a practitioner describing business cases built on "incremental gains on automations, something like 5–15% of every human doing an ops job," tallying to substantial annual savings — and then: "in the real world, we couldn't remove those humans from the system. So most people who put in an AI business case failed to deliver it." Time saved is not money saved unless roles are redesigned or headcount actually changes. State explicitly what the freed capacity will be used for.

The double-counting trap. When several initiatives each claim efficiency in the same function, the same saving is counted repeatedly and the aggregate becomes fictional. Oxford's recommended remedy is to evaluate AI initiatives programmatically as well as case by case — which both prevents double counting and allows enabling investments that generate no standalone return to be funded on the strength of the programme.

Individual business cases produce a collection of local optima. Portfolio management produces capability. A workable structure:

  • Balance horizons. Roughly: 60% near-term efficiency with measurable payback, 30% capability building with indirect return, 10% exploratory. Adjust to appetite, but hold the discipline that not everything must have a standalone business case.
  • Fund enabling infrastructure at portfolio level — data platform, feature store, model serving, monitoring, evaluation harness. These fail every individual ROI test and make everything else possible.
  • Track reuse. EY reports an institution reaching over 50% model reuse and 30–40% lower marginal cost per use case through a centralised platform, achieving measurable returns within 18–24 months. Reuse rate is the clearest single indicator that you are building capability rather than accumulating projects.
  • Review and terminate. A portfolio requires the discipline to stop things. Institutions that never cancel are not managing a portfolio.

A credible quarterly AI report to a board contains, on one page:

  1. Portfolio position — initiatives by stage, with movement since last quarter.
  2. Financial outcomes realised — against baselines, with attribution assumptions stated.
  3. Efficiency ratio trajectory, with commentary on AI's contribution.
  4. Risk position — models by tier, validation status, incidents, monitoring exceptions.
  5. Capability indicators — reuse rate, cycle time from approval to production, trained staff.
  6. Decisions required — what the board must actually decide.

What should not appear: model counts, pilot counts, or vendor names presented as achievements. Boards that receive activity reporting eventually conclude AI is expensive and unaccountable, and they are not wrong to.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: instrument the baseline before the build
practitioner.text: The single highest-return four weeks in any AI programme are the four weeks spent measuring the current process before anything changes — cycle time, cost per unit, error rate, volume, and the specific decision quality metric that matters. It costs almost nothing, requires no technology, and it is the difference between a defensible business case and an anecdote. Institutions that skip it discover, eighteen months later, that they cannot prove what they achieved.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: For one AI initiative in your institution, construct the four-level value chain: the activity metric, the operational outcome, the business outcome, and the financial outcome — plus the mechanism linking each level to the next. Then stress-test it: is the freed capacity explicitly redirected? Is any of this benefit already claimed by another initiative? If either answer is unsatisfactory, you have found why the business case will not survive.

takeaways: 55% of industry and 76% of large institutions find AI value difficult to measure — solve it or lose the budget argument
Define one metric at each of four levels — activity, operational, business, financial — and the mechanism linking them
The efficiency ratio is unavoidably honest and captures both sides of the AI thesis; PwC estimates up to 15 points available
62% of organisations spending over USD 100,000 annually reach advanced maturity and report higher profitability
Modest spend buys capability; sustained spend buys profitability — the gap is integration and change management
Time saved is not money saved unless roles are redesigned; state what freed capacity will do
Evaluate programmatically to prevent double counting and to fund enabling infrastructure
Model reuse rate is the clearest indicator of capability rather than project accumulation

finance-advanced.title: Leading the AI Transformation in a Nepali Institution
objectives: Synthesise the programme into a coherent institutional strategy
Apply the emerging-market advantage realistically rather than aspirationally
Sequence a credible three-horizon roadmap
Anticipate the specific obstacles Nepali institutions encounter
Understand the leadership behaviours that determine whether transformation succeeds
Complete a defensible enterprise AI strategy for your own institution

sections.h: The strategic position of a Nepali bank
sections.html:
Pull the evidence together honestly.

Working in your favour: the Cambridge finding that EMDE institutions report higher deployment levels than advanced-economy peers; the collapse in entry cost, with 53% of respondents spending under USD 100,000 while reporting high GenAI and agentic maturity; less accumulated legacy technical debt than a two-hundred-year-old European bank; a young, digitally fluent workforce; rapid growth in digital payments generating genuinely valuable behavioural data; and NRB having issued AI Guidelines, which resolves the ambiguity that 79% of regulators globally say they want resolved.

Working against you: scarce specialist talent competing against outbound migration; fragmented core systems and inconsistent customer identifiers; limited local validation capability; dependence on foreign providers with negligible negotiating power; small individual institution scale limiting investment; and thin local evidence, since almost nothing is validated on Nepali populations.

The honest conclusion is that Nepali institutions can reach Scaling maturity within a few years on modest budgets — but only by being disciplined about sequencing, because they cannot afford the expensive parallel experimentation that larger institutions use to find their way.

Horizon 1 — Foundations and credible wins (0–12 months).

  • Compile the model and AI inventory, including AI embedded in purchased software
  • Issue the acceptable-use policy for generative AI and provide an approved alternative tool
  • Establish decision rights, the AI committee, and risk tiering
  • Build the decision inventory (Module 2)
  • Fix entity resolution and the consistent customer identifier
  • Instrument baselines for two or three candidate processes
  • Deliver two internal, low-risk, measurable use cases — document processing, alert prioritisation or an internal policy assistant

Horizon 2 — Decisioning and scale (12–30 months).

  • Stand up shared platform components: feature store, model serving, monitoring, evaluation harness
  • Build independent validation capability, whether internal or contracted
  • Deploy decision-support models with humans deciding — early warning, alert scoring, a credit challenger model
  • Run a first agentic deployment at Level 1 autonomy on a bounded internal process
  • Begin measuring reuse rate and cycle time from approval to production
  • Report AI to the board using the value framework rather than activity counts

Horizon 3 — Business model (30 months onward).

  • Automated decisioning within defined limits, fully governed
  • Personalised propositions and risk-based pricing, fairness-tested
  • New products enabled by AI — the 51% of mature adopters piloting AI-powered products
  • Embedded finance and partner ecosystems
  • Only here does the institution begin crossing from the 86% into the 14%

• Starting with the most exciting use case. Customer-facing generative AI is the most visible and the least forgiving. Earn the right to it.
  • Waiting for core replacement. Build the data layer beside the core (Module 2).
  • Buying a platform before knowing the decisions. The decision inventory should precede the procurement.
  • Hiring data scientists into an institution with no data foundation. They will spend two years on plumbing, become frustrated, and leave — taking the capability with them.
  • Running pilots without baselines. Guarantees an unprovable outcome.
  • Treating governance as a later phase. Retrofitting governance onto deployed systems costs several times more than building it in.

Across every source in this programme, the same behaviours recur among institutions that succeed:

  • Leadership from the top, explicitly. SAS quotes Banorte's Abraham Izquierdo: "Innovation and AI must be recognised as a pillar of the strategy in the institution... leadership from the top is non-negotiable."
  • Business fluency in the AI team — the 40–50% benchmark, and AI leaders who understand banking raising use-case conversion by 20–30%.
  • Honest measurement, including of failures, with baselines instrumented before the build.
  • Willingness to stop projects and to say so publicly.
  • Openness about employment effects rather than allowing rumour to fill the silence.
  • Patience with foundations and impatience with unmeasured activity — most institutions have this precisely backwards.

sections.h: What to do about the evidence gap
sections.html:
A closing point specific to institutions in markets like Nepal. Almost no AI tool sold to you has been validated on a Nepali population. That is a risk, and it is also an opportunity.

The institution that builds genuine local validation capability — the ability to evaluate any model, from any vendor, on its own customers — acquires something that does not depreciate, cannot be bought off the shelf, and improves every subsequent procurement decision. It is the highest-return capability investment available, and it is entirely achievable at modest cost.

Consider also publishing what you learn. The evidence base for AI in South Asian financial populations is thin partly because evaluations conducted here are rarely documented. A well-conducted local validation — including one showing that a tool does not transfer — is a genuine contribution and a reputational asset.

Twelve modules reduce to five propositions:

  1. Adoption is not transformation. 81% are adopting; 14% are transforming. The gap is execution and business integration, and closing it is a board responsibility.
  2. Capability beats use cases. The stack performs at its weakest layer; reuse rate reveals whether you are building or accumulating.
  3. Governance enables scale. The bank that tripled applications without proportional incidents did so because of its framework.
  4. Value must be instrumented before it can be claimed. Baselines first; the efficiency ratio does not lie.
  5. Judgement remains accountable. Explainability, human oversight and named accountability are not constraints on advanced AI — under NRB's framework and every convergent international model, they are its licence to operate.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the twelve-month test
practitioner.text: Whatever strategy you write, apply one test to it: if we execute this perfectly for twelve months, what will be measurably different? If the honest answer is "we will have more pilots and a better understanding," the strategy is a research agenda rather than a plan. A good twelve-month answer names two processes with improved measured outcomes, one governance artefact in operation, and one foundational capability built — modest, specific and defensible.

activity.title: Capstone: your enterprise AI strategy
activity.text: Produce a five-page enterprise AI strategy for your institution containing: (1) an honest maturity assessment against the four-stage ladder with evidence; (2) your weakest capability-stack layer and why; (3) a decision-rights table; (4) a risk-tiered model inventory summary, even if partial; (5) a three-horizon roadmap with named owners and dates; (6) the value framework for your two priority initiatives, with baselines you will instrument; (7) your concentration and dependency assessment; and (8) the twelve-month test — what will be measurably different. This is the deliverable of the programme, and it is written to be presented to your management committee or board.

takeaways: Nepali institutions can reach Scaling maturity on modest budgets, but only with disciplined sequencing
Horizon 1 is foundations and two credible internal wins; Horizon 2 is decisioning and shared platforms; Horizon 3 is business model
The most common sequencing errors are starting with customer-facing GenAI, waiting for core replacement, and hiring data scientists before data foundations
Leadership from the top is non-negotiable; business fluency in AI teams raises conversion by 20–30%
Local validation capability is the highest-return, non-depreciating investment available
Publishing local evaluations, including negative results, strengthens the regional evidence base
Adoption is not transformation; capability beats use cases; governance enables scale; instrument value; judgement remains accountable

opts: Optional guidance for small banks

education.title: What AI Actually Is — and What It Means for Your Classroom
education.summary: The foundations every teacher needs, and none of the ones they don't
objectives: Distinguish the kinds of AI you will actually meet in a school or college
Understand precisely what these tools can and cannot do, in classroom terms
Recognise why 'the process is the purpose' is the central principle of this programme
Understand the scale of student AI use already happening around you
Speak accurately enough to lead a staffroom conversation or challenge a vendor

sections.h: What this programme is, and who it is for
sections.html:
This programme is written for teachers, lecturers, heads of department, principals and education administrators — people who must decide how artificial intelligence enters their classroom, their marking, their planning and their institution. It assumes no technical background and requires none.

You will not learn to write code. You will learn to plan and differentiate faster, give better feedback, redesign assessment that AI has broken, teach your students to use these tools honestly and well, protect the children in your care, and lead adoption in your school or college. Every module ends with something you can use on Monday, and the programme concludes with an implementation plan for your own institution.

The programme takes a clear position, and it is worth stating at the outset. AI is genuinely useful to teachers and genuinely dangerous to learning — and the difference between the two is almost entirely a matter of how a teacher designs the task. That is a professional judgement, not a technical one, which is precisely why it belongs to you.

sections.h: This is already happening in your classroom
sections.html:
Whatever your school's policy says, your students are using these tools. In a December 2024 survey reported by the Higher Education Policy Institute, 92% of British undergraduates reported using AI tools — up sharply in a single year. As Washington University professor Ian Bogost observed in August 2025, the technology is no longer a curiosity or merely a way to cheat; it has become a habit, as ordinary on campus as scrolling social media.

School-level adoption follows the same curve, and institutional response has been chaotic. Districts worldwide banned ChatGPT from school devices in early 2023, then reversed within months as the futility became clear. IDC's Future Enterprise Resiliency Survey of August 2025 found 58% of education respondents reporting that their AI programmes had grown (26%) or improved (32%) in the preceding twelve months — while 35% reported slowing down and 7% cutting back.

The practical consequence for you is simple. The choice is not whether AI enters your classroom. It is whether it enters with your guidance or behind your back.

sections.h: The three kinds of AI you will meet
sections.html:
• Predictive AI / machine learning. Systems that learn patterns from data to forecast something. In education: early-warning systems flagging students at risk of dropping out, attendance pattern analysis, timetabling optimisation, enrolment forecasting. It answers "how likely is X?"
  • Generative AI. Systems that produce new content — text, images, audio, slides. This is the wave that changed teaching: lesson plans, worksheets, differentiated texts, question banks, report comments, parent letters, feedback drafts. It answers "draft this, adapt this, explain this." Almost everything in this programme concerns this category.
  • Agentic AI. Systems that pursue a goal across several steps rather than answering one request — for instance, marking a whole class set against a rubric, then compiling a gap analysis, then drafting differentiated follow-up tasks. Newest, most powerful, and requiring the most oversight.

A fourth term you will hear is the intelligent tutoring system (ITS) — software that guides a student through problems, diagnoses errors and adapts what comes next. These are not new; they descend from rule-based systems built in the 1970s. What has changed is that conversational AI has made them dramatically cheaper and more flexible to build.

sections.h: What these tools genuinely do well for a teacher
sections.html:
• First drafts of anything. Lesson plans, worksheets, rubrics, comprehension questions, parent letters, report comments, revision guides, exam questions. Never finished work — always a starting point that saves the blank page.
  • Adaptation and differentiation. Taking one text and producing it at three reading levels; converting a task for a student with dyslexia; translating a letter home for a family that does not read English.
  • Explanation at infinite patience. A student can ask the same question nine times without embarrassment. For a shy student in a class of fifty, this is not a small thing.
  • Generating variation. Twenty more practice problems of the same type; five different worked examples; alternative analogies for a concept a student has not grasped.
  • Summarising and organising. Turning your messy notes into a scheme of work; extracting the key points from a long policy document.

sections.h: What they cannot do — and why this matters more in education than anywhere else
sections.html:
• They are not reliably accurate. Generative systems produce confident, fluent, well-formatted statements that are simply wrong — invented dates, misattributed quotations, fabricated citations, incorrect worked solutions. In a classroom this is uniquely damaging, because students cannot yet tell the difference and because your authority is what they are calibrating against.
  • They do not know your students. No model knows that Sita has been absent for a fortnight, that Ram's mother died in March, or that this class needs the concept re-taught rather than extended.
  • They do not know your curriculum. Output aligned to a foreign syllabus is worse than useless — it is confidently misaligned.
  • They have no stake in the conversation. As Tom Chatfield puts it in AI and the Future of Pedagogy, a large language model "has no stake in a conversation and no mind to change. It will flatter, cajole or concede points in line with its training. But it can neither care nor know anything about a learner's life beyond the screen."
  • They cannot take responsibility. If a report comment is wrong, a grade is unfair, or a resource contains an error, the teacher who sent it answers for it. No parent has ever accepted "the computer wrote it."

The working rule for every teacher

Treat AI output as work from an enthusiastic, fast, well-read trainee teacher who has never met your class, sometimes invents facts, and will never tell you when they are out of their depth. You would read that person's worksheet before photocopying it for thirty children. Apply the same standard and most of the risk in this programme disappears.

sections.h: The principle that governs everything that follows
sections.html:
There is one idea this programme returns to in every module, and it is worth installing now.

Learning cannot be automated or outsourced. To learn is to acquire knowledge and understanding through the effortful exercise of skills. As the writer Nicholas Carr put it in May 2025, "to automate learning is to subvert learning."

Chatfield states the corollary precisely: when children at a primary school write stories and draw pictures, the point is not to supply the world with more stories and pictures. It is to help them become literate, reflective participants in their society. Undergraduates do not write essays because the world needs more essays. The process is the purpose.

This gives you a test you can apply to any proposed use of AI in your classroom, and it takes five seconds:

The two-question test

(1) Whose cognitive effort is this task designed to exercise? If it is the student's, and AI does it, the learning has been destroyed. (2) Is this effort the point, or is it overhead? Writing the essay is the point. Formatting the bibliography is overhead. Automate the overhead without hesitation; protect the point without exception.

Applied consistently, this single test resolves the great majority of the dilemmas teachers report — and it explains why using AI to draft your own lesson plan is entirely legitimate while letting a student use it to draft their own essay may not be.

sections.h: The vocabulary that makes you effective
sections.html:
• Prompt — the instruction you give the system. The main determinant of output quality, and a teachable skill (Module 8).
  • Hallucination — a confident, fluent, factually wrong output. Use the word with students; naming it makes it visible.
  • Training data — the material the model learned from. Explains why models are strong on English and weak on Nepali, strong on American curricula and weak on yours.
  • Human in the loop — a person reviews before the output takes effect. The central recommendation of the US Department of Education's guidance, and of this programme.
  • AI literacy — the capacity to use, evaluate and critique these systems. A curriculum outcome, not a technology skill.
  • Algorithmic bias — systematic unfairness produced by patterns in training data. Covered in Module 9.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: start with your own work, not your students'
practitioner.text: Nearly every teacher who has a bad first experience with AI began by pointing it at students. Begin instead with something that is entirely yours and entirely low-stakes: next week's lesson plan, a set of comprehension questions, a letter to parents. You will learn the tool's strengths and its failure modes on work where a mistake costs you ten minutes rather than a child's understanding. Teachers who use these tools themselves make far better decisions about student use — and are far more credible when they set rules.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: List the five tasks that consumed most of your time last week outside actual teaching. For each, apply the two-question test: whose cognitive effort does this exercise, and is that effort the point or overhead? You have just produced your own shortlist of legitimate AI uses — and you will return to it in Module 3.

quiz.fb: An adult professional can often spot an error. A learner, by definition, cannot — which is why teacher verification is non-negotiable.

quiz.fb: It will flatter, cajole or concede in line with its training, and can neither care nor know anything about a learner's life beyond the screen.

quiz.fb: 26% growing and 32% improving — though 35% reported slowing down and 7% cutting back. Adoption is real but uneven.

education.title: How People Learn: The Evidence AI Must Serve
education.summary: The cognitive science that decides whether a tool helps or harms
objectives: Understand cognitive load and why it governs whether a resource helps or overwhelms
Apply the five evidence-based learning techniques AI can genuinely support
Understand why metacognition becomes more important, not less, in an AI age
Recognise the instructional principles that make feedback effective
Understand the social and emotional dimension AI cannot replicate
Evaluate any AI tool against what is actually known about learning

sections.h: Why this module comes before any tool
sections.html:
Most AI training for teachers begins with tools. That is exactly backwards, and it is why so much of it produces enthusiasm followed by disappointment.

Chatfield's AI and the Future of Pedagogy is built on two principles, and the first is that innovation must draw on what we know about how humans learn. Without that grounding, a teacher cannot tell the difference between a tool that supports learning and one that merely feels productive — and these two feel almost identical in the moment.

This module gives you the evidence base. It is the most important module in the programme, and the one you will use most often without noticing.

The Australian educational psychologist John Sweller established that the brain is a natural information-processing system with a sharply limited working memory — one that easily becomes overwhelmed in the face of distraction or too much information.

This single fact explains a great deal of classroom failure. A worksheet crowded with decorative images, a slide with nine bullet points, an instruction containing four separate tasks, a classroom with a screen playing in the background — each consumes working memory that was needed for the actual learning.

The AI implication is direct and double-edged. These tools can generate enormous quantities of material instantly, and quantity is precisely what a learner cannot absorb. A teacher who generates a six-page differentiated resource pack has not helped a struggling student; they have buried one. Used well, however, AI is exceptionally good at the opposite: breaking a topic into a sequence, stripping a text to its essentials, and producing the one clear worked example that carries the concept.

Deeper dive: worked examples

Sweller's worked example effect is one of the most robust findings in educational psychology. Taking students step-by-step through a solved problem allows them to focus on reasoning and strategy rather than expending all their working memory on reaching an answer. Novices learn more from studying worked examples than from solving problems unaided. AI generates high-quality worked examples on demand — arguably its single most valuable and most underused classroom application.

sections.h: The five techniques with the strongest evidence
sections.html:
Each of these is supported by substantial research, and each maps onto something AI can help you produce:

  1. Worked examples. Step-by-step solutions that relieve the pressure to leap to answers. Ask AI for three worked examples of increasing difficulty, each with the reasoning made explicit.
  2. Spacing. Distributing practice over time inculcates knowledge more effectively than massed practice. Ask AI to build a retrieval schedule that revisits Week 2's content in Weeks 4, 7 and 11.
  3. Interleaving. Mixing different problem types rather than blocking them together helps learners discriminate between ideas and strategies. Ask AI to produce a mixed problem set drawing on three topics rather than one.
  4. Elaboration. Explaining how new information relates to what is already known makes knowledge more applicable. Ask AI for questions that force students to connect today's concept to last term's.
  5. Retrieval practice. Recalling information strengthens it far more than re-reading. Ask AI for low-stakes recall questions rather than another summary.

Notice the pattern. In every case, the instruction is to produce something that makes the student work harder in a productive way — not something that makes the work easier. That distinction is the whole of good AI use in teaching.

sections.h: Metacognition: the skill that matters most
sections.html:
Underlying all of the above is metacognition — the ability to think about your own thinking. As Chatfield notes, metacognition is neither distinct from nor detachable from recall and knowledge; but by learning to monitor their understanding and adjust their strategies, learners acquire a form of educational agency that goes beyond any particular subject.

UCL Professor Emerita of Learner Centred Design Rose Luckin put the AI-age case for it directly in June 2025:

"As our world integrates more AI into every aspect of life and work, our students need something deeper than efficient content delivery. They need sophisticated meta-learning capabilities — the ability to adapt, change, and evolve their thinking as the world transforms around them."

This is the strategic answer to the anxiety many teachers feel. If AI can produce the essay, what is left to teach? The answer is: the judgement to know whether the essay is any good, the knowledge to see what it has missed, and the self-awareness to know what you have and have not understood. Those are teachable, and they are what your students most need.

Where cognitive science tells us how minds learn, instructional research — synthesised across thousands of studies — converges on a small number of principles:

  • Clarity of purpose. Students need to understand not just what they are learning but why. Clear goals give direction and form to effort.
  • Scaffolding. The careful structuring of tasks so that each builds on the last. Badly designed tools and resources "overwhelm and demoralize learners, leaving them struggling to work out what is required."
  • Well-calibrated feedback. Feedback must show learners both what they have achieved and how to improve. Critically, the best feedback creates a dialogue, turning assessment into a continuation of learning rather than merely its measurement.

That last point governs Module 5 entirely. An AI system that returns a grade and three generic comments has measured. It has not taught. The difference is not a technical limitation — it is a design choice you control.

Human learning is never purely cognitive. People are sociable, embodied creatures who thrive on constructive debate and meaningful feedback and suffer in their absence.

  • Engagement follows respect. When students see their perspectives treated seriously and their struggles understood, engagement tends to follow. The classroom becomes a space for sociable sense-making, not only individual achievement.
  • Emotional safety is a precondition. Learning requires acknowledging error and uncertainty in front of others. Classrooms that treat mistakes as useful information rather than evidence of failure make vulnerability productive.
  • Surveillance corrodes it. Chatfield warns specifically that classrooms which surveil and penalise students for infractions of a system they have little agency within — or which fail to offer guidance, trust and access around tools already integral to life and work — are likely over time to fall behind. This is the direct argument against detection-led policy, developed fully in Module 6.

The design conclusion is that the back-and-forth of debate and the building of common understanding are not inefficiencies to be optimised away. They are the mechanisms through which learning occurs. When students challenge one another's assumptions and construct reasoned arguments, they are not exchanging information. They are learning to think.

sections.h: Evaluating any tool against the evidence
sections.html:
You now have a rubric. When a vendor, a colleague or a ministry circular proposes an AI tool, ask:

  1. Does it reduce extraneous cognitive load, or add to it? More content is not more learning.
  2. Does it make the student work productively, or work less? Effort in the right place is the mechanism.
  3. Does its feedback open a dialogue, or close one?
  4. Does it build metacognition, or bypass it?
  5. Does it protect the social dimension, or substitute for it?
  6. Is it scaffolded toward a goal, or an undifferentiated firehose?

A tool that fails three or more of these will not improve outcomes however impressive the demonstration. This rubric costs nothing and is more predictive than any feature list.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: put the pedagogy in the prompt
practitioner.text: Most disappointing AI output for teachers comes from prompts that describe a topic rather than a pedagogy. Compare "Make a worksheet on photosynthesis for Grade 8" with "Create a Grade 8 photosynthesis worksheet using two worked examples with reasoning made explicit, followed by six interleaved problems mixing photosynthesis with respiration from last term, ending with three retrieval questions. Keep each instruction to one step. No decorative content." The second produces a genuinely better resource because it encodes what you know about learning. Your pedagogical expertise is the input that makes these tools worth using.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take a worksheet or resource you already use. Score it against the six-point rubric above. Then rewrite the prompt you would give an AI to produce a better version — explicitly naming worked examples, interleaving, spacing or retrieval as appropriate. Generate it, compare the two, and note honestly which is better and why.

takeaways: Working memory is easily overwhelmed; AI's ability to generate volume is a hazard, not a feature
Worked examples let novices focus on reasoning rather than exhausting working memory reaching an answer
Spacing, interleaving, elaboration and retrieval practice are the techniques with the strongest evidence
Good AI use makes students work harder in a productive way, not less
Metacognition is the strategic answer to 'what is left to teach' — judgement, knowledge and self-awareness
The best feedback creates dialogue; a grade with generic comments has measured, not taught
Debate and shared sense-making are the mechanism of learning, not inefficiency to be optimised away

opts: Assigns an accurate numerical grade
