quiz.fb: An AI system returning a grade and generic comments has measured but not taught — and that is a design choice, not a technical limit.

quiz.q: Chatfield warns that classrooms which surveil and penalise students around AI, without offering guidance and trust, are likely to:
opts: Achieve higher integrity standards
Improve examination results
Fall behind over time, because emotional safety is a precondition for learning
Reduce teacher workload
quiz.fb: Learning requires acknowledging error and uncertainty in front of others. Surveillance frames the relationship as conflict rather than collaboration.

education.title: Reclaiming Your Time: AI for Teacher Workload
education.summary: The strongest evidence in the field, and a prompt library you can use today
objectives: Understand where teacher time actually goes, and which parts AI can safely take
Apply a tested prompt library across planning, communication, admin and reporting
Understand the measured workload results achieved by real school systems
Distinguish tasks that are safe to delegate from those that are not
Protect the reclaimed time rather than allowing it to be absorbed
Build a personal weekly workflow that compounds over a term

sections.html:
The US Department of Education's Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Teaching and Learning reports the figure that frames this module: teachers work about 50 hours a week, spending less than half of that time in direct interaction with students.

The report, drawing on McKinsey research, concludes that AI's initial benefit could be to improve teaching jobs by reducing low-level burdens in administrative and clerical work — and adds a crucial condition: that recovered time should be rededicated toward more meaningful work rather than simply absorbed.

This is the least controversial and best-evidenced application of AI in education. It is also where you should start, for a reason that has nothing to do with technology: a teacher who is not exhausted teaches better. Every other module in this programme depends on you having the capacity to think about your practice, and that capacity is what workload has taken.

sections.h: What real school systems have measured
sections.html:
Three systems documented by IDC in December 2025 give you defensible numbers rather than vendor claims.

  • Brisbane Catholic Education (Australia) — 146 schools, 13,000 staff, 20,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot licences, one of the largest educational deployments in the world. Measured outcome: a reduction of up to nine hours per week in administrative workload for teachers, alongside qualitative reports of improved work–life balance and more time available for personalising learning.
  • Broward County Public Schools (United States) — over 20,000 Copilot licences across the district. Measured outcome: 75% of teachers and administrators actively use the tool, reporting an average saving of over two hours per week on lesson planning and administrative tasks.
  • Coquitlam School District (Canada) — a deliberate "go slow to go fast" programme that established data readiness and cybersecurity before introducing tools to educators, prioritising trust over speed.

Note the honest spread: two hours a week in one system, up to nine in another. The difference is not the software — Brisbane and Broward deployed the same product. It is training, workflow redesign and time to learn. A licence alone buys very little, a point Module 11 develops.

Before the prompt library, the rule that governs its use. Sort every task into three categories:

  • Delegate freely. No student-specific judgement, no confidential data, errors are obvious and cheap. Drafting a scheme of work, generating practice questions, rewriting a text at a lower reading level, drafting a newsletter, summarising a policy document, producing a rubric skeleton, translating a general letter home.
  • Delegate with mandatory review. AI drafts, you verify and adapt, always. Report comments, feedback drafts, worked solutions, subject-specific factual content, anything a parent or student will read.
  • Never delegate. Final grades and rank ordering. Safeguarding and pastoral judgements. Decisions about a child's placement, referral or discipline. Anything requiring knowledge of a student's circumstances. Anything containing a named student's personal information typed into a public tool.

The data rule, stated once and applying throughout

Do not type a student's name, examination number, medical or family information, safeguarding detail, or any identifiable personal data into a general public AI tool. Describe the situation generically instead — "a Grade 9 student who has missed three weeks and is anxious about returning" — and add the specifics yourself afterwards. This costs you nothing and protects both the child and you.

Copy these, replace the bracketed parts, and adjust. The specificity is what makes them work.

  • Scheme of work. "You are an experienced [subject] teacher. Draft a [6]-week scheme of work for Grade [8] on [topic], aligned to these learning outcomes: [paste]. For each week give the objective, one worked example, the key misconception to pre-empt, a retrieval question from a previous week, and a 5-minute exit check. Class size [45], mixed ability, English is a second language for most students."
  • Single lesson. "Plan a 40-minute lesson on [topic] for Grade [7]. Structure: 5-min retrieval starter on [prior topic], 10-min explanation with one worked example, 15-min paired task, 5-min whole-class check, 5-min consolidation. I have a blackboard and no projector. Give me exactly what to write on the board."
  • Misconception hunt. "List the eight most common misconceptions students hold about [topic] at Grade [9] level. For each, give the misconception, why it is intuitive, and one diagnostic question that would reveal it." — This is among the highest-value prompts in the library and has no equivalent shortcut.
  • Worked examples. "Produce three worked examples of [problem type] at increasing difficulty. Make the reasoning explicit at every step, including why each step is chosen, not only what it is. Then give three parallel problems with no solutions."
  • Question bank. "Generate 20 questions on [topic] for Grade [8], graded across recall, application and analysis, with an answer key. Mark which are suitable for oral questioning."

sections.h: The prompt library — communication and administration
sections.html:
• Report comments. "Draft three report comment templates for a Grade [6] [subject] student: one performing above expectation, one at expectation, one below. Each 60–80 words, specific about skills rather than personality, ending with one concrete next step. Warm and professional; no clichés." Then personalise every one by hand — this is a mandatory-review task.
  • Difficult parent letter. "Draft a letter to a parent about a student who has stopped submitting homework. Firm but not accusatory, assumes good faith, invites a meeting, offers two practical supports. 200 words. Do not use the student's name — I will add it."
  • Translation. "Translate this letter into [Nepali] for parents who do not read English. Use simple everyday language, not formal or literary register." Always have a fluent colleague check regional-language output before it goes home — model performance in Nepali and other regional languages is materially weaker than in English.
  • Policy digest. "Summarise this [policy document] in 200 words for busy teachers. Then list the five things it actually requires us to do differently."
  • Meeting and minutes. "Turn these rough notes into structured minutes with decisions, owners and deadlines separated: [paste]."
  • Newsletter. "Write a 300-word parent newsletter section covering these three items: [list]. Warm, concrete, no jargon, readable by a parent with limited formal education."

This is the step that determines whether any of this matters, and it is the step almost everyone skips.

The US Department of Education's condition — that recovered time be rededicated — is not a pleasantry. Time saved that is not deliberately reassigned is absorbed within weeks by whatever else is waiting, and the teacher ends the term exactly as tired, now with an additional tool to maintain and no evidence that it helped.

Decide in advance where the time goes. IDC's recommendation for school leaders is to shift the teacher's role from content deliverer to facilitator and relationship builder — using AI to handle administrative overhead so teachers can reclaim time for what brought them into the profession: building meaningful relationships with students and providing individualised support, "getting back to real teaching" rather than being overburdened by paperwork.

Concretely, name the destination: two more one-to-one conversations a week with the students who need them; one properly planned practical lesson instead of three rushed ones; leaving at a reasonable hour on Fridays. Write it down and defend it.

1. Sunday or Monday, 30 minutes. Generate the week's planning skeleton, worked examples and question banks in one sitting. Batching is far more efficient than reaching for the tool ad hoc.
  2. Build a personal prompt file. Keep the prompts that worked in a single document. Within a term you will have a library tuned to your subject, your grade level and your students — the compounding asset of this entire module.
  3. Verify before duplicating. Never photocopy a generated resource you have not read end to end. This is not optional.
  4. Keep one honest note per week. What did it do well, what did it get wrong. After a term you will have a genuine evidence base — for yourself and for the colleagues who will ask.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the misconception prompt
practitioner.text: If you take one prompt from this module, take the misconception hunt: "List the eight most common misconceptions students hold about [topic] at [grade] level, why each is intuitive, and one diagnostic question that would reveal it." Experienced teachers accumulate this knowledge over a decade of marking. It does not make you a worse teacher to have it in thirty seconds — it makes your first lesson on an unfamiliar topic behave like your fifth. For an early-career teacher, or one teaching outside their specialism, this is the single most valuable thing in the programme.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Pick next week's most demanding lesson. Use three prompts from this module — the misconception hunt, the worked examples prompt, and the single-lesson plan — and build the lesson. Time yourself against how long it normally takes. Then write down, specifically, what you will do with the time saved, and defend that decision for the rest of the term.

takeaways: Teachers work around 50 hours a week and spend less than half of it interacting with students
Brisbane Catholic Education measured up to nine hours per week saved; Broward measured over two
The difference between two hours and nine is training and workflow redesign, not software
Sort every task: delegate freely, delegate with mandatory review, or never delegate
Never type identifiable student data into a public AI tool — describe the situation generically
The misconception hunt makes a first lesson behave like a fifth
Time saved that is not deliberately reassigned is absorbed within weeks and proves nothing

quiz.q: Brisbane Catholic Education and Broward County deployed the same product but measured very different time savings (up to nine hours versus just over two). This indicates that:
opts: Australian teachers work harder
The measurement methods were invalid
One system exaggerated its results
The determining factor is training and workflow redesign, not the software
quiz.fb: A licence alone buys very little. The difference between the two figures is professional learning and deliberate redesign of how the work is done.

quiz.q: Which task falls into the 'never delegate' category?
opts: A safeguarding or pastoral judgement about a specific child
Generating practice questions
Summarising a policy document
Drafting a scheme of work
quiz.fb: Final grades, safeguarding, placement and discipline decisions all require contextual judgement AI does not possess and cannot be accountable for.

quiz.q: A teacher wants AI's help with a struggling student. The correct approach is to:
opts: Type the student's name and full background into the tool for better personalisation
Describe the situation generically without identifiable details, then add specifics yourself
Ask the student to enter their own details
Avoid using AI for any student-related task
quiz.fb: Generic description costs nothing, produces equally useful output, and protects both the child and the teacher.

quiz.q: The US Department of Education attaches which condition to AI-driven workload reduction?
opts: That it must be approved by parents
That only senior teachers should use it
That recovered time should be rededicated toward more meaningful work rather than simply absorbed
That it must save at least five hours
quiz.fb: Unreassigned time is absorbed within weeks, leaving the teacher equally tired with an extra tool to maintain and no evidence of benefit.

quiz.q: The 'misconception hunt' prompt is valuable primarily because:
opts: It saves photocopying
It works without electricity
It generates more questions than a textbook
It supplies in seconds the diagnostic knowledge experienced teachers accumulate over years of marking
quiz.fb: It makes a first lesson on an unfamiliar topic behave like a fifth — especially valuable for early-career teachers or those teaching outside their specialism.

quiz.q: IDC recommends that AI-enabled workload reduction should be used to shift the teacher's role toward:
opts: Facilitation and relationship building — individualised support and meaningful student relationships
Content delivery at greater speed
Administrative supervision
Technology management
quiz.fb: The stated aim is 'getting back to real teaching' rather than being overburdened by paperwork.

education.title: Planning, Differentiating and Resourcing
education.summary: Reaching every student in a class of fifty
objectives: Use AI to differentiate a single resource across a wide ability range
Adapt materials for multilingual learners and students with additional needs
Apply Universal Design for Learning principles with AI support
Build resources that work in low-resource classrooms without projectors or devices
Understand the adaptivity that intelligent tutoring systems offer, and its limits
Avoid the differentiation traps that widen rather than close gaps

sections.h: The problem AI is genuinely well suited to
sections.html:
Differentiation is the thing every teacher is told to do and almost no teacher has time to do properly. In a class of fifty with a five-year spread of reading ages, several students learning in their second or third language, and two or three with unidentified additional needs, producing three versions of every resource is not a workload problem — it is an impossibility.

This is the clearest case in the whole programme where AI does something that was previously out of reach rather than merely faster. Producing a text at three reading levels, or a task in four versions, takes minutes instead of hours. The US Department of Education identifies adaptivity as "a key way in which technology can improve learning" — improving a resource's ability to meet students where they are, build on their strengths, and grow their knowledge.

The core move, with the prompts:

  • Reading level. "Rewrite this passage at three levels: (a) two years below grade level with simpler sentence structure and vocabulary, (b) at grade level, (c) extended with more demanding vocabulary and one additional idea. Keep all three factually identical and the same length so they are not visibly different in class." That last instruction matters more than it looks — a visibly shorter or simpler sheet is a public label.
  • Second-language support. "Produce a glossary of the 12 words in this text most likely to block comprehension for a student learning in English as a second language. Give a one-line definition in simple English and a Nepali equivalent."
  • Scaffolded task versions. "Take this task and produce four versions: heavily scaffolded with sentence starters and a worked model; moderately scaffolded with prompts only; unscaffolded; and an extension that requires synthesis across two topics. All four must assess the same objective."
  • Concrete to abstract. "Give me three ways to introduce [concept] — one fully concrete using objects available in a rural Nepali classroom, one pictorial, one abstract — and tell me what the student must understand before moving from each to the next."

The Department of Education's report names Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as one of the frameworks AI-supported adaptivity should be built on. UDL asks you to provide multiple means of engagement (the why of learning), representation (the what) and action and expression (the how).

AI makes UDL affordable for the first time in an ordinary classroom:

  • Multiple representations. "Explain [concept] four ways: as a short narrative, as a diagram description I can draw on the board, as a real-world analogy from daily life in Nepal, and as a step-by-step procedure."
  • Multiple means of expression. "Give me five ways a student could demonstrate mastery of [objective] that are not a written essay — including one oral, one visual, one practical and one collaborative — with a common rubric that applies fairly across all five."
  • Multiple entry points to engagement. "Suggest three opening questions for [topic] that connect to the everyday experience of a 14-year-old in a small town, and would provoke disagreement."

• Dyslexia and reading difficulty. "Reformat this worksheet for a student with dyslexia: shorter sentences, one instruction per line, no dense blocks, key terms defined at first use, generous spacing."
  • Attention difficulties. "Break this 40-minute task into five separately completable chunks, each with its own success criterion, so a student who loses focus can re-enter without starting over."
  • Anxiety and low confidence. "Rewrite these six questions so that each begins with something the student can almost certainly do, before increasing demand."
  • Gifted and rapidly-finishing students. "Give me three genuine extension tasks for [topic] that deepen rather than merely add more of the same — each requiring synthesis, evaluation or transfer to an unfamiliar context."

The limit you must respect

AI can adapt materials. It cannot diagnose a learning difficulty, design a formal support plan, or replace specialist assessment — and it will confidently pretend otherwise if asked. Adapting a worksheet for a student you know has dyslexia is good practice. Asking a chatbot whether a student has dyslexia is not, and typing that student's details in to find out compounds the error.

Much AI-in-education material silently assumes a device per student, reliable electricity and fast internet. Most classrooms in Nepal and comparable systems have none of these, and this does not disqualify them — it changes where the tool sits.

The most important reframing in this module: the AI can be entirely on the teacher's side of the classroom. A teacher with a phone and intermittent connectivity, preparing at home, can bring in printed differentiated worksheets, worked examples on the board and a bank of oral questions. Every student benefits and not one of them touches a device.

  • "Design this activity for a classroom with no electricity, no projector and no student devices. Everything must work with a blackboard, chalk and printed sheets."
  • "Give me 15 oral questions on [topic] I can ask around a class of 50, sequenced so that early questions build the vocabulary needed for later ones."
  • "Design a group task for 50 students in fixed rows who cannot move furniture."
  • "Adapt this practical experiment to use only materials available in a Nepali market for under 500 rupees."

Beyond your own resource-making sits a category of software that adapts automatically to each student: intelligent tutoring systems. The Department of Education's report treats these as the clearest established example of AI models in education, descending from cognitive-science-based systems for mathematics problem solving.

What they do well is narrow and real: in well-structured domains — arithmetic, algebra, grammar, vocabulary — they diagnose the specific step a student is failing on and supply targeted practice, indefinitely and without judgement.

What you must ask before adopting one:

  • Whose curriculum is it built on? A system aligned to a foreign syllabus will teach confidently misaligned content.
  • What does it do when a student is stuck? Escalating hints that eventually give the answer teach helplessness.
  • Can the teacher see and override it? The Department's recommendation is explicit: AI in education should be inspectable, explainable and overridable.
  • Does it adapt pace in a way that could widen gaps? The report's specific warning is that if a system speeds the pace for some students and slows it for others on the basis of incomplete data or biased assumptions, achievement gaps could widen. This is developed in Module 9.

• Permanent ability labelling. Differentiation should be responsive to a task, not a caste. Generating three fixed versions and assigning each child permanently to one is a way of guaranteeing the gap.
  • Differentiating the demand instead of the support. The lower-attaining student should get more scaffolding toward the same objective, not a lesser objective. AI makes it very easy to do the wrong one.
  • Visible difference. If the sheets look different, every child in the room knows. Match length and formatting.
  • Volume as differentiation. More questions is not extension. Extension requires synthesis, evaluation or transfer.
  • Generating without reading. A differentiated pack you have not checked may contain a factual error propagated across all four versions.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: differentiate the support, not the objective
practitioner.text: When you write the prompt, state the objective once and ask for varied support toward it: "All four versions must assess the same objective — [state it]. Vary only the scaffolding." Without that instruction, AI will quietly lower the demand for the weaker versions, because that is the most common pattern in its training data. One sentence in the prompt prevents you from institutionalising low expectations at scale — which is the single largest risk of AI-assisted differentiation.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take one text or task you will teach in the next fortnight. Produce four scaffolded versions holding the objective constant, plus a 12-word glossary for second-language learners, plus three genuine extension tasks requiring synthesis rather than volume. Teach it. Note which version each student chose or was given, and whether the visible-difference problem arose.

takeaways: Differentiation is the clearest case where AI does something previously out of reach, not merely faster
Hold the objective constant and vary only the scaffolding — state this explicitly in the prompt
Match length and formatting across versions, or the sheets themselves become a public label
AI adapts materials; it cannot diagnose a learning difficulty and will pretend otherwise if asked
In low-resource classrooms the AI sits on the teacher's side — printed sheets, board work, oral questions
Adaptive systems must be inspectable, explainable and overridable by the teacher
Pace-adaptation built on incomplete data or biased assumptions can widen achievement gaps

quiz.q: When generating differentiated versions of a task, the instruction most important to include is:
opts: 'Use simpler vocabulary throughout'
'All versions must assess the same objective; vary only the scaffolding'
'Add more questions to the extension'
'Make the easier version shorter'
quiz.fb: Without it, AI quietly lowers the demand for weaker versions — institutionalising low expectations at scale.

quiz.q: Why should differentiated worksheets match in length and formatting?
opts: To simplify photocopying
Because regulations require it
Because visibly different sheets publicly label the students who receive them
To save paper
quiz.fb: Every child in the room can see which sheet is the 'easy' one. Matching format preserves dignity without reducing support.

quiz.q: A teacher asks a chatbot whether a particular student has dyslexia. This is:
opts: Acceptable if the parents consent
An efficient use of AI for early identification
Standard practice in adaptive learning
Inappropriate — AI cannot diagnose, and entering the student's details compounds the error
quiz.fb: Adapting materials for a student you know has dyslexia is good practice. Diagnosis requires specialist assessment, and AI will confidently pretend otherwise.

quiz.q: The US Department of Education recommends that AI systems used in education be:
opts: Inspectable, explainable and overridable by educators
Purchased only from large vendors
Restricted to secondary schools
Fully autonomous to reduce teacher workload
quiz.fb: Teachers must be able to see what the system is doing, understand why, and override it when their judgement differs.

quiz.q: In a classroom with no electricity, projector or student devices, AI is:
opts: Useful only if the school buys tablets
Still highly useful, sitting entirely on the teacher's side — printed differentiated sheets, board work and oral question banks
Of no practical use
Only useful for administration
quiz.fb: A teacher preparing at home with a phone can bring the whole benefit into a classroom where no student touches a device.

quiz.q: Which is a genuine extension task rather than a differentiation trap?
opts: A neater version of the worksheet
Twenty more questions of the same type
A task requiring synthesis across two topics or transfer to an unfamiliar context
The same task with a longer time limit
quiz.fb: Volume is not extension. Extension requires synthesis, evaluation or transfer.

education.title: Feedback, Marking and the Limits of Automated Assessment
education.summary: Where AI helps most — and where it must never be left alone
objectives: Use AI to produce feedback that opens a dialogue rather than closing one
Understand what automated essay scoring can and cannot measure
Recognise and mitigate bias in automated assessment
Design rubrics that make AI-assisted marking defensible
Keep the teacher meaningfully in the loop rather than nominally
Build a marking workflow that reduces load without surrendering judgement

sections.h: The tension at the centre of this module
sections.html:
Marking is the largest single component of teacher workload and the one teachers most want to delegate. It is also the activity where delegation does the most damage, because feedback is not administration — it is teaching.

Module 2 established the principle: the best feedback creates a dialogue, turning assessment into a continuation of learning rather than merely its measurement. An AI system that returns a score and three generic comments has measured. It has not taught. Resolving this tension is what this module is for, and the resolution is not "use AI for marking" or "never use AI for marking" — it is a precise division of labour.

The US Department of Education's report treats automated essay scoring as a well-established example worth understanding honestly. Such systems have existed for decades and work by learning statistical associations between features of student writing and the scores human markers previously gave.

That description contains the limitation. The system is not reading for meaning. It is predicting what a human marker would have said based on surface features that historically correlated with quality — sentence length, vocabulary range, structural markers, organisational signals.

The practical consequences:

  • It is reasonably good at conventions — grammar, spelling, structure, paragraphing, register. These are genuinely surface features and it detects them well.
  • It is poor at argument quality. A fluent, well-structured essay that is entirely wrong will often score well. An awkwardly written essay containing an original insight will often score badly.
  • It cannot recognise what it has not seen. The unusual answer, the culturally specific example, the student who has understood something the marking scheme did not anticipate — all get penalised.
  • It rewards length and elaboration because those historically correlated with effort. Students learn this quickly, and it teaches them to pad.

The consequence for your students

If students believe an algorithm is scoring their work, they will optimise for the algorithm. They will write longer, use more connectives, and deploy sophisticated vocabulary they do not control — because those things move the number. You will have taught them to produce the appearance of quality instead of quality. This is the strongest single argument for keeping the final judgement visibly human.

The Department of Education's recommendation here is explicit: harness assessment expertise to reduce bias. The report warns of "algorithmic discrimination" — systematic unfairness in the opportunities or resources recommended to some populations of students — and offers concrete examples: a voice recognition system that works less well with regional dialects; an exam monitoring system that unfairly identifies some groups of students for disciplinary action.

In assessment specifically, bias enters through several doors:

  • Language background. Systems trained mainly on first-language English writing systematically under-score competent second-language writers whose grammar is non-standard but whose reasoning is sound. In a Nepali classroom this is not a marginal concern — it is the majority case.
  • Dialect and register. Writing that is regionally natural but not standard-academic is penalised as error.
  • Cultural reference. An example drawn from a local festival, an agricultural practice or a religious tradition may be scored as irrelevant because the pattern is unfamiliar.
  • Name and identity signals. Where any identifying information reaches the system, historical patterns can attach to it.

The mitigation is procedural and cheap: never let an automated score stand as a final grade; sample-check across groups; and specifically compare outcomes for your second-language learners against your judgement. If the system is systematically harsher on them, you have found real bias in ten minutes of checking.

sections.h: The division of labour that works
sections.html:
Here is the practical resolution, and it is the core of the module.

Let AI do the first pass on the mechanical layer. Keep the judgement, the grade and the relationship.

  • AI does well: flagging surface errors, checking against a structural checklist, identifying which rubric criteria appear unaddressed, generating a bank of feedback phrases you can select from, spotting that fourteen students in the class made the same mistake, summarising class-wide patterns you would otherwise miss.
  • You do: reading for meaning, recognising the unusual insight, knowing that this particular student has improved enormously even if the piece is still weak, deciding the grade, choosing the one comment that will actually move this child forward.

The highest-value application is not marking individual scripts at all — it is class-level pattern analysis. Paste twenty anonymised responses and ask: "What are the three most common conceptual errors in this set, ranked by frequency? For each, give the likely misconception behind it and one re-teaching activity." That is thirty seconds of work producing something a teacher rarely has time to do properly, and it changes what you teach next lesson.

• Dialogue feedback. "Here is a Grade 10 student's paragraph and the rubric. Give feedback in this form: one specific thing done well with evidence quoted from the text, one specific area to improve with a concrete example of how, and one question that makes the student think rather than telling them the answer. No grade. Under 80 words."
  • Class pattern analysis. "Here are 25 anonymised student answers to [question]. Identify the three most common errors ranked by frequency, the misconception behind each, and one five-minute re-teaching activity for each."
  • Rubric stress-test. "Here is my rubric. Identify any criteria that are vague, overlapping, or that a student could not self-assess against. Rewrite the weakest three in student-facing language."
  • Feedback bank. "Generate 15 feedback comments for [skill] at Grade [8] — five for work below expectation, five at, five above. Each must name a specific next step, not a judgement. I will select and adapt."
  • Self-assessment scaffold. "Turn this rubric into six student-facing questions a Grade 9 student could ask of their own draft before submitting." — This is among the most valuable uses in the module, because it moves work from your marking pile to their metacognition.

sections.h: Keeping the human meaningfully in the loop
sections.html:
The Department of Education's first recommendation is to emphasise humans in the loop — people remaining part of the process of noticing patterns and assigning meaning to them, with teachers "at the helm of major instructional decisions."

The failure mode to guard against is nominal rather than absent oversight: a teacher who approves every AI-generated grade because it is usually about right, under time pressure, at eleven at night. The oversight exists on paper and does nothing.

Three practical tests of genuine oversight:

  1. Do you ever disagree? If you have never changed an AI-suggested comment or score, you are not reviewing — you are rubber-stamping. Track it honestly.
  2. Do you have the time to disagree? Oversight that is not resourced is not oversight. If the workflow only works when you accept everything, it is designed wrongly.
  3. Would you defend it to the parent? Every comment that leaves your hands must be one you would stand behind in a meeting. If you would not, do not send it.

sections.h: A marking workflow that reduces load honestly
sections.html:
1. Before marking: stress-test the rubric with AI, and convert it into student-facing self-check questions. Give those to students before they submit. This measurably reduces the volume of poor work reaching you.
  2. First pass, whole class: anonymised pattern analysis. Decide what you will re-teach before you mark a single script.
  3. Second pass, individual: mark yourself, but with an AI-generated feedback bank open. Selecting and adapting a comment is far faster than composing one, and the quality is more consistent across a set of fifty.
  4. Grades: yours alone. Always.
  5. Follow-up: the re-teaching activity generated in step 2 becomes next lesson's starter. The loop closes, which is the point of formative assessment and the part most often lost.

Teachers who adopt this report the load falling not because the marking is automated but because the rubric was better, the students self-corrected more before submitting, and the re-teaching was targeted rather than guessed.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: move the work upstream
practitioner.text: The highest-leverage change in this module happens before students submit, not after. Convert your rubric into six student-facing self-check questions and require students to answer them on the front of their work. The quality of what arrives improves, the volume of avoidable error falls, and — the real prize — the students have practised metacognition on their own writing. You have reduced your marking by improving their thinking, which is the only workload reduction in teaching that is also a pedagogical gain.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take a rubric you already use. Stress-test it with AI for vagueness and overlap, rewrite the three weakest criteria, then convert the whole thing into student-facing self-check questions. Use it with your next assessment. Separately, run an anonymised class-pattern analysis on a set of responses and compare what it found to what you expected — note anything you would have missed.

takeaways: Feedback is teaching, not administration, which is why delegation does the most damage here
Automated scoring predicts what a human marker would have said from surface features; it does not read for meaning
Students who believe an algorithm is scoring will optimise for it and learn to produce the appearance of quality
Language-background bias is not marginal in a second-language classroom — it is the majority case
The highest-value use is class-level pattern analysis, not marking individual scripts
If you never disagree with the AI, you are rubber-stamping rather than reviewing
Move the work upstream: student-facing self-check questions reduce marking by improving thinking

quiz.q: Automated essay scoring systems work primarily by:
opts: Reading the essay for meaning and argument quality
Checking facts against reference sources
Comparing the essay to a database of model answers
Predicting what a human marker would have said, based on surface features that historically correlated with quality
quiz.fb: This explains why a fluent but wholly incorrect essay often scores well, while an awkward essay containing an original insight often scores badly.

quiz.q: In a classroom where most students write in their second language, automated scoring bias is:
opts: The majority case, since such systems systematically under-score competent second-language writers
Eliminated by modern models
Only relevant to spoken assessment
A marginal concern affecting few students
quiz.fb: Non-standard grammar with sound reasoning is penalised as error. Sample-checking outcomes for these students against your own judgement exposes it quickly.

quiz.q: The highest-value marking application of AI for a teacher is:
opts: Ranking students against one another
Anonymised class-level pattern analysis that identifies common errors and their underlying misconceptions
Detecting whether students used AI
Grading individual scripts to save time
quiz.fb: Thirty seconds of work producing something teachers rarely have time to do properly — and it changes what you teach next lesson.

quiz.q: A teacher has approved every AI-suggested comment for a whole term without changing one. This indicates:
opts: Efficient workflow design
That the rubric is well written
Oversight has become nominal — rubber-stamping rather than reviewing
The system is performing excellently
quiz.fb: Genuine oversight requires that you sometimes disagree, that you have time to disagree, and that you would defend every comment to a parent.

quiz.q: Converting a rubric into student-facing self-check questions before submission is valuable because:
opts: It allows AI to mark more accurately
It satisfies inspection requirements
It shortens the assignment
It reduces marking load by improving student thinking — a workload gain that is also a pedagogical gain
quiz.fb: Quality improves, avoidable error falls, and students practise metacognition on their own writing.

quiz.q: Who should decide the final grade on a piece of student work?
opts: The teacher, always
Whichever is faster under time pressure
The AI system, for consistency
The school's software policy
quiz.fb: AI may support the mechanical layer. Judgement, grade and relationship remain with the teacher.

education.title: Academic Integrity: Beyond the Arms Race
education.summary: Why detection fails, and what actually works instead
objectives: Understand why AI detection tools are unreliable and can be discriminatory
Recognise why a surveillance-led response damages learning
Implement an AI maturity matrix that makes expectations unambiguous
Redesign tasks so that integrity is built in rather than policed
Hold an honest conversation with students about AI use
Write a workable academic integrity policy for AI

sections.h: The crisis is real — and the usual response makes it worse
sections.html:
It is worth acknowledging the depth of the problem before proposing anything. A May 2025 feature in New York Magazine, headlined "Everyone Is Cheating Their Way Through College," captured the bleakness: the speed with which AI proved able to do college-level work exposed pre-existing weaknesses in assessment — and multiple platforms now offer tools to leave AI-generated feedback on students' essays, raising the possibility that AI systems are evaluating AI-generated papers, "reducing the entire academic exercise to a conversation between two robots."

The institutional reflex has been defensive: proctored exams, AI-detection software, handwritten requirements. Chatfield acknowledges that in the immediate term some return to basics is understandable. But he is unambiguous that as a strategy this fails, and it is worth understanding exactly why, because most schools are currently choosing it.

• Practically, it is unsustainable. Detection tools are, in Chatfield's assessment, "at best unreliable and at worst actively discriminatory." They produce false positives on genuine student work and false negatives on lightly edited AI text. Every improvement in the models degrades the detectors.
  • It discriminates. The documented pattern is that detectors disproportionately flag second-language writers, whose more formulaic sentence construction resembles machine text. In a Nepali or comparable classroom, a detection-led policy will systematically accuse your most vulnerable students.
  • Pedagogically it is counterproductive. It frames the relationship between learners and institution as conflict rather than collaboration — which, as Module 2 established, attacks the emotional safety that learning requires.
  • It fails on its own terms. Those determined to cheat will find a way. Meanwhile the majority — who want to learn — are denied the guidance they actually need.

The professional judgement this requires of you

A detection score is not evidence. It is a probability estimate from an unreliable instrument. Never accuse a student on the basis of a detector alone, never let a number substitute for a conversation, and be aware that if your school acts on detector output at scale, it will produce wrongful accusations — disproportionately against second-language learners and students who write in a formal register.

Chatfield makes an observation that reframes the whole problem, and it is uncomfortable:

"If a student uses AI to complete an assignment, the problem is not just the tool. It is also that the assignment may no longer measure those things it was designed to measure."

He goes further. A student who can carefully prompt an AI to output an eloquent, appropriate analysis is demonstrating certain capabilities: crafting clear requirements, understanding the topic well enough to evaluate outputs, iterating and improving in the light of these. These are not the same skills as writing a traditional essay — but nor are they meaningless.

The philosopher Luciano Floridi named this mode "distant writing": a hybrid composition in which the human becomes less an author than a designer, someone who "sets requirements" rather than composing directly. Floridi describes it as "a significant evolution in authorship, not replacing but expanding human creativity within a design paradigm."

None of this means the traditional essay should be abandoned. It means you must decide, explicitly, which skill each task is assessing — and then design accordingly. That decision is what the rest of this module operationalises.

sections.h: The AI maturity matrix — the single most useful tool in this module
sections.html:
Brisbane Catholic Education's approach, documented by IDC, is the practical answer, and it is simple enough to implement next week. They developed a maturity matrix clarifying when AI is prohibited, when it may be used for planning only, when for writing assistance, and when for feedback.

Adapted for classroom use, print this and put it on every assignment:

  • Level 0 — No AI. This task assesses your unaided ability. Completed in class or under supervision. Use when: you need to know what a student can do alone; foundational skills; anything that must be verifiable.
  • Level 1 — AI for planning only. You may use AI to brainstorm, structure or clarify the question. All writing is yours. Submit your AI conversation alongside. Use when: the writing is the assessed skill but the blank page is a barrier.
  • Level 2 — AI for assistance. You may use AI to check grammar, suggest vocabulary, or improve a draft you wrote. Highlight what changed and explain why you accepted or rejected each suggestion. Use when: you are teaching revision and editing.
  • Level 3 — AI as collaborator. You may use AI throughout. You are assessed on the quality of your prompts, your evaluation of its output, what you rejected and why, and the final result. Submit the full log. Use when: the assessed skill is direction, judgement and critical evaluation.

Two things make this work. First, every task carries a visible level, so no student can claim confusion. Second, Levels 1–3 require disclosure of the conversation, which converts hidden use into visible, discussable, teachable use — and is far more informative to you than any detector.

sections.h: Designing tasks where integrity is built in
sections.html:
Better than policing is designing tasks AI cannot complete on the student's behalf. Practical moves, all of which work without technology:

  • Anchor to the specific and local. "Analyse the water supply problem in our ward using the data we collected on Tuesday." AI has never seen your data.
  • Anchor to the personal. "Connect this concept to something that happened in your own family or community, and explain the limits of the comparison."
  • Anchor to the class's shared experience. "Referring to the argument Bishal made in Wednesday's discussion, explain where you agree and where you would push back."
  • Assess the process. Require drafts, notes, a planning sheet, a reflection on what changed between versions.
  • Require the student to critique AI output. "Here is an AI-generated answer to this question. Identify three weaknesses and rewrite the weakest paragraph." Now AI use is the assignment.
  • Add an oral component. Two minutes of questioning about a submitted piece tells you more than any detector — and, as Module 7 develops, is a genuine skill worth developing in its own right rather than a surveillance device.

sections.h: The conversation to have with your students
sections.html:
Have it early, once, and honestly. The elements that make it land:

  1. Acknowledge that they are already using it. Pretending otherwise destroys your credibility in the first thirty seconds.
  2. Explain the two-question test from Module 1 in their terms: "When I ask you to write this, the writing is the exercise. Getting a machine to do your push-ups does not make you stronger." Students find this argument persuasive because it is true and because it treats them as capable of understanding their own interest.
  3. Be explicit that you will teach them to use it. They will need this skill; you are not withholding it, you are sequencing it.
  4. Set out the maturity matrix and commit to marking every task with a level.
  5. State the consequence honestly — and state clearly that you will not accuse anyone on the basis of software. Say that you will ask them about their work instead. This does more for integrity than any threat, because it makes the system feel fair.

Six clauses. One page. Written for students and parents, not lawyers.

  1. Every assessed task states its AI level (0–3). If a task carries no level, ask before assuming.
  2. Where AI is permitted, disclosure is required. Submit the conversation or a short statement of what you used it for. Undisclosed use of permitted AI is the integrity breach — not the use itself.
  3. You are responsible for everything you submit, including errors AI introduced. "The AI said so" is not a defence.
  4. Never submit AI text as your own words at Levels 0–2.
  5. No accusation rests on detection software. Concerns are addressed through a conversation about the work.
  6. Ask when unsure. Asking is always safe and never penalised.

Clause 5 is the one that will be argued about in your staffroom. Hold it. A policy that permits accusation on the basis of an unreliable, discriminatory instrument will eventually produce a wrongful accusation against a real child — and the damage from that will exceed anything the policy was designed to prevent.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: put the level on the sheet
practitioner.text: The single change with the largest immediate effect costs nothing: print the AI level on every assignment sheet, in a box, at the top. Most student "cheating" in the first year of a technology like this is genuine ambiguity — a student who used AI for planning, believed that was fine, and never mentioned it. Removing the ambiguity removes most of the problem, and what remains is a much smaller number of deliberate cases you can address individually rather than through a policy of general suspicion.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take the next four tasks you will set. Assign each an AI level (0–3) and write the level on the sheet with one line explaining why that level fits what the task assesses. Then redesign one of them using an anchoring technique — local, personal, or class-shared — so that AI could not complete it on the student's behalf. Note how much the task improved as a task, independently of the integrity question.

takeaways: Detection tools are unreliable at best and discriminatory at worst; a score is not evidence
Detectors disproportionately flag second-language writers — your most vulnerable students
Surveillance frames learning as conflict and attacks the emotional safety learning requires
If AI can complete the assignment, the assignment may no longer measure what it was designed to measure
The AI maturity matrix (Levels 0–3) removes ambiguity and converts hidden use into teachable use
Anchor tasks to the local, the personal and the class's shared experience
Never let an accusation rest on detection software — have a conversation about the work instead

quiz.q: AI detection tools are described in the research as unreliable and potentially discriminatory. The group most likely to be wrongly flagged is:
opts: High-attaining students
Second-language writers, whose more formulaic construction resembles machine text
Students using handwriting
Students who write very short answers
quiz.fb: In a second-language classroom, a detection-led policy will systematically accuse your most vulnerable students.

quiz.q: Chatfield argues that when a student successfully uses AI to complete an assignment, the deeper problem is that:
opts: The student lacks moral character
The task was too long
The assignment may no longer measure what it was designed to measure
The school's software is outdated
quiz.fb: This reframes integrity as an assessment design question rather than purely a disciplinary one.

quiz.q: In the AI maturity matrix, Level 3 ('AI as collaborator') assesses:
opts: Nothing meaningful
The student's unaided writing ability
Only the final product's grammar
The quality of the student's prompts, evaluation of output, and what they rejected and why
quiz.fb: When the assessed skill is direction, judgement and critical evaluation, full AI use with a submitted log is the appropriate design.

quiz.q: Under a well-designed AI policy, where AI use is permitted, the integrity breach is:
opts: Undisclosed use — failing to declare permitted AI use
Using AI at all
Discussing AI with classmates
Using AI for grammar checking
quiz.fb: Disclosure converts hidden use into visible, discussable, teachable use — and is far more informative than any detector.

quiz.q: Which task design makes AI completion genuinely difficult without any technology?
opts: A multiple-choice test
'Analyse the water supply problem in our ward using the data we collected on Tuesday'
An essay on a very obscure topic
A longer essay with a stricter word count
quiz.fb: Anchoring to local, personal or class-shared material means AI has never seen the source. It also improves the task independently of integrity.

quiz.q: Luciano Floridi's term 'distant writing' describes:
opts: Writing done remotely from home
Plagiarism from online sources
Hybrid composition where the human sets requirements as a designer rather than composing directly
Handwritten work under supervision
quiz.fb: Floridi frames it as an evolution in authorship — expanding human creativity within a design paradigm rather than replacing it.

education.title: Redesigning Assessment for an AI World
education.summary: From 'What do you know?' to 'How do you think?'
objectives: Understand why traditional assessment assumptions no longer hold
Design process-based and portfolio assessment supported by AI
Use oral and viva-style assessment as development rather than surveillance
Build a bank of AI-resistant and AI-integrated task designs
Apply mastery-based progression concepts to your own subject
Sequence a realistic transition rather than changing everything at once

sections.html:
Traditional examinations assume a world in which information is scarce and retrieval is difficult. Essays test the ability to construct arguments without assistance. Both assumptions were true for centuries and are no longer true.

Chatfield argues that transforming assessment may prove AI's greatest impact within education, and the reasoning is worth following carefully. Creating assessments adequate to this challenge means focusing not only on products but on processes. This has long been an aspiration for educators; AI makes it at once necessary and possible. Necessary because traditional assessments can no longer measure what they once did. Possible because AI can support forms of evaluation that were previously impractical at scale.

The reframing he proposes is the organising idea of this module: assessment as conversation rather than surveillance. The underlying question moves from "What do you know?" to "How do you think?" — and, more precisely, "How are you thinking about your thinking, and about its entwining with the very different forms of intelligence AI tools possess?"

The practical shift is to assess the journey, not only the destination. Concretely:

  • Staged submission. Plan, then annotated bibliography, then draft, then final. Each stage carries marks. A student who produces a polished final piece with no preceding stages has not completed the assessment.
  • Annotated drafts. Require students to mark what changed between versions and why. The reasoning is the assessed object.
  • Process logs. Where AI is permitted, the log of prompts and responses is submitted. Wharton's Ethan Mollick has student venture teams keep records of their queries alongside responses; these are handed in with the final business plan, together with reflections analysing which machine-generated ideas they modified, kept or discarded, and whether they found hallucinations or biases.
  • Reflective commentary. A short piece explaining the choices made, the alternatives rejected, and what the student would do differently. AI can generate a reflection; it cannot generate your student's reflection on their specific process, and the difference is visible.

Mollick's framing is worth noting for teachers: reviewing those student reports, he observes, "can also give you a sense of where students are in their learning journey so that you can modify your lessons accordingly." The process log is not only an integrity device — it is formative data you never previously had.

Portfolio-based assessment enacts the process principle at scale. Students document their learning journey across a term or year; AI can help identify patterns and growth across a large body of work. But — and Chatfield is explicit — the business of reflection and curation remains irreducibly human.

A workable portfolio structure for a school or college:

  1. Five to eight pieces across the term, of varied type — at least one oral, one collaborative, one practical or visual.
  2. For each piece: the artefact, the process evidence, and a 100-word reflection.
  3. A closing synthesis: the student selects their strongest and weakest pieces and argues why, identifying the specific skill that improved most.
  4. Assessment: weighted toward the synthesis and the trajectory rather than any single artefact.

This is more demanding to administer than a single exam and considerably more informative. It is also far harder to fake, because the fabrication would have to be sustained and coherent across months.

sections.h: Oral assessment — as development, not policing
sections.html:
Viva-style defences and discussions gain new significance precisely because written work may be AI-assisted. The critical design point, which most schools get wrong: the best implementations treat this as an opportunity for developing distinctively human skills, not as surveillance.

If students experience an oral component as an interrogation to catch cheats, you have imported all the damage of the detection approach with additional anxiety. If they experience it as the place where they explain and defend their thinking — a skill that will matter in every interview and meeting of their adult lives — it becomes the most valuable part of the course.

Practical formats that work in large classes:

  • Two-minute defence. Every student answers two questions about their submitted work. In a class of fifty this is achievable across two lessons with the rest of the class working independently.
  • Peer viva. Students question each other against a supplied question frame; you circulate. Preparing to question someone else requires understanding the topic thoroughly.
  • Structured debate. Students argue a position they were assigned rather than chose, then swap. Assesses reasoning and flexibility together.
  • Teach-back. The student explains the concept to a younger student or a peer who has not studied it. Notoriously difficult to fake and among the most reliable indicators of genuine understanding.

Emerging platforms are beginning to use AI itself not as a substitute for discussion but as a moderator and evaluator of small-group discussion, providing individual post-discussion feedback against a rubric — an approach that makes oral assessment more tractable at scale.

The cognitive co-pilot developed by Chatfield with Dr Timo Hannay, Sage and City St George's, University of London, illustrates a further possibility. By tracking how students engage with concepts through adaptive, Socratic questioning, it sidesteps the authentication problem entirely.

The logic is elegant. Progress is not about producing correct factual answers — it is about demonstrating that you can apply concepts in novel contexts and connect disparate ideas. A "mastery gate" in the system's instructions ensures a student cannot progress until understanding has been shown. Assessment becomes an ongoing measure of mastery integrated into each interaction, rather than a discrete event that can be outsourced.

You do not need such a system to apply the principle. In your own classroom:

  • Define mastery for each unit as application in an unfamiliar context, not recall.
  • Use short, frequent, low-stakes checks rather than infrequent high-stakes ones.
  • Allow re-attempts. If mastery is the goal, the timing of arrival matters less than arrival.
  • Assess transfer explicitly: "Here is a situation we have never discussed. Apply what you learned."

Note that the prototype was well received but modestly so — twelve students across six disciplines rated it 7.6 out of 10. That is a realistic figure for an early prototype and a useful corrective to vendor claims of transformation.

AI-resistant (the assessed skill must be exercised unaided):

  • In-class writing under supervision, with the planning done at home
  • Analysis of data the class collected itself
  • Response to a text or artefact introduced in the lesson and not published online
  • Critique of a specific argument made by a named classmate
  • Practical demonstration, performance or fieldwork
  • Oral defence of any submitted work

AI-integrated (using AI well is the assessed skill):

  • Prompt-and-critique: generate an answer, then identify and correct its three weakest claims
  • Fact-check an AI-produced text against primary sources and document every error
  • Use AI to generate three counter-arguments to your position, then rebut the strongest
  • Compare two AI systems' answers to the same question and account for the differences
  • Build a resource with AI assistance and submit the full log with a rationale for every rejection
  • Design a prompt that reliably produces a high-quality output for a stated purpose, and justify each element of it

Do not redesign everything at once. A realistic three-term sequence:

  1. Term 1. Label every task with an AI level. Add an oral component to one assessment. Change nothing else. This alone resolves most ambiguity.
  2. Term 2. Convert one major assessment to staged submission with process evidence. Introduce one AI-integrated task so students learn the skill explicitly.
  3. Term 3. Pilot a portfolio in one class or one year group. Evaluate honestly against the previous year's assessment before extending it.

Teachers who attempt total redesign in a single term generally abandon it by mid-year, and the failure discredits the approach for colleagues who were watching.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the two-minute defence
practitioner.text: If you change one thing about your assessment this year, add a two-minute oral defence to one written task per term. Ask each student two questions: "Explain the choice you made in this section" and "What would you do differently?" It is achievable in a large class across two lessons, it tells you more about understanding than the script did, it develops a skill your students will use for the rest of their lives — and, as a side effect that you should never present as its purpose, it makes outsourced work immediately apparent.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take your most important assessment this year. Redesign it in three ways: convert it to at least two staged submissions with process evidence; add a two-minute oral defence; and write one AI-integrated alternative task from the bank above. Then define what mastery of this unit means as application in an unfamiliar context, and write the transfer question you would use to test it.

takeaways: Traditional assessment assumed scarce information and difficult retrieval; both assumptions have failed
Assess the process, not only the product — staged submission, annotated drafts, process logs, reflection
Process logs are formative data about where students are, not merely an integrity device
Oral assessment must be framed as developing a human skill, never as an interrogation to catch cheats
Mastery-based progression sidesteps authentication: demonstrate application in novel contexts
Build both AI-resistant tasks and AI-integrated tasks — students need both experiences
Sequence the transition across three terms; total redesign in one term generally collapses

quiz.q: Chatfield reframes assessment as moving from 'What do you know?' toward:
opts: 'What can you memorise?'
'Can you avoid using AI?'
'How fast can you work?'
'How do you think — including about your own thinking?'
quiz.fb: Focusing on process rather than only product is now both necessary, because products can be outsourced, and possible, because AI supports evaluation at scale.

quiz.q: Ethan Mollick has students submit their AI query logs alongside final work. Beyond integrity, the value of this is that:
opts: It gives the instructor formative insight into where students are in their learning journey
It proves the AI was accurate
It satisfies university regulations
It reduces marking time
quiz.fb: The log is data about student thinking that teachers previously had no access to at all.

quiz.q: The most important design consideration when adding oral assessment is:
opts: Recording every session for evidence
Framing it as development of a human skill rather than as surveillance to catch cheating
Using it only for suspected cases
Making it as long as possible
quiz.fb: Framed as interrogation, it imports all the damage of detection with added anxiety. Framed as explaining and defending thinking, it becomes the most valuable part of the course.

quiz.q: A 'mastery gate' in an adaptive tutoring system means that:
opts: Students pay to unlock content
Content is locked by grade level
Students cannot progress until they have demonstrated understanding, typically by applying a concept in a novel context
The teacher approves each step manually
quiz.fb: Because progress requires application rather than correct recall, the authentication problem is largely sidestepped.

quiz.q: Which is an AI-integrated task rather than an AI-resistant one?
opts: An oral defence
Analysis of data the class collected
In-class supervised writing
Fact-checking an AI-produced text against primary sources and documenting every error
quiz.fb: AI-integrated tasks make skilled, critical AI use the assessed object. Students need experience of both categories.

quiz.q: The recommended pace for redesigning assessment is:
opts: A three-term sequence beginning with labelling AI levels and adding one oral component
Complete redesign in a single term for consistency
No change until national guidance arrives
Redesign only for senior year groups
quiz.fb: Total redesign in one term generally collapses by mid-year, and the failure discredits the approach for colleagues who were watching.

education.title: Teaching Students to Use AI Well
education.summary: AI literacy as a curriculum outcome, with ready-to-run lessons
objectives: Design age-appropriate AI experiences for under-13 and 13-plus learners
Teach prompting, verification and critical evaluation as explicit skills
Apply the seven pedagogical roles AI can play for a student
Run classroom activities that build critical AI literacy
Address the equity dimension of AI literacy directly
Connect AI literacy to workforce preparation and digital citizenship

sections.html:
IDC's recommendation to school leaders is blunt: reframe AI literacy as workforce preparation and digital citizenship, recognising that students who graduate without AI capabilities may be at a disadvantage in college and in establishing careers across industries that already use these tools to formulate ideas, solve problems and enhance productivity.

There is an equity argument that makes this urgent rather than merely desirable. The University of Rochester's AI4Education working group documents the shape of the problem: AI-related jobs in the United States increased by almost 80% in a single year between 2017 and 2018, while only 22% of AI jobs are held by women and fewer than 6% of PhD students in AI programmes are Hispanic or African-American. Their conclusion is direct — if such inequality continues, rapid societal AI adoption will widen the gap between rich and poor, as the latter have limited opportunity to develop AI skills.

They also identify a structural barrier that will be familiar: more than 75% of K-12 schools in the United States do not offer a computer science curriculum, and most existing AI learning activities assume prior block-based programming skills. Requiring programming as a prerequisite for AI literacy, they warn, inevitably increases AI inequality among young learners — and research finds children of low and median socioeconomic status find AI concepts harder precisely because they lack that programming background and prior exposure.

Why this matters for your school

If AI literacy is only available through a computer science pathway, it will reach the students who need it least. AI literacy must be taught across the curriculum by ordinary subject teachers — in English, in social studies, in science — and it must not require programming. Everything in this module is designed on that basis.

IDC's guidance separates two bands, and the distinction is both pedagogical and a matter of policy compliance, since most major AI tools set a minimum age of 13.

Under 13 — teacher-facilitated, scaffolded, no independent accounts.

  • The teacher operates the tool on a single screen; children direct it collectively.
  • Emphasis on curiosity, metacognition and basic digital citizenship.
  • Guided storytelling, reading and numeracy support, "let's see if it gets this right" activities.
  • No open-ended chatbot accounts that exceed age or policy limits. This is not negotiable, and a school that permits it has a safeguarding problem rather than a pedagogical one.

13 and above — expanded use with explicit instruction.

  • Research, drafting, code generation, data analysis, content creation.
  • Approved tools within a school-managed environment where possible.
  • Explicit teaching of verification, responsible use, disclosure, and assignment-level AI maturity expectations.
  • The balance IDC names: creativity with academic integrity.

sections.h: The three skills to teach explicitly
sections.html:
1. Prompting. Treat this as a writing skill, because it is one. Teach five moves:

  • Give a role and a context. "You are a science tutor helping a Grade 8 student who has understood photosynthesis but not respiration."
  • Supply your own material. Paste your notes, your data, your draft. Grounded output is far more reliable.
  • Specify the output. "Three points, each with one example, under 100 words."
  • Require gaps to be flagged. "Where you are unsure, say so rather than guessing."
  • Iterate. The first answer is a draft. "That is too general. Use the data I gave you."

2. Verification. The most important and least taught. A four-step routine students can memorise:

  1. Identify every factual claim, number, date, name and quotation.
  2. Check each against an independent source — textbook, teacher, primary document.
  3. Ask: does this contradict anything I already know?
  4. Ask: what has it left out that I would expect to be here?

3. Critical evaluation. Whose perspective is this? What is missing? Would this answer be different if the question had been asked from a Nepali rather than an American standpoint? Whose examples does it use by default?

sections.h: The seven roles AI can play for a student
sections.html:
Ethan and Lilach Mollick's 2023 framework, Assigning AI: Seven Approaches for Students, with Prompts, gives you a design vocabulary. Each role has distinct pedagogical benefits and distinct risks:

  • AI-tutor. Explains and questions Socratically. Risk: giving answers too readily.
  • AI-coach. Prompts reflection on the student's process. Risk: generic encouragement.
  • AI-mentor. Gives feedback on work. Risk: the student adopts suggestions uncritically. Mollick's remedy: students report their interactions and reflect on what guidance they will and will not incorporate.
  • AI-teammate. Contributes to a group task. Risk: displacing a human contributor's thinking.
  • AI-tool. Performs a defined function — translation, formatting, calculation. Lowest risk.
  • AI-simulator. Plays a scenario, a historical figure, a customer, a patient. Excellent for practice; risk of anachronism and invented detail.
  • AI-student. The learner teaches the AI, which asks naive questions. Powerful — teaching is the strongest test of understanding.

The AI-student role deserves particular attention in large classes. "Explain this to an AI playing a confused Grade 6 student, and correct it when it misunderstands" produces genuine cognitive work, requires no marking, and is nearly impossible to complete without understanding the material.

Activity 1 — The bias audit (Grades 9–12, 60 minutes). Adapted from literature scholar Christopher D. Jimenez's 2023 capstone, Teaching Social Identity and Cultural Bias Using AI Text Generation. Students answer six autobiographical questions about their interests and daily life. These are fed to an AI with a prompt asking it to guess their age, gender, background, religion and socioeconomic status, with explanations and confidence levels. Students then debrief with the class about the model's assumptions and produce a written reflection.

The questions that emerge are the lesson: why did it confidently assign a socioeconomic class based on these answers? Why did it attach assumptions to an ambiguous name? By treating outputs as evidence of an algorithmic process to be interpreted rather than products to be accepted or rejected, students trace how training data relates to stereotype and debate what authorship means when mediated by an algorithm. Run it with the teacher's own answers first if student privacy is a concern — it works nearly as well.

Activity 2 — Catch the hallucination (any subject, 30 minutes). You generate an AI answer on a topic the class has studied, containing errors you have verified. Students work in pairs to find every error and rank them by seriousness. Debrief on which errors were easy to catch, which were nearly invisible, and what that implies about using AI on topics you do not already understand. The concluding insight is the one that matters: you can only safely check AI in a domain where you already have knowledge — which is an argument for learning things.

Activity 3 — The prompt improvement ladder (any subject, 40 minutes). Give students a deliberately poor prompt. In pairs they improve it four times, recording the output each round, and annotate what each change achieved. Ends with a class-built list of prompting principles in the students' own words — which they will remember far better than yours.

This is the part of AI literacy most often omitted and, for adolescents, arguably the most important.

Chatfield's warning is specific: modern generative AI systems are "all too adept at simulating emotion, empathy and interest. And the feelings these simulations call forth are all too real." Their bottomless attentiveness is both why they can be so effective and why it is vital to preserve human connection alongside an informed awareness of these machines' actual nature, limitations and manipulative power.

He notes a further risk that applies directly to students: the more people share their thoughts and data with AI, the more value it provides — but this risks both a distorting anthropomorphism and the displacement of conversations that might otherwise have been had with peers, teachers or family.

Teach students plainly: it is not your friend, it does not remember you the way a person does, it is designed to be agreeable, and its endless patience is a product feature rather than affection. Students find this genuinely useful — most have sensed the strangeness and have had no adult name it for them.

One study is worth teaching to older students because it captures both the danger and the opportunity in a single result.

In 2025, researchers at the University of Zurich covertly deployed AI-powered bots on a Reddit forum devoted to changing people's minds. On that forum, humans change one another's minds at a baseline rate of about 3%. The generic bots achieved 17%; personalised bots, which tailored messages using details from users' profiles, achieved 18%. Across four months, nobody noticed.

The ethics of the deception are indefensible and worth discussing with students on their own terms. But the neuroscientist David Eagleman drew out a more interesting finding: the bots did not succeed by hacking people's brains or feeding disinformation. "They made better arguments. The bots presented their points calmly, rationally, and persuasively." Users did not change their minds because they were fooled — they recognised that their views might need updating in light of a better argument.

Chatfield's conclusion is the note to end this module on. So long as the purpose of automation is to elevate rather than displace human skill, it can feed a culture of excellence. He offers chess as the analogy: superhuman AI did not destroy interest in the game. It made leading human players stronger, helped legions of others learn faster, and deepened appreciation of top-level play. That is the version of AI literacy worth teaching for.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: teach verification before you teach prompting
practitioner.text: Most AI literacy teaching begins with prompting, because it produces impressive results quickly. Reverse the order. A student who can prompt well but not verify is more dangerous to their own learning than a student who cannot prompt at all — they will produce confident, fluent, wrong work at speed and believe it. Teach the four-step verification routine first, run "catch the hallucination" before anything else, and only then teach them to get better output. Scepticism first, capability second.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Plan and run one of the three activities with a real class. Before you do, decide which of Mollick's seven roles you want students to experience and design the task accordingly. Afterwards, record honestly: what did students already know, what surprised them, and what misconception did they hold about these tools that you had not anticipated?

takeaways: If AI literacy is only available through a computer science pathway it will reach the students who need it least
More than 75% of US K-12 schools offer no computer science curriculum; requiring programming increases AI inequality
Under 13: teacher-facilitated only, no independent accounts. 13+: expanded use with explicit instruction

opts: Improve rigour and outcomes
Inevitably increase AI inequality among young learners
