education.title: Equity, Safety and Student Data
education.summary: Protecting the children in your care
objectives: Understand algorithmic discrimination and how it appears in education specifically
Recognise how adaptive systems can widen rather than close achievement gaps
Apply the four foundations of trustworthy AI in education
Protect student data in practical, everyday classroom terms
Address the access gap so AI does not become another advantage for the advantaged
Know what to check before any tool touches a child

sections.html:
The US Department of Education sets out three reasons to address AI in education now, and only the first is optimistic.

  1. AI may enable educational priorities to be achieved better, at scale, and at lower cost — improving adaptivity, supporting teachers, and allowing resources to be customised to local needs.
  2. System-level risks are already visible. Students may become subject to greater surveillance. Algorithmic bias is demonstrable. Some AI is infrastructural and invisible, creating problems of transparency and trust. AI often arrives "with the aura of magic," while educators and procurement policies properly require evidence of efficacy.
  3. The scale of unintended consequences. When instructional decisions are automated at scale, unwanted effects propagate to every student at once.

On the anxiety many teachers feel, the report is worth quoting for reassurance: "the Department firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers." That position is consistent across every serious source in this programme.

The report defines the central risk precisely: the risk of scaling pattern detectors and automations that result in "algorithmic discrimination" — systematic unfairness in the learning opportunities or resources recommended to some populations of students.

Its examples are concrete and worth carrying with you:

  • A voice recognition system that does not work as well with regional dialects — penalising students for how they speak.
  • An exam monitoring system that unfairly identifies some groups of students for disciplinary action — the detection problem of Module 6, in a different form.
  • An AI-enabled teacher hiring system assumed to be more objective than human résumé screening, which, if built on poor-quality historical data, "might de-prioritize candidates who could bring both diversity and talent to a school's teaching workforce."

The common structure is important to grasp because it lets you spot new instances: the system learns what happened before and reproduces it, while wearing the appearance of neutrality. A human who under-serves a group can be challenged. A system that does so at scale, with an interface that looks objective, is far harder to argue with — and that difficulty is itself the harm.

sections.h: The warning every teacher should memorise
sections.html:
How adaptive learning can widen the gap it was bought to close

The Department's specific caution: "if AI adapts by speeding curricular pace for some students and by slowing the pace for other students (based on incomplete data, poor theories, or biased assumptions about learning), achievement gaps could widen."

Follow the mechanism, because it is not obvious and it is entirely plausible. A student arrives with weaker prior attainment — often for reasons of poverty, language, attendance or disrupted schooling rather than capability. The adaptive system detects lower performance and slows the pace, offering easier content. The student receives less curriculum than their peers. The gap widens. The system reports success, because the student is now answering more questions correctly.

This is the same trap as the differentiation trap in Module 4 — differentiating the demand instead of the support — but automated, invisible, and applied to every child simultaneously. It is the single most serious risk in this programme, precisely because it looks like personalisation working.

What to check with any adaptive system:

  • Does it slow the pace or increase the support? These are not the same and only one is defensible.
  • Can a student ever be permanently routed onto a lower track by early performance?
  • Can the teacher see and override the routing?
  • Over a term, has the content coverage of the lowest quartile fallen behind the rest?

That last question is the one to actually run. If nobody in your school can answer it, the system is not being monitored.

The Department's framework gives you a checklist that applies to any tool:

  1. Centre people — educators and learners. Humans remain in the loop; teachers stay at the helm of major instructional decisions.
  2. Advance equity. Ask who benefits and who is disadvantaged, before adoption rather than after.
  3. Ensure safety, ethics and effectiveness. Demand evidence of efficacy. "AI often arrives in new applications with the aura of magic" — that aura is not evidence.
  4. Promote transparency. Students, teachers and families should know when AI is being used and what it does. Invisible, infrastructural AI is the hardest to hold accountable.

Alongside these sit the Department's key recommendations most relevant to a classroom teacher: human in the loop; AI models aligned to a vision for learning; and AI that is inspectable, explainable and overridable.

Stated concretely, because policy documents rarely are:

  • Never enter identifiable student information into a general public AI tool. Names, examination numbers, dates of birth, addresses, medical information, family circumstances, safeguarding detail, disability status, photographs. Describe generically instead.
  • Assume anything you type may be retained and may be used to improve the service. Free consumer tools frequently permit this by default.
  • Uploading a class list, a mark sheet or a set of scripts is a data transfer to a third party in another country. Treat it with the seriousness you would treat handing a stranger a folder of student records — because that is the accurate analogy.
  • Age limits are legal thresholds, not suggestions. Most major tools require users to be 13 or older. A teacher who creates accounts for younger children has assumed a liability the school did not agree to.
  • Photographs and voice are personal data. Uploading a child's image or recording to a tool requires far more care than uploading text, and generally consent.
  • Prefer school-managed environments. The reason Brisbane and Broward deployed within their own institutional tenancy rather than telling staff to use public tools is precisely this — the data stays inside a governed boundary.

Deeper dive: the generic-description habit

Almost every legitimate classroom use survives anonymisation with no loss of quality. "Draft a supportive letter to the parent of a Grade 8 student whose attendance has dropped from 95% to 60% since January, where the family situation is difficult" produces exactly the same quality of letter as the version with the child's name in it. Building this habit costs nothing and eliminates the majority of data risk in teaching. Make it automatic.

There is a version of AI in education that makes inequality worse, and it is the default version. It runs on a personal device, a data connection and a paid subscription; it performs best in English; and it assumes a home environment where a parent can help.

The systematic review by Ikram and colleagues, published in Frontiers in Education in 2026, flags this at national scale: while research is broadening beyond China, the United States and Europe into wider Asia, the rapid expansion of AI combined with persistent concerns about educational standards in developing countries may create additional institutional pressures on effectiveness. Adoption pressure is arriving faster than capacity.

Practical mitigations available to an individual school:

  • Keep AI on the teacher's side by default. As Module 4 argued, a teacher with a phone can bring differentiated printed resources to a class where no student owns a device. Every student benefits equally.
  • Never set homework that requires AI access. This converts a home advantage directly into a grade.
  • If students use AI, do it in school on shared devices in supervised time, so access is equal.
  • Test regional-language performance before relying on it. Model quality in Nepali and other regional languages is materially weaker than in English. Verify on your own material rather than a demonstration.
  • Teach AI literacy in ordinary subject lessons, not as an optional club or an elective, so it reaches everyone.

Before any AI tool is used with students in your school, answer these eight questions in writing. It takes an hour and it is the highest-value hour in this module.

  1. What is the minimum age, and do all our users meet it?
  2. What student data does it collect, where is it stored, and does it leave the country?
  3. Is our data used to train the vendor's models? (Frequently permitted by default.)
  4. What evidence of educational efficacy exists, from someone other than the vendor?
  5. Can a teacher see what it recommended and why, and override it?
  6. Whose curriculum is its content aligned to?
  7. How would we detect it performing worse for one group of students than another?
  8. Who at this school is accountable for it, and how do we switch it off?

A vendor unwilling to answer questions 2, 3 and 5 in writing should be declined regardless of how impressive the demonstration was. Question 7 is the one nobody asks and the one that catches algorithmic discrimination before it compounds.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: run the coverage check
practitioner.text: Once a term, if your school uses any adaptive learning system, ask for one number: how much curriculum content the lowest-attaining quartile has covered compared with the highest. If the gap is growing, the system is slowing pace rather than increasing support, and it is widening the gap it was purchased to close. If nobody can produce the number, the system is not being monitored — which is itself the finding, and one worth putting in writing to your leadership.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Complete the eight-question pre-adoption checklist for one AI tool already in use in your school or one you are considering. Identify which questions you cannot currently answer. Then audit your own recent practice honestly: have you entered any identifiable student information into a public AI tool? Write the generic-description version of the three prompts you use most often.

takeaways: Algorithmic discrimination reproduces past patterns while wearing the appearance of neutrality
Adaptive systems that slow pace rather than increase support can widen the gaps they were bought to close
Ask the coverage question: has the lowest quartile fallen behind in content covered this term?
The four foundations: centre people, advance equity, ensure safety and efficacy, promote transparency
Never enter identifiable student data into a public tool; generic description costs nothing and works as well
Age limits are legal thresholds; uploading class data is a cross-border data transfer
Never set homework requiring AI access — it converts home advantage directly into a grade

opts: Reduce teacher workload
Improve outcomes for all students
Violate copyright law
Cause achievement gaps to widen
quiz.fb: The lower-attaining student receives less curriculum, the gap grows, and the system reports success because accuracy rose. It looks like personalisation working.

quiz.q: 'Algorithmic discrimination' in education refers to:
opts: Systematic unfairness in learning opportunities or resources recommended to some populations of students
Unequal internet speeds between schools
Teachers being replaced by software
Students refusing to use AI tools
quiz.fb: The system learns what happened before and reproduces it while wearing the appearance of neutrality — which makes it far harder to challenge than a human decision.

quiz.q: A teacher wants AI help drafting a letter about a specific student's attendance. Best practice is to:
opts: Avoid AI for all parent communication
Describe the situation generically without identifiable information, then personalise afterwards
Include full details for a better letter
Ask the student to write it
quiz.fb: Almost every legitimate classroom use survives anonymisation with no loss of quality. Make the habit automatic.

quiz.q: Setting homework that requires students to use an AI tool at home is problematic because:
opts: It takes too long to mark
AI works better at school
It converts a home advantage in devices, connectivity and subscriptions directly into a grade
Parents may complain
quiz.fb: If students are to use AI, do it in supervised school time on shared devices so that access is equal.

quiz.q: Which pre-adoption question most directly guards against algorithmic discrimination?
opts: Does it have a mobile app?
What is the annual licence cost?
How many schools use it?
How would we detect it performing worse for one group of students than another?
quiz.fb: It is the question nobody asks, and the one that catches discrimination before it compounds across a whole cohort.

quiz.q: On the question of whether AI will replace teachers, the US Department of Education's position is that it:
opts: Firmly rejects the idea that AI could replace teachers
Has not taken a position
Expects gradual replacement in administrative roles
Recommends reducing teacher numbers by 20%
quiz.fb: This position is consistent across every serious source in this programme.

education.title: What Has Actually Worked: Global Case Studies
education.summary: Real systems, measured results, and what transfers
objectives: Examine three documented school-system AI programmes and their measured outcomes
Understand the implementation approaches that produced those results
Learn from higher education and edtech examples beyond K-12
Distinguish evidence from vendor narrative
Identify what transfers to a resource-constrained context and what does not
Extract the common pattern across every successful programme

sections.html:
Scale. 146 schools, 13,000 staff, 20,000 Microsoft 365 Copilot licences — one of the largest educational deployments in the world.

Approach. An explicitly ethics-led programme. Guided by the Rome Call for AI Ethics framework, staff completed mandatory ethics training before receiving their tool licences — a sequencing decision worth pausing on, since almost every organisation does the reverse. The system also conducted a "digital renovation": cleaning data, establishing robust system permissions and retiring legacy systems to prepare the digital ecosystem before deployment.

Delivery was organised through four workstreams:

  • AI Foundations — infrastructure, data cleanup, permissions, security
  • AI Enablers — change management with school personnel and tailored training
  • Evaluation, Monitoring and Reporting — governance, quality assurance, impact measurement, user feedback
  • Creative AI Lab — ideation and prototyping of purpose-built tools with human oversight, supported by an ideation agent called "Sparky," giving schools a shared space to propose, refine and scale promising use cases

Academic integrity was handled through a maturity matrix clarifying when AI is prohibited, when staff may use it for planning only, when for writing assistance, and when for feedback — the model adapted for classroom use in Module 6.

Measured outcomes. A reduction of up to nine hours per week in administrative workload for teachers. Student academic results improved by 10–30%. A 275% increase in student agency for students using AI for learning, as measured by the University of Melbourne's New Metrics Success project, which focuses on student confidence and reduced stress during assessments. Educators reported improved work–life balance and more time to personalise learning.

Read these numbers carefully

These are strong results from a well-resourced system, self-reported through a vendor-sponsored study. The 10–30% range is wide, and neither a control group nor an isolation of AI's contribution from the concurrent "digital renovation," ethics training and change programme is available. Treat this as evidence that a serious, well-sequenced programme can produce meaningful gains — not as a forecast of what a licence purchase will deliver. That distinction is the difference between learning from a case study and being sold one.

sections.h: Case 2 — Broward County Public Schools, United States
sections.html:
Scale. Over 20,000 Copilot licences, one of the largest US districts to embrace generative AI at scale.

Approach. Board-level mandate — "Broward powered by AI" — explicitly tying AI to core academic goals (English language arts, algebra and science proficiency, college and career readiness) and to operational efficiency including energy optimisation and overtime reduction. Delivery mechanisms:

  • AI ambassadors on every campus — educators who lead professional learning, support peers and act as liaison between district leadership and schools
  • Monthly communities of practice to share what works
  • Mandatory AI training for principals and assistant principals, with micro-credentialing aligned to ISTE and state standards
  • Vendor and resource audits twice a year, with disciplined procurement to prevent shadow AI
  • A school-based AI liaison to mitigate the implementation dip and sustain adoption
  • Students in AI Academies engaged to vet tools before district-wide student adoption — students as evaluators, not only end users

Measured outcomes. 75% of teachers and administrators actively use the tool, reporting an average saving of over two hours per week on lesson planning and administration. A partnership with Willow for energy and HVAC optimisation reduced district-wide energy costs by 12% in the first year. Early classroom pilots showed increased engagement and improved writing outcomes in Grades 8–12, with targeted support ensuring multilingual learners and students with disabilities benefited.

The honest part. IDC records that Broward's journey "has not been without challenges" — the district prioritised myth-busting, supported reluctant adopters, and built feedback cycles to improve implementation. Note also that the energy saving has nothing to do with teaching. Operational AI wins are often easier, faster and more measurable than instructional ones, which is a legitimate strategy and worth naming honestly rather than presenting energy savings as an educational result.

Approach. Deliberately the slowest of the three — a "go slow to go fast" programme that first established AI-ready data and strengthened cybersecurity before introducing tools to educators. Privacy-by-design vendor vetting. A broad educational technology committee including teachers, administrators, parents and district leadership co-designing direction. A dedicated pedagogical help desk. Classroom exemplars and monitored channels for educators to share problems. Incremental annual device refresh cycles rather than a single large purchase.

Outcome. An improved security posture and readiness to scale, with adoption following trust rather than preceding it.

Why this case matters most for a Nepali school. Brisbane and Broward are large, well-funded systems whose approaches are not directly replicable. Coquitlam's core insight is: sequence foundations before tools, involve parents from the start, and accept slower adoption in exchange for durable trust. That is available to any school at any budget, and it is the case study to study if you are starting from a standing start.

sections.h: Beyond schools — higher education and operations
sections.html:
• Georgia State University (United States). Adopted AI-driven tools analysing enrolment trends and student progress to forecast course demand, optimise faculty assignment and schedule classroom space — addressing overcrowded classes, underused facilities and students unable to enrol in courses they need. An institutional rather than instructional application, and among the most immediately transferable to a Nepali college.
  • City St George's, University of London, with Sage. The "cognitive co-pilot" described in Module 7 — Socratic tutoring anchored to a curated knowledge base, with progress tracking and a mastery gate. Tested with 12 students across medicine, biomedical science, international politics, financial economics, speech and language therapy, and mathematics, who rated it 7.6 out of 10. A faculty workshop found alignment between students and instructors on AI's potential as an explainer, alongside shared concerns about over-reliance, accuracy and trust. Notably, a majority of students were already using tools like ChatGPT to digest what they perceived as poorly designed or overwhelming course materials — effectively creating their own resources.
  • The Wharton School. Ethan Mollick's embedding of AI across entrepreneurship courses through seven distinct personas, with student teams submitting query logs and reflections alongside final business plans (Modules 7 and 8).
  • Intelligent tutoring systems. The oldest documented category, descending from rule-based systems of the 1970s and grounded in cognitive learning theory. Genuine evidence of effectiveness exists in well-structured domains such as mathematics.

That finding about students building their own materials from poor course resources deserves attention from every teacher reading this. Students are not only using AI to avoid work. A substantial part of the usage is remedial — compensating for teaching materials that did not work. That is uncomfortable, and it is also actionable.

sections.h: What transfers, and what does not
sections.html:
Does not transfer directly: 20,000 enterprise licences; dedicated data engineering teams; district-wide device refresh programmes; partnerships with global technology firms; a full-time pedagogical help desk.

Transfers completely, at no or minimal cost:

  • Ethics and training before tools. Brisbane's sequencing is free to copy and is the single most replicable decision in all three cases.
  • The AI maturity matrix. Costs one page and resolves most integrity ambiguity.
  • Champion networks. Two or three enthusiastic teachers as ambassadors, with monthly sharing. Broward's most effective mechanism and effectively free.
  • Including parents in the committee. Coquitlam's approach; costs nothing and prevents the trust problem that otherwise arrives later.
  • Communities of practice and lunch-and-learns. Brisbane turned staff success stories into momentum this way.
  • Measuring and communicating both wins and failures. IDC's recommendation is explicit — communicate the key learnings and areas for improvement, not only the successes, to earn and sustain trust.
  • Feedback loops every five weeks. IDC's specific cadence recommendation, requiring nothing but discipline.

sections.h: The pattern across every successful programme
sections.html:
Strip away scale and budget and the same five elements appear in all three systems:

  1. A clear educational purpose stated first. IDC's test is the sharpest formulation in the whole literature: "Prioritize student outcomes above all else. If you can't answer 'How will this support improved student learning and well-being?', deprioritize it."
  2. Foundations before tools — data, permissions, security, ethics training.
  3. Teacher-led adoption through ambassadors and communities of practice, not mandate alone.
  4. Explicit guardrails — maturity matrices, vetted tools, transparent communication with families.
  5. Measurement and honest communication, including of what failed.

None of the five is a technology decision. All five are available to a school with no budget. That is the finding to take from this module — and it is why Module 11 is about leadership rather than software.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: separate the operational win from the instructional claim
practitioner.text: Broward's 12% energy reduction is real, measurable and has nothing whatsoever to do with teaching. When you make the case for AI in your own institution, keep these categories separate. Operational wins — scheduling, enrolment forecasting, energy, administration — are faster, cheaper and far easier to evidence, and they are a perfectly legitimate place to start. But do not let them be presented as evidence that learning improved. Leaders who blur the two lose credibility precisely when they need it to fund the harder instructional work.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Choose the two mechanisms from the "transfers completely" list that your school could adopt this term. For each, write who would own it, what the first step is, and what you would measure after five weeks. Then apply IDC's test to every AI use currently proposed or running in your institution: can you answer "How will this support improved student learning and well-being?" Deprioritise anything that fails.

education.title: Leading AI Adoption in Your School or College
education.summary: The six characteristics of institutions that got this right
objectives: Apply the six foundational characteristics of advanced school AI strategies
Build guardrails and a governance approach proportionate to your institution
Establish champion networks and communities of practice
Communicate with parents and families in a way that builds trust
Design professional learning that actually changes practice
Avoid pilot purgatory and move to sustained adoption

sections.html:
IDC's analysis of advanced AI strategies across K-12 systems worldwide identifies six foundational characteristics common to institutions that have moved beyond pilots to results:

  1. Functional area focus — AI tied to specific, named academic and operational goals rather than adopted in general
  2. Guardrails — governance frameworks and usage guidelines for staff, students, and families
  3. Learning communities — open groups and channels for sharing practice and lessons learned
  4. Change management and training — continuous, role-specific professional learning that meets people where they are
  5. Strategic partnerships — external expertise from companies, employers and universities
  6. Leadership and champion networks — executive ownership combined with grassroots, educator-led champions

Note that five of the six are about people. This is the most consistent finding in the entire programme and the one most often ignored in favour of procurement.

Functional area focus means naming what AI is for. IDC's strategic recommendations are worth following closely:

  • Align AI investment with the school's broader strategic goals, and focus where it drives greatest value — faculty burnout and attrition, learning loss and chronic absenteeism, or resource-intensive administrative challenges.
  • Create compelling narratives so the case becomes "Why not?" rather than "Why?"
  • Adopt a flexible, iterative approach allowing quick pivots — and specifically avoid rigid plans that lock the school into strict three-to-five-year roadmaps, while still maintaining a long-term vision.
  • Democratise access so that all students, faculty and staff have access regardless of background or subject area.

Guardrails for a school of any size need only three documents:

  1. A one-page acceptable use policy covering approved tools, what must never be entered, mandatory verification, teacher responsibility, disclosure, and blame-free reporting of problems.
  2. The AI maturity matrix (Module 6), printed on assignment sheets.
  3. A register of AI tools in use — including AI features quietly added to software you already own. Most schools cannot currently answer "what AI are we using?", and building the register takes a fortnight and produces the most surprising findings of the exercise.

These two produce most of the adoption, and both are effectively free.

Learning communities. Brisbane implemented cross-functional professional learning communities, lunch-and-learns, and communication channels monitored for rapid support — which "turned staff success stories into momentum." Coquitlam runs a broad committee including teachers, administrators, parents and district leadership, with a pedagogical help desk and shared classroom exemplars.

Champion networks. Broward's model combines executive ownership with school-based AI ambassadors: educators who lead professional learning, support peers and act as liaison to leadership. IDC's phrasing is precise — the district "reinforced top-down direction with bottom-up credibility." Broward extended this to students, engaging those in AI Academies to vet tools before wider student adoption.

For a single school starting now:

  • Identify two or three genuinely interested teachers — not the most senior, the most curious.
  • Give them time, not titles. An hour a fortnight of protected time is worth more than a designation.
  • Run a monthly 30-minute sharing session: two teachers, one thing that worked, one that did not.
  • Keep a shared prompt library the whole staff can add to. This becomes the school's most valuable AI asset within a term.

Broward's approach: mandatory AI training for principals and assistant principals, micro-credentialing aligned to ISTE and state standards, tiered programming combining internally-curated and vendor-led sessions, embedded coaching, and a school-based liaison to mitigate the implementation dip.

That phrase — the implementation dip — names the thing that kills most school initiatives. Performance falls before it rises, because people are doing something unfamiliar badly. Teachers who are not warned about this conclude the tool does not work and stop. Teachers who are warned persist. Telling staff explicitly that the first three weeks will feel slower is one of the highest-value sentences a school leader can say.

Design principles that matter more than content:

  • Role-specific. A primary teacher, a science head and a school accountant need different things.
  • On real work. Bring next week's actual lesson. Abstract training does not transfer.
  • Address the fear directly. IDC notes a direct and intentional effort in leading systems to dispel myths and address ethical concerns among all stakeholders, particularly teachers and parents. Teachers worry about being replaced; the honest answer — that this is not what the evidence shows, and that the goal is returning them to relationship-building work — must be said aloud rather than assumed.
  • Continuous, not one-off. A single INSET day produces enthusiasm and no change.

IDC's recommendation is specific and frequently ignored: educate parent communities not only about the risks and guardrails but also about the benefits and pedagogical rationale — helping families understand how AI amplifies existing educational strategies and can assist them directly, for example by translating school content for parents who do not read the language of instruction or communicating more effectively with administrators.

That last point is the one that changes the conversation in a Nepali context. A parent who has been told AI is a cheating risk hears a threat. A parent who receives their child's school newsletter in Nepali for the first time because of it has experienced a benefit. Lead with what it does for them.

A workable parent communication, one page, four sections:

  1. What we are doing and why — teachers using AI to plan and differentiate so they have more time with your child.
  2. What this means for your child's work — every assignment states what AI use is permitted; we teach them to use it honestly.
  3. How we protect your child — no personal data entered into these tools; age limits observed; tools vetted before use.
  4. What it does for you — communications available in Nepali; help understanding school documents; a named person to ask.

IDC's warning is direct: "Don't get stuck in an infinite loop of pilots; develop a clear strategy to move from the pilot phase to full-scale implementation."

The mechanisms that prevent it:

  • Measure from the start. Establish clear metrics and collect data every five weeks to enable continuous improvement — IDC's specific cadence.
  • Define in advance what would make you stop. A pilot without a stopping condition cannot fail, and therefore cannot succeed.
  • Name who decides to scale, before the pilot begins.
  • Communicate wins and learnings. IDC: continuously share compelling quantitative and qualitative data, and communicate "both the wins and the key learnings and areas for improvement to earn and sustain trust." A school that only reports successes is not believed for long.
  • Allocate adequate resources — budget, time and ongoing support to maintain and scale, not only to launch.

sections.h: A 90-day plan for a school starting now
sections.html:
Days 1–30: understand and decide.

  • Build the register of AI already in use, including features in existing software
  • Survey staff anonymously: who is already using what, and for what
  • Name the two or three problems AI is meant to address — most likely teacher workload, differentiation and integrity
  • Identify two or three teacher champions and protect an hour a fortnight for them

Days 31–60: guardrails and first practice.

  • Issue the one-page acceptable use policy
  • Adopt the AI maturity matrix and require the level on every assignment sheet
  • Run the first professional learning session on real work — workload and planning first, because it earns goodwill
  • Send the parent communication
  • Start the monthly sharing session

Days 61–90: measure and extend.

  • Collect the first five-week feedback
  • Report honestly to staff and governors — including what has not worked
  • Choose one instructional application to pilot properly, with a stopping condition and a named decision-maker
  • Review the register and retire anything unused

Nothing in this plan requires a budget, a vendor or a technical specialist.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: warn them about the dip
practitioner.text: Before any professional learning session, say this plainly: "For the first two or three weeks this will feel slower than doing it your usual way. That is normal and it is not evidence that it does not work. Come back to me in week four." Broward built an entire liaison role to mitigate the implementation dip; you can capture most of the benefit with one honest sentence. Teachers who are warned persist through it. Teachers who are not warned conclude the tool is useless and quietly stop — and you will never find out why adoption failed.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Write your school's one-page acceptable use policy and begin the register of AI tools already in use — ask every department head directly, including about AI features in software you already own. Then draft the four-section parent communication, leading with what AI does for families rather than with the risks. Identify your two or three champions by name and decide what protected time you can actually give them.

takeaways: Five of IDC's six foundational characteristics are about people, not technology
Avoid rigid three-to-five-year roadmaps; stay iterative while holding a long-term vision
Guardrails need only three documents: acceptable use policy, maturity matrix, and a register of tools in use
Champion networks and communities of practice produce most adoption and are effectively free
Warn staff explicitly about the implementation dip — performance falls before it rises
Lead the parent conversation with benefits to families, not with risks
Collect feedback every five weeks; define stopping conditions; report failures as well as wins

opts: None
Three of six
One of six

opts: Every two years

quiz.fb: Frequent feedback loops enable continuous improvement and are one of the main mechanisms preventing pilot purgatory.

opts: Because a school that only reports successes is not believed for long, and trust is what sustains adoption

quiz.fb: IDC recommends communicating both the wins and the key learnings and areas for improvement to earn and sustain trust.

education.title: Your Implementation Plan
education.summary: Bringing it together into something you will actually do
objectives: Synthesise the programme into a term-by-term plan for your own practice
Understand what the evidence collectively supports and what it does not
Apply the considerations specific to schools in Nepal and comparable systems
Build the habits that sustain practice beyond the first enthusiasm
Prepare to lead colleagues rather than only change your own teaching
Complete your capstone implementation plan

sections.html:
Six independent sources have informed this programme, and their conclusions converge more than one might expect:

  • IDC and Microsoft, from systems that have actually done this: the determinants of success are leadership, guardrails, training and champion networks — not software. Five of six foundational characteristics concern people.
  • Chatfield and Sage: the danger is that AI hollows out the very skills needed to navigate an AI age. Innovation must be grounded in how humans actually learn. Surveillance fails; assessment redesign is the real work.
  • The US Department of Education: humans in the loop; systems that are inspectable, explainable and overridable; and a firm rejection of the idea that AI could replace teachers.
  • The AI4Education working group: AI literacy is an equity issue, and gating it behind computer science guarantees it reaches the wrong students.
  • The systematic review in Frontiers in Education: professional development must go beyond technical proficiency to pedagogical integration and digital literacy — and adoption pressure in developing countries may outrun institutional capacity.
  • MGT's analysis: the operational applications — scheduling, enrolment forecasting, resource allocation — are real, immediate and separate from instructional claims.

The common thread: this is a teaching and leadership problem that happens to involve technology. Almost every constraint identified is one a teacher or a school can act on without technical capability or significant budget.

sections.h: A term-by-term plan for your own practice
sections.html:
Term 1 — reclaim time and remove ambiguity.

  • Build your personal prompt library, starting with the misconception hunt and worked examples (Module 3)
  • Batch your planning into one weekly session
  • Put an AI level on every assignment sheet (Module 6)
  • Have the honest conversation with your classes
  • Decide where the reclaimed time goes, and defend it

Term 2 — improve what students receive.

  • Differentiate one unit properly across four scaffolded versions, holding the objective constant (Module 4)
  • Convert one rubric into student-facing self-check questions (Module 5)
  • Run one class-level pattern analysis on a set of responses and re-teach accordingly
  • Add a two-minute oral defence to one assessment (Module 7)
  • Run one AI literacy activity with a class (Module 8)

Term 3 — redesign and extend.

  • Convert one major assessment to staged submission with process evidence
  • Introduce one AI-integrated task where using AI well is the assessed skill
  • Complete the pre-adoption checklist for any tool your school uses with students (Module 9)
  • Share what worked and what did not with two colleagues

sections.h: Considerations for Nepal and comparable systems
sections.html:
• Large classes make differentiation impossible by hand and possible with AI. This is the strongest single argument for adoption in this context, and it costs nothing beyond a teacher's phone.
  • Keep AI on the teacher's side. Printed differentiated sheets, board work and oral question banks deliver the benefit into classrooms where no student owns a device — and deliver it equally.
  • Test Nepali-language output before relying on it. Performance in Nepali and other regional languages is materially weaker than in English. Have a fluent colleague check anything going to parents.
  • Second-language writing makes detection tools actively dangerous here. The population most likely to be wrongly flagged is the majority of your students. This is a policy position worth defending in your staffroom.
  • Curriculum alignment must be checked every time. Default output aligns to American or British curricula. Confidently misaligned content is worse than no content.
  • Adoption pressure may outrun capacity. The Frontiers review's warning applies directly: be willing to go slower than the marketing suggests, on Coquitlam's model.
  • There is a genuine advantage. Schools without large legacy technology investments have nothing to unwind. A teacher with a phone and a photocopier can start on Monday, which is not true of institutions with entrenched systems to migrate.

sections.h: The habits that sustain the practice
sections.html:
• Apply the two-question test to every proposed use: whose cognitive effort is this, and is that effort the point or overhead?
  • Verify before you duplicate. Never photocopy a generated resource you have not read end to end.
  • Put the pedagogy in the prompt. Name worked examples, interleaving, retrieval. Your expertise is what makes the tool worth using.
  • Never enter identifiable student data. Make generic description automatic.
  • Keep the prompt library growing. It compounds; nothing else in this programme does.
  • Keep one honest weekly note of what worked and what it got wrong. After a term you have evidence rather than impressions.
  • Protect the human parts. Discussion, disagreement, relationship, the two minutes with the student who needs them. These are the point, and they are what the reclaimed time is for.

sections.h: What to say when colleagues ask
sections.html:
You will be asked, and probably soon. Four positions worth holding clearly:

  1. "It will replace us." No serious source in the literature supports this, and the US Department of Education firmly rejects it. What the evidence shows is administrative burden reduced and time returned to teaching.
  2. "Students will cheat." They already do, detection does not work and discriminates against second-language writers, and the answer is assessment design plus explicit expectations — not surveillance.
  3. "We cannot afford it." Everything in Modules 3 through 8 works with one teacher, one phone and a photocopier. The expensive version is optional.
  4. "It is not accurate." Correct, and that is why teacher verification is non-negotiable and why it is a drafting tool rather than an authority. That limitation is manageable; it is not disqualifying.

Chatfield's closing argument is the right note to end on, and it is a demanding one.

So long as the purpose of automation is to elevate rather than displace human skill, it can feed a culture of excellence and engagement. The analogy is chess: superhuman AI did not destroy the game. It made leading players stronger, helped legions of others learn faster and deepened appreciation of the highest-level play. Taken in isolation chess is zero-sum, but as an institution it is enriched by every player who participates and every technology that widens access.

He is equally clear about what excellence now requires of educators: mastering twin domains. On the human side, deep pedagogical empathy for how people actually learn, sensitivity to individual differences, and the capacity to combine psychological safety with intellectual challenge. On the machine side, an informed strategic understanding of what AI can and cannot do, skill in prompt design, the evaluation of outputs and awareness of biases and limitations.

Intellectual excellence in an AI age is not about competing with machines on their terms. It is about developing the distinctly human capabilities they can enhance rather than replace: framing problems critically and creatively, synthesising across domains, bringing ethical judgement to bear, and collaborating and communicating richly.

Those are the things you were always teaching. The tools have changed. The job has not.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: pick one thing and start it this week
practitioner.text: The most common outcome of a course like this is a thoughtful plan that never begins, because it waits for a training day that never gets scheduled. Avoid that. Choose one item from Term 1 and start it before this week ends — the misconception prompt for your hardest upcoming lesson is usually the right choice, because it takes ten minutes, it visibly improves the lesson, and success with it makes everything else in the programme credible to you.

activity.title: Capstone: your implementation plan
activity.text: Write a plan of no more than four pages for your own practice and, if you lead others, your institution: (1) the three problems you are using AI to address, named specifically; (2) your term-by-term plan with dates; (3) your AI maturity matrix as it will appear on assignment sheets; (4) your one-page acceptable use policy and parent communication if you lead a school; (5) what you will measure at five weeks and what would make you stop; and (6) what you will do with the time you reclaim. Then give it to one colleague and ask them to hold you to it.

Term 1 reclaim time and remove ambiguity; Term 2 improve what students receive; Term 3 redesign assessment
Large classes make differentiation impossible by hand and possible with AI — the strongest local argument
Detection tools are actively dangerous where most students write in a second language
Schools without legacy technology investment have nothing to unwind and can start on Monday
Protect the human parts — discussion, disagreement, relationship — because that is what the time is for

opts: Detection software administration
Vendor negotiation
Twin domains — pedagogical empathy for how people learn, and informed strategic understanding of what AI can and cannot do

quiz.fb: The art lies in linking the two productively: using AI for routine work while reserving human attention for complex interpersonal work.

management.title: The Executive's Mental Model of AI
management.summary: What leaders actually need to understand — and what they can safely ignore
objectives: Distinguish the four kinds of AI a manager will encounter, and know which problems each solves
Understand what AI can and cannot do, in terms you can defend in a management meeting
Recognise the three eras of business AI and where your organisation currently sits
Speak precisely enough to lead vendor conversations and challenge weak proposals
Understand why AI projects behave more like research than like IT projects

sections.h: What this programme is, and who it is for
sections.html:
This programme is written for managers, senior management teams and executives — people who must decide about AI rather than build it. It assumes no technical background and requires none.

You will not learn to write code or train a model. You will learn to set strategy, allocate budget, assign decision rights, select vendors, govern risk, lead your people through change, and judge whether what you are being sold is worth buying. Every module ends with something you can apply in your own organisation, and the programme concludes with a capstone AI strategy you can take to your board or management committee.

The pressure to act is real. Capgemini Research Institute's 2026 survey of 500 CXOs, including 100 CEOs, found that more than half already use AI to support or inform strategic decision-making, with close to another third experimenting — and this is expected to more than double within three years. The question facing most leadership teams is no longer whether to engage, but whether they will do so deliberately or by accident.

sections.h: The four kinds of AI a manager will meet
sections.html:
Vendors use these terms interchangeably. Precision protects your budget.

  • Rule-based automation. Software following logic a person wrote: "if the invoice is over this amount, route it for approval." Reliable, transparent, and it does not learn. Much of what is sold as AI is this.
  • Machine learning (ML). Systems that learn patterns from historical data rather than following written rules. This is what powers demand forecasting, customer churn prediction, credit assessment and fraud detection. It answers questions of the form "how likely is X?"
  • Generative AI. Models that produce new content — text, images, summaries, code. This is the wave that made AI a boardroom topic. It answers "draft this, summarise this, explain this."
  • Agentic AI. Systems that pursue a goal across multiple steps, using tools and adapting as they go, rather than answering a single request. The newest category, the most powerful, and the one requiring the most control.

A practical translation for management: machine learning predicts, generative AI produces, agentic AI acts. Each carries a different cost profile, a different risk profile and a different governance requirement. A proposal that does not say which one it is has not been thought through.

sections.h: The three eras — and where you are
sections.html:
The evolution of AI in business has moved through recognisable phases:

  1. Rule-based systems. Automating routine tasks on predefined logic. Efficient but rigid, requiring constant manual updating.
  2. Predictive analytics and machine learning. Identifying patterns, forecasting trends and automating decisions at scale — though early applications were often siloed, operating in isolation and constrained by data quality.
  3. Enterprise AI. AI as an organisation-wide capability integrated across functions, learning from large datasets and adapting in real time — moving from static insight toward being a decision-making partner.

Most organisations in Nepal and comparable markets sit somewhere between the first and second era, with pockets of the third appearing through purchased software. That is a perfectly reasonable position. The mistake is believing you are further along than you are, which leads to buying era-three solutions that your era-one foundations cannot support.

• Finds patterns in large volumes of data that no human could hold in their head — customer behaviour, demand seasonality, quality defects, risk indicators.
  • Processes language and documents at scale — reading, summarising, extracting, drafting, translating.
  • Handles repetitive cognitive work consistently and without fatigue.
  • Makes expertise more available — putting a reasonable first answer in the hands of someone who would otherwise wait for a specialist.
  • Operates continuously — no shifts, no queue, no closing time.

sections.h: What AI does not do — and why executives get this wrong
sections.html:
• It does not understand your business. It has no model of your strategy, your customers or your constraints beyond what is in its data or what you tell it.
  • It is not reliably factual. Generative systems can produce confident, well-written statements that are simply wrong. This is the single most important limitation for a manager to internalise.
  • It is not objective. A system trained on your historical decisions will reproduce your historical preferences, including ones you would not defend publicly.
  • It does not maintain itself. Conditions change; performance quietly degrades. Deployment is the beginning of an obligation, not the end of a project.
  • It does not take accountability. When something goes wrong, the manager who authorised it answers for it. No regulator, customer or board has ever accepted "the system decided."

The executive translation

Treat AI output the way you would treat work from a capable, fast, tireless analyst who is new to your organisation, occasionally overconfident, and unable to tell you when they are out of their depth. You would not forward that person's work to a customer unread. Apply the same standard, and most AI risk management follows naturally.

sections.h: Why AI projects behave differently from IT projects
sections.html:
This is the insight that most protects a management team from disappointment. The World Economic Forum's AI C-Suite Toolkit puts it directly: AI projects often resemble research and development rather than IT projects. They are less deterministic and more experimental in nature.

The consequences are practical and financial:

  • Outcomes cannot be guaranteed in advance. Getting a system to an acceptable level of performance and robustness can be challenging and unpredictable.
  • Overruns are common. The WEF reports AI projects falling foul of data accessibility, quality and manipulation challenges, overrunning by factors of two to three times in cost and time.
  • Data work dominates. It is not uncommon for 80% of the time needed to create an AI system to be devoted to data cleansing and manipulation.
  • Maintenance is permanent. Models drift as the environment changes, undermining effectiveness unless actively managed.

If you budget and govern an AI initiative as though it were an ERP implementation with a fixed scope and a fixed date, you will be disappointed and your team will be blamed for something structural. Budget it as a portfolio of experiments with staged decision points, and you will be running it correctly.

sections.h: The vocabulary that makes you effective in the room
sections.html:
Six terms worth using precisely:

  • Model — the trained system that produces predictions or output.
  • Training data — the historical examples the model learned from. Ask what it was, and how similar it is to your situation.
  • Hallucination — a confident, fluent, factually wrong output from a generative system.
  • Human in the loop — a person reviews or approves before the output takes effect. Ask who, and whether they have the time and authority to disagree.
  • Drift — gradual degradation of performance as conditions change.
  • Use case — a specific business problem AI is applied to. Insist that proposals name one; "adopting AI" is not a use case.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the three questions that expose a weak proposal
practitioner.text: In any AI proposal meeting, ask these in order: (1) Which specific decision or task does this improve? (2) What does the system do when it is wrong, and who notices? (3) What data does it need, and do we actually have it today? A serious proposal answers all three in plain language within two minutes. A weak one retreats into technology description. You do not need technical knowledge to run this test — only the discipline to keep asking.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: List the three most repetitive, judgement-light tasks your team performs each week, and estimate the hours each consumes. For each, note whether it is fundamentally about predicting something, producing something, or acting across several steps. You have just categorised your first candidate use cases by AI type — and you will use this list again in Module 4.

takeaways: Machine learning predicts, generative AI produces, agentic AI acts — each has a different risk and cost profile
Most organisations sit between the rule-based and predictive eras; overstating your position leads to buying what you cannot support
AI is fast and tireless but not factual, not objective, not self-maintaining and never accountable
AI projects resemble R&D more than IT — they overrun by two to three times when governed as fixed-scope projects
Roughly 80% of the effort in building an AI system is data cleansing and preparation
Insist every proposal names a specific use case, a failure mode, and the data it requires

quiz.fb: Deployment is the beginning of an obligation, not the end of a project. Drift must be actively monitored and managed.

management.title: AI Strategy: Aligning Technology to Business Goals
management.summary: Turning enthusiasm into a defensible plan
objectives: Understand what an AI strategy is and why it must sit inside corporate strategy rather than beside it
Assess your organisation's AI maturity honestly
Understand the relationship between AI strategy, data strategy and change management
Design an AI roadmap and know who must be consulted in building it
Recognise the strategic options AI creates, from incremental efficiency to business-model change
Avoid the most common strategic errors

sections.h: What an AI strategy actually is
sections.html:
An AI strategy is not a list of technologies, a budget line, or a statement that the organisation will "embrace AI." It is a set of choices: which business objectives AI will serve, which problems it will be applied to first, what capability the organisation will build versus buy, what risks it will accept, and how success will be measured.

The World Economic Forum's AI C-Suite Toolkit is direct on the central requirement: an AI strategy must be aligned with the organisation's larger corporate strategy. This sounds obvious and is routinely violated. AI strategies written by technology functions in isolation optimise for technical capability; AI strategies written by business leaders without technical input optimise for things that cannot be built. Neither survives.

AI presents a spectrum of ambition, and choosing where you sit on it is the first strategic decision:

  • Efficiency. Do what you do now, faster and cheaper. Lowest risk, most measurable, and where nearly all organisations should start.
  • Effectiveness. Do what you do now, better — more accurate forecasts, better targeting, earlier problem detection.
  • Experience. Change what it feels like to be your customer or your employee — faster service, personalisation, availability outside working hours.
  • New propositions. Offer something you could not previously offer — a service that was uneconomic at your scale, or a product that requires continuous intelligence.
  • Business model. Redesign the organisation around an AI-optimised workflow, enabling a rethinking of internal economics and organisational design.

The WEF observes that these carry very different risk profiles — reimagining the business as an AI-first organisation is a fundamentally different undertaking from rolling out a customer-facing chatbot, "despite both being relevant AI strategic options." A strategy that does not state which level it is pursuing will drift toward the easiest and disappoint everyone who expected the hardest.

Strategy requires a truthful starting point. A workable four-stage assessment:

  1. Exploring. Interest and discussion. Perhaps unapproved tools in use. No owner, no governance, no measured use case.
  2. Piloting. One or more defined use cases in controlled testing, with named owners and some measurement. Value not yet proven at scale.
  3. Scaling. Proven use cases extended across functions, supported by shared data, reusable components and a governance framework.
  4. Transforming. AI materially changes products, propositions or the operating model. Strategy and AI capability are inseparable.

Assess across five dimensions rather than as a single score: strategy and sponsorship, data foundations, technology, people and skills, and governance. Most organisations discover they are further along on enthusiasm than on data — which is precisely the diagnosis that should shape the roadmap.

Deeper dive: the honest self-assessment problem

Organisations consistently overstate maturity because pilots are visible and foundations are not. A useful corrective: for each dimension, require evidence rather than opinion. "We have good data" becomes "we can produce a joined, reliable customer dataset within four weeks — yes or no?" Written, evidenced assessments circulated to the management team are uncomfortable and immediately clarifying.

sections.h: AI strategy, data strategy and change management
sections.html:
The WEF toolkit treats these as inseparable, and the relationships are worth stating plainly:

  • AI strategy depends on data strategy. AI is fuelled by data. If your data is fragmented across systems with no common identifiers, your AI ambitions are constrained regardless of budget. Data strategy is not a subordinate technical matter — it is a precondition.
  • AI strategy is a change programme. The technology is rarely the hard part. Getting people to use, trust and challenge a new system — and redesigning the work around it — is where initiatives succeed or fail.
  • AI strategy rides on digital transformation. AI typically piggybacks on investments in data platforms, cloud and process engineering. The WEF warns specifically that removing funding from these to pay for a "sexy" new AI initiative "may well prove counterproductive."

A credible AI roadmap has six components:

  1. Business objectives it serves. Stated in the language of your existing strategy — growth, cost, service, risk — not in the language of technology.
  2. Prioritised use cases, sequenced by value and feasibility (Module 4).
  3. Capability build-out. What data, technology, skills and governance must exist for each wave to be possible.
  4. Sequencing across horizons. Foundations and quick wins first; decision support second; customer-facing and transformational last.
  5. Investment and funding model, including ring-fenced capability spend that no single use case can justify alone.
  6. Measures and decision points. What will be true at six, twelve and twenty-four months, and what triggers a stop.

A roadmap designed by too few people fails on adoption; one designed by everyone never gets written. The WEF's guidance points to a defined consultation set:

  • Business function heads — they know which problems are worth solving and which processes will resist change.
  • Technology and data leadership — feasibility, foundations, sequencing.
  • Finance — funding model, and crucially the appetite for uncertainty in returns.
  • Risk, legal and compliance — early, not at approval. Late involvement is the most common source of delay.
  • HR — skills, role redesign, and the employment questions your people are already asking privately.
  • Front-line representatives — the people who will actually use the system, and who know the edge cases.

• Technology-led strategy. Starting with a tool and searching for a problem. Reverse it.
  • Everything at once. A portfolio of twelve simultaneous pilots produces twelve half-finished pilots and no capability.
  • Underfunding foundations. Data and platform work fails every individual business case and makes everything else possible.
  • Ignoring change management. Budgeting for software and not for adoption.
  • No stopping rule. Initiatives that cannot be cancelled consume budget indefinitely.
  • Copying a competitor's strategy. Their data, systems, skills and constraints are not yours.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: write the one-page strategy first
practitioner.text: Before commissioning any detailed planning, write a single page: the three business objectives AI will serve, the three use cases you will start with, the one capability gap you will close, the budget envelope, and what will be measurably different in twelve months. If your management team cannot agree on that page, no amount of detailed planning will rescue the programme — and if they can, the detail follows quickly.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Assess your organisation on the four-stage maturity ladder across all five dimensions — strategy and sponsorship, data, technology, people, governance — and write one sentence of evidence for each rating, not opinion. Identify your weakest dimension. Then draft the one-page strategy described above. Keep both; they form the opening of your capstone.

takeaways: An AI strategy is a set of choices about objectives, priorities, capability and risk — not a technology list
It must sit inside corporate strategy; strategies written in isolation by either business or technology fail
Choose your ambition level deliberately: efficiency, effectiveness, experience, new propositions or business model
Assess maturity across strategy, data, technology, people and governance — with evidence, not opinion
Data strategy is a precondition, and AI strategy is fundamentally a change programme
Do not defund the data and platform investments that AI depends on to pay for AI
Consult business heads, technology, finance, risk, HR and front-line staff early

quiz.q: The World Economic Forum emphasises that an AI strategy must above all be:
opts: Led by the technology function
Aligned with the organisation's larger corporate strategy
Focused on the newest available models
Approved by an external consultant
quiz.fb: Strategies written by technology alone optimise for capability; those written by business alone optimise for the unbuildable. Neither survives.

quiz.q: An organisation redirects funding from its data platform programme to pay for a new AI initiative. The WEF's guidance suggests this is:
opts: Required for AI success
Only a problem in large organisations
Likely counterproductive, since AI typically piggybacks on those very investments
Efficient reallocation of scarce capital
quiz.fb: AI depends on data lakes, cloud and process engineering. Defunding the foundation to buy the application undermines both.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of ambition, from lowest risk to highest?
opts: There is no meaningful difference between them
New propositions → efficiency → business model
Business model → experience → efficiency
Efficiency → effectiveness → experience → new propositions → business model
quiz.fb: Reimagining the business as AI-first is a fundamentally different undertaking from a chatbot rollout, despite both being valid strategic options.

quiz.q: When assessing organisational AI maturity, the most useful discipline is to:
opts: Require documented evidence for each rating rather than opinion
Rate the organisation as a single overall score
Ask each department for a self-rating
Benchmark only against competitors
quiz.fb: Organisations overstate maturity because pilots are visible and foundations are not. 'We have good data' must become a testable claim.

quiz.q: Which is the most common reason a technically successful AI initiative fails to deliver value?
opts: The vendor was too expensive
Change management and adoption were not funded or led
The servers were too slow
The model was not accurate enough
quiz.fb: The technology is rarely the hard part. Getting people to use, trust and challenge the system is where initiatives succeed or fail.

management.title: Decision Rights: Who Owns AI in the Leadership Team
management.summary: The evidence on which executives should hold which decisions
objectives: Understand the empirical relationship between executive decision rights and AI returns
Recognise the distinct value each senior role brings to AI investment decisions
Design a decision-rights allocation for your own leadership team
Understand where the AI or data leader should sit and report
Establish the governance forums an AI programme requires
Avoid the failure modes of siloed ownership

sections.h: The finding that should reshape your leadership discussion
sections.html:
Deloitte's Center for Integrated Research ran a predictive analysis on its Tech Value data, surveying 550 business and technology leaders in April and May 2025, to establish how the degree to which a given executive owns technology decision-making corresponds with AI outcomes. Results were measured against perceived return on technology investment, movement across 46 operational and financial indicators, and reported EBITDA gains.

Their headline conclusion is unambiguous, and it is not about technology:

"AI-driven business outcomes peak when decision rights are distributed among complementary leaders."

In other words, the strongest predictor of AI returns Deloitte found was not the sophistication of the technology, the size of the budget or the calibre of the data science team. It was who sits at the table when investment decisions are made, and how well they work together.

sections.h: What each role contributes — with the evidence
sections.html:
• Chief technology / information officer. Deloitte found CIOs and CTOs still drive most technology decisions, according to 60–80% of respondents. When CTOs shift from no control to full control of technology investment decisions, organisations are more than twice as likely to achieve "advanced" AI automation maturity. The caution: where CTOs are the primary decision-makers, companies often invest less aggressively in new data monetisation initiatives — possibly reflecting constrained budgets or a focus on maximising return from existing assets rather than pursuing growth.
  • Chief financial officer. The most striking single finding. Among organisations where the CFO had no decision-making authority over digital investment, only 18% achieved above-average profitability. Where the CFO had full authority, that figure rose to 42% — more than twice as likely to outperform. Deloitte also notes CFOs tend to forecast AI-driven returns cautiously, but that their confidence in meeting programme milestones grows when they are hands-on.
  • Chief strategy officer. The largest effect in the study. Companies with limited CSO involvement rarely excel across their KPIs. Where CSOs are given substantial authority, organisations could be up to 88 times more likely to achieve high ROI across financial, customer, operational, workforce and purpose-driven metrics. In practice the CSO is called on either to refocus investments that have plateaued, or to clarify the broader strategic value of the transformation.

Deloitte's synthesis: no single role can drive strategic alignment, technical capability growth and profitability on its own. All three are needed to deliver the full set of outcomes organisations are seeking.

sections.h: Translating this to an organisation without a formal C-suite
sections.html:
Most organisations in Nepal and comparable markets do not have a chief strategy officer or a chief technology officer. The finding still applies, because what matters is the lens, not the title. Every AI investment decision needs four perspectives present:

  • Technical feasibility — can this be built and run with what we have? (IT head, or a trusted external adviser)
  • Financial discipline — what does it cost in full, and how will we know it paid? (finance director)
  • Strategic alignment — does this advance where the business is going? (CEO or managing director)
  • Operational reality — will this survive contact with how the work is actually done? (the function head who owns the process)

If your AI decisions are being made by one person with one lens — most commonly the technology lens, or the enthusiasm of whoever attended a conference — Deloitte's evidence suggests you are systematically underperforming what the same investment could deliver.

Beyond decision rights, Deloitte's modelling identified three drivers that predict returns:

  1. Technology strategy innovation maturity — having a deliberate strategy for innovation rather than reactive purchasing.
  2. Automation budget — a higher dedicated budget for automation is associated with greater profitability.
  3. Monetisation strategy investment — deliberate investment in how data and capability generate value, not only in cost reduction.

Note that two of the three are funding decisions and one is a strategy decision. None is a technology decision. This is a recurring theme of the programme and worth internalising early.

sections.h: Where the AI or data leader should sit
sections.html:
Whoever leads AI in your organisation — whether a dedicated appointment or an existing executive with the remit added — three structural questions matter:

  • Reporting line. Deloitte's related research on digital operating models suggests a direct line to the CEO helps organisations capture more value, because digital and AI ambitions succeed when they visibly reinforce the organisation's mission. An AI leader buried three levels inside IT will deliver IT outcomes.
  • Profile. The right leader depends on your maturity. Early-stage organisations usually need a translator — someone credible with both the business and the technology — more than they need a deep technical specialist.
  • Authority. Can this person convene function heads, stop a project, and access the budget? A leader with responsibility and no authority is a coordinator with a title.

sections.h: The governance forums you actually need
sections.html:
Two, in most organisations, plus one document:

  • An AI steering group. Cross-functional — business, finance, technology, risk, HR. Meets monthly. Approves use cases, allocates budget, reviews progress, and stops things. This is where the four lenses meet.
  • Board or executive committee oversight. Quarterly. Receives a standing report on the AI portfolio, value realised, risks and incidents. Approves strategy and risk appetite.
  • A decision-rights table. One page listing every AI-related decision, the accountable role, and the evidence required. Most governance disputes are not disagreements about principle; they are ambiguity about who decides.

Deeper dive: why siloed ownership fails

Deloitte concludes that siloed leadership is unlikely to deliver the versatility, agility or strategic focus needed to achieve enterprise-wide value. The mechanism is straightforward: technology-owned AI optimises for capability and under-invests in adoption; finance-owned AI optimises for cost and under-invests in growth; business-owned AI optimises for one function and creates duplication. Each is individually rational and collectively insufficient.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: check who was in the room
practitioner.text: Take the last three technology or AI investment decisions your organisation made. For each, list who was actually in the room when the decision was taken. If the same one or two people appear every time — and particularly if the finance and strategy lenses were absent — you have found a structural cause of underperformance that costs nothing to fix. Widening the table is free; the returns evidence says it is also the highest-leverage change available.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft the decision-rights table for your organisation. List at least six AI-related decisions — approving a use case, approving spend above a threshold, approving customer-facing deployment, approving use of customer data, stopping a project, accepting a risk finding. For each, name the accountable role and the evidence required. Identify which decisions currently have no clear owner; that gap is your most urgent governance action.

takeaways: Deloitte's survey of 550 leaders found AI outcomes peak when decision rights are distributed among complementary leaders
CFO with full decision authority: 42% achieve above-average profitability, versus 18% with none
Substantial CSO involvement is associated with up to 88x greater likelihood of high ROI across metrics
No single role can deliver strategic alignment, technical capability and profitability alone
Without a formal C-suite, ensure four lenses are present: technical, financial, strategic and operational
The three predictive value drivers are innovation maturity, automation budget and monetisation investment — two funding, one strategy
A direct reporting line to the CEO helps capture more value; responsibility without authority is a title

quiz.q: Deloitte's predictive analysis of 550 leaders found that AI-driven business outcomes peak when:
opts: The CTO holds sole authority over technology decisions
Decisions are delegated entirely to the IT department
Decision rights are distributed among complementary leaders
An external consultant makes the decisions
quiz.fb: Each executive brings a distinct lens — technical capability, financial discipline, strategic alignment. Combined, they drive smarter bets.

quiz.q: In Deloitte's findings, organisations where the CFO had full decision-making authority over digital investment achieved above-average profitability at what rate, compared with those where the CFO had none?
opts: 20% versus 19%
5% versus 50%
There was no measurable difference
42% versus 18%
quiz.fb: More than twice as likely to outperform. Financial discipline in the decision process is strongly associated with financial outcomes.

quiz.q: An organisation with no chief strategy officer should conclude that:
opts: The strategic lens must still be present in every AI investment decision, typically supplied by the CEO or managing director
They should hire a CSO immediately
They cannot succeed with AI
The finding does not apply to them
quiz.fb: What matters is the lens, not the title. Four perspectives must be present: technical, financial, strategic and operational.

quiz.q: Deloitte's research on digital operating models suggests that the AI or digital leader benefits from:
opts: Reporting to an external board
A direct line to the CEO
Reporting deep within the IT function
No formal reporting line
quiz.fb: A direct line to the CEO helps organisations capture more value, because AI ambitions succeed when they visibly reinforce the mission.

quiz.q: Which of Deloitte's three predictive value drivers is a strategy decision rather than a funding decision?
opts: All three are funding decisions
Monetisation strategy investment
Technology strategy innovation maturity
Automation budget
quiz.fb: Two of the three drivers are funding decisions and one is a strategy decision. None is a technology decision.

quiz.q: Why does technology-owned AI typically underperform?
opts: Technology teams are too small
Regulators prohibit it
Technologists lack intelligence
It optimises for capability and under-invests in adoption, while lacking the financial and strategic lenses
quiz.fb: Each siloed ownership model is individually rational and collectively insufficient — which is why distributed decision rights outperform.

management.title: Finding and Prioritising Use Cases
management.summary: From vague ambition to a ranked, fundable list
objectives: Systematically identify AI opportunities across your organisation
Apply a value-versus-feasibility framework to rank candidates
Recognise the characteristics that make a use case likely to succeed
Understand where the strongest opportunities sit by function
Build a balanced portfolio rather than a collection of projects
Know which use cases to refuse

sections.h: Start with work, not with technology
sections.html:
The most common failure in use-case selection is starting from what AI can do and searching for somewhere to apply it. The disciplined approach reverses this: start from where your organisation loses time, money, accuracy or customers, and ask whether AI addresses that specific cause.

Four questions surface almost every worthwhile opportunity:

  1. Where do we do the same thing repeatedly? High-volume, rule-bounded work — data entry, document checking, routine correspondence, reconciliation, first-line queries.
  2. Where do we wait? Queues and backlogs — waiting for a report, an approval, a specialist, a translation.
  3. Where do we guess? Decisions made on instinct that could be informed by data — demand, pricing, staffing, which customer to call, which risk to investigate.
  4. Where do we get it wrong? Recurring errors, rework, complaints, missed opportunities.
