Ask these of every function head and you will typically generate thirty to fifty candidates in a fortnight. That list, not a vendor's catalogue, is the raw material of an AI strategy.

Score each candidate on two axes, each from 1 to 5.

Value — combining:

  • Volume: how often does this happen?
  • Cost or time consumed per occurrence
  • Consequence of error today
  • Strategic importance — does it serve a stated business objective?

Feasibility — combining:

  • Data: do we have it, is it accessible, is it reliable?
  • Clarity: is "correct" well defined, or a matter of judgement?
  • Workflow: can the output be acted on without redesigning everything around it?
  • Risk: what is the consequence of the system being wrong, and is it reversible?
  • Readiness: do the people involved have capacity and willingness?

Plot the results. The high-value, high-feasibility quadrant is where you start — not the most exciting quadrant, which is usually high-value and low-feasibility. Those belong on the roadmap for a later horizon, after the foundations they depend on exist.

sections.h: What a good first use case looks like
sections.html:
Six characteristics, and the strongest candidates have all of them:

  • Internal before external. Mistakes stay inside the organisation while you learn.
  • Reversible. A wrong output can be corrected before it causes harm.
  • Measurable. There is a number that will move, and you can measure it today.
  • Bounded. One process, one team, a clear definition of done.
  • Frequent. Happens often enough that improvement is visible within weeks.
  • Wanted. The people doing the work would welcome help with it.

That last point is systematically underrated. A use case the affected team actively wants will overcome implementation problems; one imposed on a resistant team will fail on adoption regardless of technical quality.

sections.h: Where the opportunities usually sit, by function
sections.html:
• Marketing. Customer segmentation, personalised content and offers, campaign optimisation, content drafting. One documented example describes AI-powered segmentation delivering personalised promotions based on browsing behaviour and increasing conversion rates by 30%.
  • Sales. Lead scoring and prioritisation using engagement history and behavioural signals, demand forecasting, proposal drafting, meeting summarisation.
  • Operations. Demand planning, scheduling, quality checking, supply chain and inventory optimisation. Accurate forecasting has been associated with inventory cost reductions of 20–50%.
  • Finance. Invoice processing, expense checking, reconciliation, variance analysis, first-draft reporting commentary.
  • Human resources. Job description drafting, initial screening support, policy question answering, onboarding material, training content.
  • Customer service. Query handling within defined limits, agent assistance, call and case summarisation, sentiment monitoring.
  • Management. Consolidated performance reporting, scenario modelling, board and committee pack preparation, competitor and market monitoring.

The functions with the highest concentration of language-heavy, repetitive work — finance operations, customer service, HR administration and marketing — usually offer the fastest measurable returns.

sections.h: Building a portfolio, not a list
sections.html:
A ranked list still produces a collection of projects. A portfolio produces capability. A workable balance for an organisation beginning this journey:

  • Roughly 60% near-term efficiency — measurable payback within twelve months, building credibility and freeing capacity.
  • Roughly 30% capability building — data foundations, skills, platform, governance. These fail every individual business case and make everything else possible.
  • Roughly 10% exploratory — deliberately uncertain, small, time-boxed, and permitted to fail.

The 30% is the discipline most organisations lack. Without a portfolio view, foundational work never survives a business-case test, and the organisation accumulates disconnected pilots that cannot scale.

• Anything where "correct" cannot be defined. If your own experts disagree on the right answer, a model cannot learn it.
  • Anything irreversible without human approval. Payments, contractual commitments, dismissals, public communications.
  • Anything requiring data you do not have. The most common quiet killer. Verify data existence before approving, not after.
  • Anything where the affected team was not consulted. It will fail on adoption.
  • Anything justified only by "our competitors are doing it." Their constraints are not yours, and you do not know whether theirs is working.
  • Anything with no measurable outcome. If success cannot be demonstrated, it cannot be defended at the next budget cycle.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: run the two-week opportunity sweep
practitioner.text: Give every function head a single page with the four questions — where do we repeat, wait, guess and get it wrong — and two weeks to answer with volumes and time estimates. It costs nothing, requires no consultant, and consistently surfaces opportunities leadership did not know existed, usually in finance operations and customer service. It also creates ownership: a use case a function head identified is one they will support.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Run the opportunity sweep for your own department. Generate at least eight candidates, then score each on value (1–5) and feasibility (1–5) using the criteria in this module. Plot them. Select your top three from the high-value, high-feasibility quadrant and, for each, write one sentence on the measure that would move and the data required. This ranked shortlist becomes the core of your capstone.

takeaways: Start from where the organisation repeats, waits, guesses and errs — not from what AI can do
Score candidates on value and feasibility; start in the high-high quadrant, not the exciting one
The best first use cases are internal, reversible, measurable, bounded, frequent and wanted by the team
Language-heavy functions — finance operations, service, HR, marketing — usually give the fastest returns
Balance the portfolio roughly 60% efficiency, 30% capability building, 10% exploratory
Foundational capability work never survives an individual business case — fund it at portfolio level
Refuse use cases with undefined correctness, no data, no measure, or no consultation with the affected team

quiz.q: The disciplined approach to identifying AI use cases begins by:
opts: Asking where the organisation repeats work, waits, guesses and gets things wrong
Benchmarking against competitors
Selecting the newest available technology
Reviewing vendor product catalogues
quiz.fb: Starting from capability and searching for an application is the most common failure. Start from where value is lost.

quiz.q: When plotting candidates on value and feasibility, an organisation should generally start with:
opts: High value, low feasibility — the most exciting opportunities
High value, high feasibility
Whichever the vendor recommends
Low value, high feasibility
quiz.fb: High-value, low-feasibility candidates belong on a later horizon, after the foundations they depend on exist.

quiz.q: Which characteristic of a first use case is most often underrated?
opts: That it uses the largest available model
That it is technically sophisticated
That the affected team actively wants the help
That it is customer-facing
quiz.fb: A wanted use case overcomes implementation problems; an imposed one fails on adoption regardless of technical quality.

quiz.q: In a balanced AI portfolio, roughly 30% should be allocated to capability building because:
opts: Vendors insist on it
Regulators require it
It is the cheapest category
Foundational work fails every individual business case yet makes everything else possible
quiz.fb: Without a portfolio view, data and platform work never survives a business-case test, and pilots accumulate without scaling.

quiz.q: Which use case should be refused outright?
opts: One where the organisation's own experts cannot agree what the correct answer is
One the affected team requested
One that improves a measurable operational metric
A high-volume internal document-checking task
quiz.fb: If correctness cannot be defined, a model cannot learn it and success cannot be evaluated.

quiz.q: 'Our competitors are doing it' is a weak justification for a use case because:
opts: It breaches confidentiality
Their data, systems and constraints differ, and you do not know whether theirs is working
Competitors are always wrong
It is unethical to follow competitors
quiz.fb: Copying a visible initiative without knowing its results or preconditions imports someone else's risk without their capability.

management.title: AI in Executive Decision-Making
management.summary: Using AI to sharpen judgement without surrendering it
objectives: Understand how senior leaders are actually using AI in strategic decisions today
Apply a framework to judge which decisions are ready for AI support
Use AI to challenge your thinking rather than confirm it
Recognise the cognitive risks specific to AI-assisted decision-making
Establish norms for disclosing AI use in executive work
Build personal fluency in the techniques that produce useful output

sections.html:
Capgemini Research Institute's 2026 research brief, based on a survey of 500 CXOs including 100 CEOs, provides the clearest available picture of AI in senior decision-making.

  • More than half of CXOs already use AI to support or inform strategic decision-making — either actively or selectively — with close to another third experimenting.
  • Use is expected to more than double within three years.
  • Today, most use it for productivity support: research, analysis and summarisation. Within three years, they expect to use it to augment and challenge their strategic thinking.
  • AI is not expected to make autonomous decisions any time soon — a finding worth quoting to anyone who fears or promises otherwise.
  • Over half report significant improvements in efficiency, creativity and foresight, with the greatest gains going to those already using AI to strengthen strategic thinking rather than merely to save time.

The research defines strategic decision-making precisely: high-impact choices that shape long-term direction, commit significant resources and carry significant risk — market entry or exit, major investments, budget shifts, mergers and acquisitions, and competitive repositioning.

Two findings from the same study deserve to be read together.

First, most organisations lack the frameworks, systems and processes needed to help leaders harness AI responsibly and confidently. Second — and this is the telling one — many CXOs continue to use AI cautiously and remain uncomfortable openly disclosing its use.

This is the pattern the report's title captures: AI is quietly reshaping executive decisions. Senior people are using these tools, deriving value from them, and not saying so. The organisational consequences are real: no shared standards emerge, mistakes are not surfaced or learned from, and junior staff receive no guidance while observing that the practice is apparently acceptable but unmentionable.

Bringing this into the open is one of the cheapest and highest-value governance acts available to a leadership team, and it is covered later in this module.

sections.h: Which decisions are ready for AI support
sections.html:
Capgemini's recommendations include building "a framework to evaluate readiness of decisions for AI support." A practical version assesses four factors:

  1. Data availability. Is there relevant, reliable information a system could actually draw on? A market-entry decision in a country with no reliable data is not made better by AI.
  2. Structure. Can the decision be broken into components — market size, cost, competitive response, capability fit? Highly structured decisions benefit most.
  3. Reversibility and stakes. Higher stakes do not disqualify AI support; they raise the standard of verification required.
  4. Verifiability. Can you check the reasoning and the facts? If a recommendation cannot be interrogated, it cannot responsibly inform a major commitment.

Decisions scoring well on structure and verifiability — pricing analysis, scenario modelling, competitor synthesis, investment option comparison — are strong candidates. Decisions dominated by relationships, politics, values or tacit knowledge are not, and no amount of prompting changes that.

sections.h: Using AI to challenge rather than confirm
sections.html:
The most valuable executive application is not generating answers. It is stress-testing the answer you already have. Capgemini's finding that the greatest gains accrue to leaders using AI to strengthen strategic thinking — rather than simply to save time — points directly at this.

Five prompts worth keeping:

  • "Here is our proposed strategy. Argue the strongest case against it."
  • "What assumptions is this plan making that we have not stated explicitly?"
  • "What would have to be true for this to fail badly? Rank by likelihood."
  • "How would our three main competitors most likely respond, and what would we do then?"
  • "What question should we be asking that we have not asked?"

Used this way, AI functions as a tireless, unintimidated devil's advocate — which is precisely the role that seniority tends to eliminate from a leadership team. Nobody's promotion depends on the model agreeing with the chief executive.

• Automation bias. Deferring to the machine because it sounds authoritative. Strongest under time pressure and when the output is well formatted.
  • Confirmation at speed. AI will happily build a compelling case for whatever you propose. Ask it to argue the opposite before you ask it to support you.
  • False precision. A number generated with three decimal places carries no more truth than the assumption behind it.
  • Persuasion effects. Capgemini's research explicitly raises concerns around AI-generated argumentation and the risk of what it terms "persuasion bombing" — being overwhelmed by fluent, confident advocacy that displaces critical evaluation. Fluency is not evidence.
  • Homogenised thinking. If every executive in your market uses similar tools on similar data, strategies converge and genuine differentiation erodes.
  • Erosion of the discipline of thinking. The strategic reasoning muscle is built by struggling with a problem. Outsourcing the struggle atrophies it.

The executive discipline

Form your own view before consulting the model, then compare. If you consult first, you will anchor on its framing and never know what you would have thought. This costs ten minutes and preserves the independent judgement your organisation is actually paying you for.

sections.h: Disclosure norms your leadership team should agree
sections.html:
Given that many executives currently use AI without disclosing it, agreeing explicit norms removes ambiguity and the low-grade discomfort that comes with it. A workable standard:

  • No disclosure needed for personal productivity — summarising your own reading, drafting your own notes, organising your own thinking.
  • Disclose the method when AI materially shaped an analysis presented to others — "the scenario ranges were generated with AI support and checked against our finance model."
  • Always disclose when AI-generated content goes to a customer, a regulator, a board, or is published externally.
  • Never present AI output as verified fact without having verified it. The person who signs the paper owns the paper.

Announcing these norms does something beyond compliance: it signals that using these tools is legitimate, which converts a quiet, unmanaged practice into a shared, improvable one.

sections.h: Personal fluency — the gap in the room
sections.html:
Capgemini found that only 38% of CXOs feel confident in prompt engineering. Given that more than half are already using these tools for strategic work, that gap is significant and easily closed.

Five techniques that account for most of the difference in output quality:

  1. Give role and context. "You are advising the management team of a mid-sized manufacturer in Nepal considering entry into a new district."
  2. Supply your own material. Paste the actual figures, the actual policy, the actual draft. Grounded output is far more reliable than general knowledge.
  3. Specify the output. "Give me three options, each with two risks and one leading indicator to monitor."
  4. Require gaps to be flagged. "Where you do not have enough information, say so explicitly rather than assuming."
  5. Iterate. The first answer is a draft. "Make the second option more concrete." "You have ignored our capacity constraint."

Capgemini's recommendations include boosting executive confidence through targeted upskilling and mentoring. Thirty minutes of structured practice moves most executives from tentative to competent — a return on time that is difficult to match elsewhere.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the pre-read challenge
practitioner.text: Before your next major decision paper goes to the management committee, have the paper's author run one prompt: "Argue the strongest case against this recommendation, and list the three assumptions most likely to be wrong." Attach the output as an appendix. It takes fifteen minutes, it consistently surfaces objections that would otherwise emerge only after the decision, and it normalises AI use as a rigour tool rather than a shortcut.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take a real decision your organisation faces in the next quarter. First, write your own view in five bullet points — before touching any AI tool. Then use the five challenge prompts from this module. Compare: what did it surface that you had not considered, and where did it merely restate your own framing back to you? Finally, draft the four disclosure norms you would propose to your leadership team.

takeaways: More than half of CXOs already use AI in strategic decision-making; use is expected to more than double in three years
AI is not expected to make autonomous strategic decisions any time soon
The greatest gains go to leaders using AI to challenge their thinking, not merely to save time
Many executives use AI without disclosing it, which prevents shared standards and learning from emerging
Assess decision readiness on data availability, structure, stakes and verifiability
Form your own view before consulting the model, or you will anchor on its framing
Only 38% of CXOs feel confident in prompting — a large, cheaply closed capability gap

quiz.q: Capgemini's survey of 500 CXOs found that within three years, executives expect to use AI primarily to:
opts: Handle only administrative tasks
Make autonomous strategic decisions
Augment and challenge their strategic thinking
Replace the management committee
quiz.fb: AI is not expected to make autonomous decisions any time soon. The shift is from productivity support toward challenging strategic thinking.

quiz.q: The finding that many CXOs remain uncomfortable disclosing their AI use matters because:
opts: It increases licensing costs
It slows down the technology
It is a legal breach
No shared standards emerge, mistakes are not surfaced, and junior staff receive no guidance
quiz.fb: Quiet use converts a potentially improvable practice into an unmanaged one. Agreeing disclosure norms is a cheap, high-value governance act.

quiz.q: The recommended discipline before consulting AI on a decision is to:
opts: Form and write down your own view first, then compare
Ask three different AI tools
Gather as much data as possible first
Delegate the question entirely
quiz.fb: Consulting first anchors you on the model's framing, and you never learn what you would independently have concluded.

quiz.q: Which decision type is LEAST suited to AI support?
opts: Scenario modelling for a pricing change
A decision dominated by relationships, organisational politics and tacit knowledge
Synthesising competitor activity
Comparing investment options against defined criteria
quiz.fb: Decisions score well when structured and verifiable. Those dominated by tacit and relational factors are not improved by prompting.

quiz.q: 'Persuasion bombing', a concern raised in the Capgemini research, refers to:
opts: A cyberattack technique
Excessive advertising spend
Being overwhelmed by fluent, confident AI-generated advocacy that displaces critical evaluation
Sending too many emails
quiz.fb: Fluency is not evidence. AI will build a compelling case for whatever position it is asked to support.

quiz.q: Capgemini found the proportion of CXOs confident in prompt engineering to be approximately:
quiz.fb: Given that more than half already use AI for strategic work, this is a significant gap — and thirty minutes of structured practice closes most of it.

management.title: The Business Case: Investment, ROI and Budgeting
management.summary: Funding AI properly and proving it worked
objectives: Build a business case that survives finance scrutiny
Understand the full cost of an AI initiative, not merely the licence fee
Understand why AI project finance differs from conventional IT finance
Avoid the efficiency trap and the double-counting of benefits
Establish baselines and measure value credibly
Design a funding model that supports capability, not only projects

sections.h: Why AI business cases fail finance review
sections.html:
The World Economic Forum identifies lack of understanding about AI project finance as one of the principal reasons AI initiatives fail to deliver business value. Three specific dynamics cause the friction:

  • AI projects need ring-fenced funding to support capacity-building, plus aligned incentives across the wider organisation — and this is frequently absent.
  • AI typically piggybacks on other investments in data platforms, cloud and process engineering. Diverting funding from those to pay for a new AI initiative "may well prove counterproductive."
  • Uncertainty is genuinely higher. The scale of outcomes can be hard to guarantee, which conflicts with the precision a finance function reasonably expects.

The WEF's practical conclusion is worth acting on directly: helping the finance department understand this dynamic can be key to a project's corporate survival. Bring finance in early, explain the R&D-like character of the work, and agree a staged funding model rather than presenting a single fixed-return case that will not hold.

sections.h: The six elements of a credible business case
sections.html:
1. The problem, in operational language. "Invoice processing takes an average of eleven days and consumes 240 staff hours per month, with a 6% error rate requiring rework."
  2. The measured baseline. Current performance, quantified before anything changes. The most commonly skipped element, and its absence makes success unprovable.
  3. The intervention. Precisely what the system does, where the human remains in the loop, and what changes in the workflow.
  4. The benefit, ranged and conservative. Expressed in the organisation's own terms — time, cost, error rate, revenue, service level — with the assumptions stated.
  5. The full lifetime cost (below).
  6. Risks and controls, with named owner and stopping criteria.

sections.h: The full cost — what proposals omit
sections.html:
Licence fees are usually a minority of total cost. A complete costing includes:

  • Data preparation. Frequently the largest line, given that roughly 80% of effort in creating an AI system goes on data cleansing and manipulation.
  • Integration with existing systems and workflows.
  • Internal staff time — subject-matter experts, IT, project management. Real cost even when it does not appear in a budget line.
  • Training and change management, including protected time for staff to learn.
  • Ongoing running costs. Generative AI in particular is charged per use, so cost scales with adoption — a pilot with fifty users is a poor guide to production with five hundred.
  • Monitoring and maintenance, indefinitely.
  • Contingency. Given documented overruns of two to three times in cost and time, a contingency below 30% on a first initiative is optimistic.

Deeper dive: the integration reality

Research from the Oxford Future of Finance and Technology Initiative records a practitioner observing that "60–70% of spend on the use case has got nothing to do with AI. It's the basic foundational middleware integration." When a proposal's costs are dominated by licence fees, it is incomplete — and the missing money will be found later, from an unbudgeted source, under pressure.

The failure mode that catches nearly everyone

Oxford's research documents a business case built on "incremental gains on automations, something like 5–15% of every human doing an ops job," which tallied to substantial annual savings — followed by: "in the real world, we couldn't remove those humans from the system. So most people who put in an AI business case failed to deliver it."

The lesson is precise. Time saved is not money saved unless the organisation acts on it. Ten minutes returned to forty people is only a benefit if roles are redesigned to absorb higher-value work, headcount genuinely changes, or the freed capacity absorbs growth that would otherwise have required hiring.

A business case claiming efficiency benefit must therefore state explicitly what the freed capacity will do. "Staff will be freed for more strategic work" is not a plan; "this absorbs the 15% volume growth forecast for next year without additional hiring" is.

sections.h: Double counting and the portfolio view
sections.html:
When several initiatives each claim to save time in the same function, the same saving is counted repeatedly and the aggregate becomes fiction. This is discovered at the worst possible moment — when the promised savings do not appear in the accounts.

Oxford's recommended remedy is to evaluate AI initiatives programmatically as well as case by case. Programme-level evaluation does two things: it prevents double counting, and it allows enabling investments that generate no standalone return to be funded on the strength of the overall programme. Without it, the data platform, the training programme and the governance framework all fail their individual business cases — and the organisation wonders why nothing scales.

Work through four levels, each closer to the accounts:

  1. Activity — tools deployed, users trained, queries handled. Useful for management, worthless as value evidence. Most reporting stops here.
  2. Operational outcome — cycle time, cost per transaction, error rate, throughput. Directly attributable if a baseline exists.
  3. Business outcome — conversion, retention, service level, capacity absorbed.
  4. Financial outcome — revenue, cost, margin. The only level a board ultimately accepts.

Define one metric at each level before deployment, plus the mechanism linking them. An initiative that cannot articulate that chain has not been thought through, however attractive the technology.

• Ring-fence a capability budget separate from use-case budgets — data, platform, skills, governance. The WEF is explicit that ring-fenced funding matters, and this is the line that dies first without protection.
  • Fund in stages with decision points. Discovery, pilot, scale — each with its own release of funds and explicit stop criteria. This matches the experimental nature of the work and gives finance appropriate control.
  • Align incentives. If a function's budget is cut the moment AI saves it money, no function will volunteer for AI. Let functions retain some benefit for a period.
  • Accept a portfolio failure rate. If every initiative succeeds, you are not attempting anything difficult. Say this to the board in advance, not after the first failure.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: bring finance in at the start
practitioner.text: Invite your finance lead into the first AI planning conversation, not the approval meeting. Explain the R&D-like character of the work, the 80% data effort, the documented two-to-three-times overrun risk, and propose stage-gated funding with explicit stop criteria. Finance leaders are rarely obstructive when they understand the shape of the uncertainty — they become obstructive when presented with a confident single-point return they know cannot be justified.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Build a full business case for the top use case you identified in Module 4. Include all six elements, and cost every line in the full-cost list — not just licences. Then apply two tests: (1) does the case state explicitly what freed capacity will be used for, and (2) is any of this benefit already claimed by another initiative? If either fails, revise before presenting.

takeaways: Lack of understanding of AI project finance is a principal reason initiatives fail to deliver value
Bring finance in early and agree stage-gated funding rather than a single fixed-return case
Licence fees are a minority of cost; integration can be 60–70% of use-case spend
Budget a contingency of at least 30% given documented two-to-three-times overruns
Time saved is not money saved unless roles are redesigned or capacity is explicitly absorbed
Evaluate programmatically to prevent double counting and to fund enabling investments
Define one metric at each of four levels before deployment — activity, operational, business, financial
Ring-fence a capability budget and align incentives so functions are not punished for saving money

quiz.q: A business case projects savings from returning ten minutes per day to forty staff. For this to become real organisational benefit:
opts: Roles must be redesigned, headcount must change, or the freed capacity must absorb defined growth
The software must be cheaper
Nothing further is required — the saving is automatic
The project must be centralised
quiz.fb: Oxford documents exactly this failure: 'we couldn't remove those humans from the system, so most people who put in an AI business case failed to deliver it.'

quiz.q: Research cited in this module suggests that in a typical AI use case, integration and foundational work account for approximately:
opts: None — modern platforms remove integration cost
60–70% of spend
5–10% of spend
Less than 1%
quiz.fb: When a proposal's costs are dominated by licence fees, it is incomplete, and the missing money will be found later under pressure.

quiz.q: The WEF identifies which finance-related factor as a principal cause of AI initiative failure?
opts: Currency fluctuations
Excessive budgets
Lack of understanding about AI project finance, including absent ring-fenced funding and misaligned incentives
Too much finance involvement
quiz.fb: Helping finance understand the R&D-like dynamic of AI work can be key to a project's corporate survival.

quiz.q: Evaluating AI initiatives programmatically rather than only case by case principally prevents:
opts: Vendor lock-in
Staff turnover
Data breaches
Double counting of the same benefit, and the underfunding of enabling investments
quiz.fb: Foundational work fails every individual business case yet makes everything else possible — programme-level evaluation is how it gets funded.

quiz.q: If a function's budget is cut immediately whenever AI saves it money, the predictable result is:
opts: No function will volunteer for AI initiatives
Lower software costs
Improved governance
Faster adoption across the organisation
quiz.fb: Incentive alignment matters. Letting functions retain some benefit for a period is what makes them willing participants.

quiz.q: Given documented overrun patterns, a reasonable contingency on a first AI initiative is:
opts: Exactly 5%
At least 30%
Zero — modern tools are predictable
Contingency is not appropriate for technology projects
quiz.fb: AI projects have been documented overrunning by factors of two to three in cost and time, driven largely by data challenges.

management.title: Data, Technology and Organisational Readiness
management.summary: What must be true before AI can work
objectives: Assess your organisation's readiness across the dimensions that actually determine success
Understand why data is the binding constraint and what to do about it
Judge build, buy and partner options without technical expertise
Conduct vendor due diligence as a non-technical executive
Understand what technology foundations are genuinely required
Sequence foundational work so it does not block all progress

sections.h: Readiness is not a technology question
sections.html:
The World Economic Forum lists unavailable or poor-quality data and technology foundations not in place among the principal reasons AI initiatives fail — alongside capability gaps, poor governance, and weak project finance and management. Note that only two of the six are technical.

A practical readiness assessment covers four dimensions. Rate each honestly, with evidence:

  1. Data. Do we have relevant data, can we access it, is it reliable, and can we link records about the same customer or product across systems?
  2. Technology. Can data be extracted from core systems? Do we have somewhere to run things? Can systems talk to each other?
  3. People and skills. Do we have anyone who can evaluate a proposal, run a pilot, and challenge a vendor? Does the affected team have capacity?
  4. Governance and process. Do we have decision rights, a policy on acceptable use, and a way to stop something that is going wrong?

Most organisations score adequately on technology and poorly on data and governance. That diagnosis should determine the roadmap — and it usually does not, because data and governance work is invisible and unexciting.

The WEF is direct that data is the key fuel for AI, and identifies the specific problems that recur:

  • Accessibility. Data stored in multiple, disparate legacy silos with little linkage between datasets, limiting any consolidated picture.
  • Quality and representativeness. Understanding data lineage, quality and statistical representativeness is necessary — and rarely documented.
  • Labelling effort. Extensive resources, often including manual labour, are needed to label datasets so they can train models.
  • Regulation. Increasing regulation of personal data use requires a clear understanding of what you hold and on what basis.

For most organisations the practical priority is unglamorous and specific: a consistent way to identify the same customer, product or transaction across systems. Without it, every analysis is quietly wrong. With it, a surprising amount becomes possible. It is also useful independently of AI, which makes it the easiest foundational investment to justify.

sections.h: Do not wait for perfect foundations
sections.html:
The opposite error is equally damaging: concluding that nothing can begin until data is fixed. Two considerations resolve the tension:

  • Different use cases have different data requirements. Building a demand-forecasting model requires clean, joined historical data. Using AI to draft correspondence, summarise documents or answer policy questions requires almost none of your structured data at all. The second category can proceed while the first waits.
  • Build alongside, not after. Extract and standardise the data specific use cases need, rather than attempting an enterprise-wide data programme first. Enterprise data programmes have a poor completion record; targeted extraction delivers value and builds the foundation incrementally.

The sequencing rule: start with use cases that need documents and language, while building the data foundations that structured use cases will require.

Three options, and for most organisations the answer is clear:

  • Buy. Purchase software with AI built in, or a ready application. Fastest, lowest risk, least differentiation. Correct for the overwhelming majority of first initiatives.
  • Partner. Work with an external provider to configure or develop something for your context. Moderate cost, moderate control. Appropriate where the need is specific but the capability is not core.
  • Build. Develop internally. Only justified where the capability is a genuine source of competitive advantage and you can attract and retain the people. Rarely true for organisations of moderate size.

The honest test: is this capability something customers would choose us for? If not, buy it. Organisations routinely build things that are available off the shelf, because building feels strategic — and then spend years maintaining something a vendor would have maintained for them.

sections.h: Vendor due diligence for the non-technical executive
sections.html:
You do not need technical expertise to run a rigorous vendor process. Ask these, and require written answers:

  1. Show me an organisation like ours using this. Similar size, similar sector, similar country if possible. Then contact them directly.
  2. What data do you need from us, where is it processed and stored, and does it leave the country?
  3. Will our data be used to train models serving your other clients? A surprising number of contracts permit this by default.
  4. What happens when the system is wrong? Who notices, and how?
  5. What does year three cost, in full? Including usage growth, support and any per-user or per-transaction charges.
  6. What happens if we leave? Can we retrieve our data in a usable form?
  7. What do we need to do for this to work? A vendor who says "nothing" is either mistaken or selling.
  8. What training and knowledge transfer is included?

A vendor unwilling to answer the data-use, exit and total-cost questions in writing should be excluded regardless of how impressive the demonstration was.

sections.h: The technology foundations that actually matter
sections.html:
The WEF notes that ambitious organisations digitise and architect their platforms, processes and tools to enable rapid roll-out — with typical foundations including data storage, access and cleansing capability, algorithmic frameworks, and access to AI-as-a-service solutions. It also warns that not all organisations have these foundations and "may be trying to run before they can walk."

Translated to a practical minimum for a mid-sized organisation:

  • A way to get data out of core systems without a manual export every time
  • A consistent identifier linking records across systems
  • Somewhere to store and process data securely, with defined access control
  • An approved, safe generative AI tool that staff can actually use — which removes the incentive for unapproved use
  • Basic security hygiene: access management, logging, backup

Notably, none of this is exotic or expensive. It is ordinary institutional discipline, and its absence — not the absence of advanced technology — is what stops most organisations.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: test the data claim
practitioner.text: When someone says "we have plenty of data," convert it into a testable request: "Please produce a single spreadsheet listing our top 200 customers with their total revenue, product holdings and last transaction date — by Friday." How long that takes, and how many people it involves, is your real data-readiness assessment. Organisations are routinely surprised, and the exercise costs nothing but a few hours.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Complete a readiness assessment across the four dimensions — data, technology, people, governance — rating each 1–5 with written evidence. Then run the data test above on a real request relevant to your priority use case. Finally, for that use case, decide build, buy or partner using the competitive-advantage test, and list the eight vendor questions you would require in writing.

takeaways: Only two of the WEF's six failure causes are technical; data and governance are usually the weak dimensions
The practical data priority is a consistent identifier linking records across systems
Document and language use cases need almost none of your structured data — start there while building foundations
Buy for the overwhelming majority of first initiatives; build only where customers would choose you for the capability
Require written answers on data use, processing location, total three-year cost and exit terms
A vendor who says you need to do nothing is either mistaken or selling
The required foundations are ordinary institutional discipline, not exotic technology

quiz.q: For most organisations, the single most valuable data foundation to establish first is:
opts: A large data warehouse
Cloud infrastructure
A consistent identifier linking the same customer or product across systems
A data science team
quiz.fb: Without consistent identifiers every analysis is quietly wrong. It is also valuable independently of AI, which makes it easy to justify.

quiz.q: An organisation with poor structured data should conclude that:
opts: It should buy more data
No AI work can begin until data is fixed
AI is not suitable for them
Document and language use cases can proceed now while structured-data foundations are built in parallel
quiz.fb: Drafting, summarising and policy question-answering require almost none of your structured data. Sequencing matters more than waiting.

quiz.q: The clearest test for whether to build rather than buy an AI capability is:
opts: Whether customers would choose your organisation because of that capability
Whether a vendor exists
Whether building is cheaper in year one
Whether the IT team wants to build it
quiz.fb: Organisations routinely build available capabilities because building feels strategic, then spend years maintaining what a vendor would have maintained.

quiz.q: Which vendor question most often reveals an unacceptable contract term?
opts: What colour is the interface?
Will our data be used to train models serving your other clients?
How long have you been in business?
How many staff does your company employ?
quiz.fb: A surprising number of contracts permit this by default. It must be answered in writing before signing.

quiz.q: A vendor tells you that no effort is required from your organisation for the system to work. This indicates:
opts: A good value proposition
That you should sign immediately
They are either mistaken or selling — every deployment requires data, integration and change effort
An unusually well-designed product
quiz.fb: Data preparation, integration, training and workflow change are always required. A vendor denying this is not a reliable partner.

quiz.q: The WEF warns that organisations without adequate technology foundations may be:
opts: Overspending on governance
Too focused on data quality
Excessively cautious
Trying to run before they can walk
quiz.fb: Typical foundations include data storage, access and cleansing capability. Ambition without foundations produces expensive disappointment.

management.title: People, Culture and Change Management
management.summary: The dimension that decides whether any of it works
objectives: Understand why culture and adoption determine AI outcomes more than technology
Address employment anxiety honestly and effectively
Decide whether to hire, train or outsource AI capability
Understand the role of executive sponsorship and what it requires in practice
Design an AI change programme with the right sequence and pace
Build AI literacy across the organisation at the right depth for each group

sections.html:
The WEF's toolkit devotes an entire chapter to people and organisation, and identifies capability gaps as the first of its principal failure causes — noting that these emerge at several levels, and that "a lack of education about the role of AI in an organisation can lead to negative impacts on employee morale and even attempts to sabotage roll-out."

That word — sabotage — is unusually direct for a WEF publication, and it should be taken seriously. Resistance to AI is rarely irrational. It is a reasonable response to a change whose implications for one's job have not been explained. The management task is not to overcome resistance but to remove its cause.

sections.h: The employment conversation you must have
sections.html:
Your people are already discussing whether AI will replace them. Silence does not prevent that conversation; it only removes management from it.

An honest position, which most organisations can defend:

  • Some tasks will be automated. Name them. Vagueness generates more fear than specificity.
  • Most roles will change rather than disappear — but changed roles require new skills, and the organisation will invest in providing them.
  • Some roles will change substantially. Say so, and say what support exists.
  • Here is what we commit to — retraining, redeployment, notice, or whatever your organisation can genuinely promise. Promise only what you will honour.

The WEF also flags a subtler risk: over-hasty deployment may "sideline the very internal domain experts required to ensure high-quality deployment." The people who understand the work best are both your greatest implementation asset and the most likely to feel threatened. Involving them early converts a risk into a resource.

sections.h: Executive sponsorship — what it actually requires
sections.html:
Every framework cites executive sponsorship. Few define it. In practice it means five observable behaviours:

  1. Visible personal use. A leader who talks about AI but has never used it is not credible. Executives who use these tools themselves lead the change materially better.
  2. Protected budget that is not raided when quarterly pressure arrives.
  3. Attendance. Turning up to the steering group consistently, not delegating it after the launch.
  4. Removing obstacles. When a function refuses to share data or release a subject-matter expert, the sponsor resolves it — this is the main practical function of sponsorship.
  5. Public support after a failure. The single most powerful signal available. If the first setback produces blame, all subsequent honesty disappears.

The WEF poses this question directly, and for most mid-sized organisations the practical answer is a combination:

  • Train your existing people for the majority of the need. People who understand your business and are taught to use AI tools generally outperform newly hired specialists who must learn your business. This is the highest-return option and the most commonly overlooked.
  • Hire selectively — perhaps one person who can evaluate, translate and challenge, rather than a team. Recruiting a data science team into an organisation without data foundations produces frustration and departure within two years.
  • Outsource specialist and infrequent work — building, validating, integrating — while insisting on knowledge transfer and documented handover so capability accrues to you rather than to the vendor.

The WEF also flags retention explicitly: the people you train become externally marketable. Career path, interesting work and recognition matter more than incremental salary, and losing your trained people to a competitor is a predictable cost of doing this well.

sections.h: AI literacy at the right depth
sections.html:
A single training programme serves nobody. Segment by what each group must do:

  • Board and executive — enough to govern: what AI is, what it risks, what to ask, how to read a proposal. Two to three hours, ideally with peers.
  • Managers — enough to specify, prioritise and challenge: use-case identification, business cases, vendor questions, change leadership. This programme.
  • Staff who will use AI — practical fluency: how to prompt, how to check, what never to enter, when to escalate. Short, hands-on, on real work.
  • Specialists — technical depth appropriate to their role.

Two design principles that materially improve outcomes. First, train on real work, not abstract exercises — people learn the tool when it solves a problem they actually have. Second, train the challenge, not just the use: staff must be able to recognise when output is wrong and be genuinely empowered to override it. Training that produces compliant users rather than critical ones has created a new risk.

Sequence matters more than intensity:

  1. Explain the why before the what. Connect AI to a business challenge people already recognise.
  2. Address employment early — before the first deployment, not after rumours circulate.
  3. Start where it is wanted. Volunteers first. Their success recruits the sceptics far more effectively than mandate.
  4. Give people time. Change introduced without protected time is change that does not happen.
  5. Redesign the work, not just the tool. If the process stays identical and a tool is added, you have added a step rather than removed one.
  6. Make results visible. Show what improved and who benefited. Nothing sustains adoption like a colleague's demonstrated success.
  7. Close the loop. Collect what users find frustrating and fix it. Unacknowledged frustration becomes quiet abandonment.

The WEF's guidance is unusually pointed here, and it belongs in this module rather than a risk module:

"The AI journey is a learning journey, and learning is all about taking risks. Managers must have room to fail, as long as they can course-correct and learn. Shutting down all risk will likely lead to the firm falling behind in the competitive race."

This requires a specific management behaviour: defining in advance what an acceptable failure looks like. A small, time-boxed, well-governed initiative that does not work is a successful experiment. An uncontrolled, unbudgeted failure is not. Making that distinction explicit lets you encourage the first without appearing to license the second — and it is what makes "permission to fail" a governance position rather than a slogan.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: use it yourself, visibly
practitioner.text: The most effective single act of AI sponsorship costs nothing: use the tools yourself, and say so in a management meeting — including where they were unhelpful. Leaders who advocate AI without using it are transparently unconvincing, and their teams know it. Leaders who describe a real task they attempted, what worked and what did not, establish both credibility and permission to experiment in a single sentence.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft the message you would give your team about AI and their jobs — no more than 200 words, specific about which tasks change, honest about what you do not yet know, and clear about what the organisation commits to. Then list the three people in your organisation who best understand the work you want to improve, and plan how you would involve them from the start rather than presenting to them at the end.

takeaways: Capability gaps are the WEF's first-listed failure cause; poor education can damage morale and provoke resistance
Resistance is rarely irrational — it is a response to unexplained implications for people's jobs
Name which tasks change, commit only to what you will honour, and involve domain experts early
Sponsorship means visible personal use, protected budget, attendance, obstacle removal and public support after failure
Train existing people for most of the need; hire selectively; outsource with mandatory knowledge transfer
Segment literacy by group, train on real work, and train challenge rather than compliance
Define in advance what an acceptable failure looks like — this makes permission to fail a governance position

quiz.q: The WEF warns that a lack of education about AI's role in an organisation can lead to:
opts: Negative impacts on employee morale and even attempts to sabotage roll-out
Higher licensing costs
Slightly slower adoption
Regulatory penalties
quiz.fb: Resistance is a reasonable response to unexplained change. The management task is to remove its cause, not to overcome it.

quiz.q: For most mid-sized organisations, the highest-return approach to building AI capability is to:
opts: Wait for the market to mature
Train existing people who already understand the business
Outsource everything permanently
Hire a full data science team immediately
quiz.fb: People who know your business and learn AI tools generally outperform specialists who must first learn your business.

quiz.q: Which behaviour is the most powerful signal of genuine executive sponsorship?
opts: Approving the budget
Appointing a project manager
Publicly supporting the team after a failure
Announcing the programme at a town hall
quiz.fb: If the first setback produces blame, all subsequent honesty disappears — and you lose the information you most need.

quiz.q: Training staff to use AI without training them to challenge its output:
opts: Is the efficient approach
Is required by most vendors
Reduces change management costs
Creates a new risk by producing compliant rather than critical users
quiz.fb: Staff must be able to recognise when output is wrong and be genuinely empowered to override it.

quiz.q: The WEF's position on risk in AI initiatives is that:
opts: Managers must have room to fail and course-correct; shutting down all risk will likely leave the firm behind
Risk is irrelevant for small projects
All risk should be eliminated before proceeding
Only the board should take risks
quiz.fb: Defining in advance what an acceptable failure looks like turns permission to fail into a governance position rather than a slogan.

quiz.q: When introducing AI to a team, the recommended starting point is:
opts: Start with the most resistant team to prove the point
Start with volunteers, whose success recruits the sceptics
Mandate use across all departments simultaneously
Start with the largest process
quiz.fb: Voluntary early adopters demonstrate value credibly to peers in a way that management mandate cannot.

management.title: Responsible AI and Governance for Leaders
management.summary: Building the framework before you need it
objectives: Understand what responsible AI means in operational rather than aspirational terms
Build a governance structure proportionate to your organisation's size
Write an acceptable use policy your staff will actually follow
Understand how governance must adapt for agentic AI
Establish board and executive oversight that is meaningful rather than ceremonial
Know the questions a leader must be able to answer about any deployed system

sections.h: Why governance is a value question, not a compliance one
sections.html:
The WEF lists poor governance structure among the principal reasons AI initiatives fail to deliver business value — not among the reasons they create risk. That framing matters. Weak governance does not merely expose you; it stops things working. Projects stall in unresolved disputes about data access. Deployments are blocked at the last moment by risk functions consulted too late. Nobody can authorise the decision to stop, so failing initiatives consume budget indefinitely.

Capgemini's 2026 research reaches the same place from the other direction: most organisations lack the frameworks, systems and processes needed to help leaders harness AI responsibly and confidently. Their first recommendation to CXOs is to revamp AI governance and accountability frameworks for the agentic era.

Governance is what converts scattered enthusiasm into an institutional capability. It is also what allows you to move faster, because pre-agreed rules remove the need to relitigate every decision.

sections.h: The principles, and what they mean operationally
sections.html:
Responsible AI principles are widely published and largely convergent. What distinguishes serious organisations is translating each into an operational requirement:

  • Fairness → we test outputs for disparate impact across groups we can identify, and we record the result.
  • Transparency → people affected by an automated or AI-assisted decision are told, and can ask why.
  • Accountability → every deployed system has a named accountable owner. Not a committee — a person.
  • Privacy → we know what data each system uses, on what legal basis, where it is processed, and who can access it.
  • Safety and robustness → we know how the system fails, we monitor for it, and we can switch it off.
  • Human oversight → a person can review and override, and has the time, information and authority to do so.

A principle that has not been converted into a testable requirement is a statement of intention, and will be treated as such by everyone in your organisation.

Governance should scale with the organisation, not with the ambition of the framework document.

For a smaller organisation (under roughly 200 staff), three things suffice:

  1. A named executive owner for AI, with authority to convene and to stop.
  2. A one-page acceptable use policy every employee has read.
  3. A register of AI systems in use, with owner, purpose, data used and risk rating — reviewed quarterly.

Larger organisations add:

  1. A cross-functional steering group approving use cases and allocating budget.
  2. A risk classification framework determining the approval and monitoring each use case requires.
  3. A pre-deployment review covering data, testing, failure modes, oversight and rollback.
  4. Standing board reporting on portfolio, value and incidents.

The register is the item most often missing and most immediately useful. Many organisations cannot answer the simple question "what AI systems are we currently using?" — including software their vendors have quietly added AI features to. Building the register takes a fortnight and frequently produces the most surprising findings of the entire governance exercise.

Applying the same controls to a meeting-summary tool and a customer-facing decision system wastes effort on one and under-protects the other. A three-tier model works for most organisations:

  • Low risk — internal productivity, human reviews everything, no personal data, easily reversible. Control: acceptable use policy and basic training.
  • Medium risk — informs decisions about people or money, uses internal or personal data, errors are correctable but costly. Control: documented owner, pre-deployment testing, human approval before effect, periodic performance review.
  • High risk — materially affects customers, employees or the organisation's standing; uses sensitive data; errors are hard to reverse. Control: full pre-deployment review, explicit executive approval, continuous monitoring, defined rollback, incident procedure, board visibility.

Classification should be driven by consequence, not by technology. A simple system making consequential decisions requires more control than a sophisticated one drafting internal memoranda.

One page, written in plain language. Six clauses cover most of the need:

  1. Approved tools. These are the tools you may use. Others require approval. Provide a genuinely usable approved option — the main driver of unapproved use is the absence of a sanctioned alternative.
  2. Never enter. Customer personal data, employee records, confidential commercial information, credentials, or anything under a confidentiality obligation — unless using a specifically approved system where this has been assessed.
  3. Always verify. Check facts, figures, names, calculations and citations before using AI output in any work product.
  4. You remain responsible. The person who submits the work owns it, regardless of how it was produced.
  5. Disclose when it matters. Say when AI materially shaped analysis presented to others, and always for external or customer-facing content.
  6. Report problems. Tell your manager when output was wrong in a way that mattered — without blame. This is your early warning system, and it only works if reporting is genuinely safe.

Shadow AI

If your staff have no approved tool, they are using unapproved ones on their personal accounts with your data, and you have no visibility of it. Prohibition without provision does not reduce risk; it relocates it somewhere you cannot see. Providing a safe, approved tool is a risk control, not a convenience.

Capgemini's first recommendation is specifically about the shift to agentic AI — systems that pursue goals across multiple steps, use tools, and act rather than merely answer. Existing governance frameworks generally assume a human reviews each output. That assumption breaks.

Four additions are required:

  • Scope limits. Define explicitly what an agent may and may not do, which systems it can access, and what value or category of action requires human authorisation.
  • Logging. Every action taken must be recorded and reviewable after the fact. Where a human no longer reviews each step in advance, the audit trail becomes the primary control.
  • Circuit breakers. A defined condition — volume, value, error rate, anomaly — that halts the agent automatically and escalates to a person.
  • Accountability that survives autonomy. A named owner accountable for the agent's actions, with the authority and the technical means to stop it immediately.

The governing principle is straightforward: an agent should never be able to take an action that the person accountable for it could not reverse. If it can, either the scope is too wide or the oversight is too thin.

sections.h: Board and executive oversight that is meaningful
sections.html:
A quarterly AI report to the board or executive committee should contain five items and fit on two pages:

  1. Portfolio. What is in progress, at what stage, consuming what budget.
  2. Value. What has been measured against baseline — not activity metrics.
  3. Risk. The register by tier, changes since last quarter, and any high-risk system approved.
  4. Incidents. What went wrong, what it cost, what changed as a result. A report with no incidents over several quarters usually means incidents are not being reported.
  5. Decisions required. What the board must approve or resolve.

Seven questions any board member should be able to ask, and any executive should be able to answer:

  • What AI systems are we using, and who owns each?
  • Which of them affect customers or employees directly?
  • What data do they use, and where is it processed?
  • How would we know if one started performing badly?
  • Who can switch it off, and how quickly?
  • What has this cost us in total, and what value have we measured?
  • What is our largest single AI-related exposure?

An executive team that cannot answer these does not have a governance problem to solve later. It has one now.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: build the register first
practitioner.text: Before writing a policy or convening a committee, spend two weeks building the register of AI systems already in use — including AI features vendors have added to software you already own, and tools individuals have adopted informally. Ask every function head directly. Organisations are routinely surprised by what is already running, on what data, with no owner. You cannot govern what you have not inventoried, and the register makes the rest of the framework concrete rather than theoretical.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft your organisation's one-page acceptable use policy using the six clauses. Then start the register: list every AI system or AI-enabled feature you know is in use, with owner, purpose, data used and a low/medium/high risk rating. Identify which entries have no owner — that is your first governance action. Finally, answer the seven board questions honestly for your own organisation and note which you cannot yet answer.

takeaways: The WEF lists poor governance as a cause of value failure, not merely of risk
Convert each principle into a testable operational requirement or it will be treated as intention
Smaller organisations need only three things: a named owner, a one-page policy, and a register
Risk-tier by consequence, not by technology sophistication
Prohibition without provision relocates risk rather than reducing it — an approved tool is a control
Agentic AI requires scope limits, logging, circuit breakers and accountability that survives autonomy
An agent should never take an action its accountable owner could not reverse
A quarterly report with no incidents usually means incidents are not being reported

quiz.q: The WEF cites poor governance structure primarily as a cause of:
opts: Regulatory penalties only
Higher software costs
AI initiatives failing to deliver business value
Slower model training
quiz.fb: Weak governance stalls projects in unresolved disputes, blocks late-stage deployments, and prevents anyone authorising a stop.

quiz.q: An organisation prohibits AI tools but provides no approved alternative. The most likely outcome is:
opts: Risk is eliminated
Productivity improves
Compliance is achieved
Staff use unapproved tools on personal accounts with company data, invisible to management
quiz.fb: Prohibition without provision relocates risk somewhere you cannot see. Providing a safe approved tool is a risk control.

quiz.q: AI use cases should be risk-tiered principally according to:
opts: The consequence of the system being wrong
The sophistication of the underlying technology
The size of the vendor
The cost of the licence
quiz.fb: A simple system making consequential decisions needs more control than a sophisticated one drafting internal memos.

quiz.q: Which control becomes the PRIMARY safeguard for agentic AI, where a human no longer reviews each step in advance?
opts: Model accuracy testing
Comprehensive logging and a reviewable audit trail
User training
Vendor reputation
quiz.fb: When pre-approval of each action is no longer possible, after-the-fact reviewability plus circuit breakers carry the control burden.

quiz.q: A quarterly AI report to the board shows zero incidents across four consecutive quarters. The most likely explanation is:
opts: AI is not risky
The systems are too small to fail
Incidents are not being reported
Excellent risk management
quiz.fb: Reporting must be genuinely blame-free to function as an early warning system. Silence is usually a reporting failure, not an absence of problems.

quiz.q: The governing principle for agentic AI scope is that an agent should never:
opts: Use more than one data source
Interact with customers
Operate outside business hours
Take an action the person accountable for it could not reverse
quiz.fb: If it can take irreversible action, either the scope is too wide or the oversight is too thin.

management.title: Managing AI Risk: What Actually Goes Wrong
management.summary: The failure modes, in order of likelihood
objectives: Understand the six principal reasons AI initiatives fail, and diagnose which apply to you
Recognise the operational, legal and reputational risks of deployed systems
Manage third-party and vendor concentration risk
Design an incident response process before you need one
Understand the risks specific to generative and agentic systems
Balance risk management against the cost of inaction

sections.h: The six reasons AI initiatives fail
sections.html:
The World Economic Forum's toolkit sets these out directly. Read them as a diagnostic checklist against your own organisation:

  1. Capability gaps. Insufficient skills at multiple levels, and inadequate education about AI's role — which damages morale and can provoke resistance to roll-out.
  2. Unavailable or poor-quality data. Fragmented legacy silos, undocumented lineage and quality, and the labelling burden. Around 80% of the effort in building an AI system goes here.
  3. Technology foundations not in place. Organisations attempting sophisticated deployment without the platforms, storage, access and integration to support it — "trying to run before they can walk."
  4. Poor governance structure. Unclear decision rights, late involvement of risk functions, no mechanism to stop.
  5. Lack of understanding about AI project finance. Absent ring-fenced funding, misaligned incentives, and cannibalisation of the very data and cloud investments AI depends on.
  6. Lack of understanding about AI project management. Managing R&D-like work as deterministic IT projects, producing overruns of two to three times in cost and time.

Note what is absent from this list: the technology not working. In practice, models rarely fail. Organisations fail to prepare for them, fund them, govern them, manage them or adopt them.

• Silent degradation. Performance declines gradually as conditions change. Nobody notices because nobody is measuring. This is the most common live-system risk and the easiest to control — define a performance metric and a threshold at deployment.
  • Automation bias in operation. Human reviewers who approve everything because the system is usually right. Human oversight becomes a formality. Test this deliberately: track how often reviewers override, and investigate if the rate approaches zero.
  • Scale of error. A human error affects one case; a systematic model error affects every case until detected. Speed of detection matters more than probability of error.
  • Dependency. Once a process is built around an AI system, the manual capability atrophies. What happens when the vendor has an outage, changes the model, or raises prices sharply?
  • Data leakage. Staff entering confidential information into external tools. Usually inadvertent, occasionally catastrophic, and best addressed through provision and training rather than prohibition.

Capgemini's research identifies the leading CXO concerns as legal risks, explainability, data transparency and governance. In practice:

  • Data protection. Requirements on personal data use are tightening across jurisdictions. Know what data each system uses, on what basis, and where it is processed — including whether it leaves the country.
  • Explainability. If a decision affecting a person cannot be explained, it is difficult to defend to that person, to a regulator or to a court. This constrains which use cases are appropriate for opaque systems.
  • Contractual exposure. Vendor terms frequently disclaim liability for output. Read who bears the loss when the system is wrong; it is usually you.
  • Intellectual property. Both the status of AI-generated content and the risk of generated content resembling protected material.
  • Reputation. Often the largest practical exposure. A discriminatory outcome, a fabricated statement sent to a customer, or a data leak becomes a story about your judgement, not about the technology. Reputational damage does not require legal breach.

Most organisations will access AI through third parties, which transfers execution but not accountability. Five questions worth answering before signing and reviewing annually:

  • Continuity. How dependent are we, and how quickly could we operate without them? Many AI vendors are young and unprofitable.
  • Change. Can they alter the underlying model, and would we know? Behaviour can shift materially with no change on your side.
  • Data. Where is it processed, who can access it, and is it used to train models for others?
  • Pricing. Usage-based costs scale with adoption. What is the exposure if usage triples?
  • Exit. Can we retrieve our data in a usable form, and what would migration actually cost?

Concentration is the under-considered risk. If several critical processes depend on one provider, you have created a single point of failure across your operations — a position you would not accept in any other supplier relationship.

sections.h: Risks specific to generative and agentic systems
sections.html:
• Fabrication. Confident, fluent, false output — including invented figures, citations, regulations and names. The defining risk of generative systems.
  • Prompt injection. Instructions hidden in a document, email or web page that the system reads and follows, causing it to behave contrary to your intent. Materially more dangerous where the system can act rather than only respond.
  • Inconsistency. The same question can produce different answers. Problematic wherever consistency is a fairness or compliance requirement.
  • Scope creep in agents. A system given a goal may take an unanticipated route to achieve it. Constrain by explicit permission rather than by prohibition — define what it may do, not what it may not.
  • Compounding errors. In multi-step agentic work, an early mistake propagates and amplifies through subsequent steps.

Design this before you need it. Six steps:

  1. Detect. Monitoring thresholds, plus a genuinely safe channel for staff to report bad output.
  2. Contain. A named person who can suspend the system immediately, without a committee.
  3. Assess. What was affected, over what period, how many cases, what harm.
  4. Remediate. Correct affected cases, notify those affected where appropriate.
  5. Learn. Why did detection take as long as it did? That is usually the more important question than why the error occurred.
  6. Report. To the executive and, for material incidents, to the board.

Test the containment step in advance. The number of organisations that discover mid-incident that nobody actually has the technical ability to switch a vendor system off is not small.

sections.h: The other side: the cost of inaction
sections.html:
A module on risk must state the counterweight, and the WEF states it plainly: managers must have room to fail, as long as they can course-correct and learn. Shutting down all risk will likely lead to the firm falling behind in the competitive race.

The risks of excessive caution are real and less visible than the risks of action:

  • Competitors build capability and cost advantage while you deliberate
  • Your people use unapproved tools anyway, without training or oversight
  • You lose the staff who wanted to work somewhere that was learning
  • You skip the small, cheap mistakes that build institutional judgement — and make your first mistake a large one

The correct posture is neither prohibition nor enthusiasm. It is controlled experimentation: small, bounded, well-governed initiatives with real stopping criteria, which build capability and judgement while limiting exposure. That is a management discipline, not a technology strategy.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: run the switch-off drill
practitioner.text: Pick one AI system currently in use and ask, in a management meeting: "If this started producing harmful output at nine tomorrow morning, who switches it off, how, and how long would it take?" If the answer requires a vendor support ticket, a committee, or a person who is on leave, you have found a serious gap that costs nothing to fix and would cost a great deal to discover during a live incident.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Score your organisation against each of the six WEF failure causes on a scale of 1 (fully exposed) to 5 (well controlled), with one line of evidence for each. Identify your two weakest. Then write the incident response process for your highest-risk system — naming the person who can suspend it, the detection threshold, and the escalation path. Verify the containment step is actually possible.

takeaways: None of the WEF's six failure causes is 'the technology did not work' — organisations fail, models rarely do
Silent degradation is the most common live-system risk and the easiest to control with a metric and a threshold
If human reviewers never override the system, oversight has become a formality — track the override rate
Vendor arrangements transfer execution but not accountability; concentration across processes is a single point of failure
Prompt injection is materially more dangerous where a system can act rather than only respond
Test containment in advance — many organisations cannot actually switch a vendor system off
Excessive caution is itself a risk; controlled experimentation with real stopping criteria is the correct posture

quiz.q: Reviewing the WEF's six principal causes of AI initiative failure, which is notably absent?
opts: The technology itself not working
Weak governance
Capability gaps
Poor data quality
quiz.fb: Models rarely fail. Organisations fail to prepare for, fund, govern, manage or adopt them.

quiz.q: A human reviewer approves virtually every AI recommendation without amendment. This indicates:
opts: Training was effective
Human oversight has become a formality and the override rate should be investigated
No further action is needed
The system is performing excellently
quiz.fb: Automation bias converts oversight into rubber-stamping. Track override rates and investigate if they approach zero.

quiz.q: 'Prompt injection' describes:
opts: A method of improving output quality
A pricing model
Hidden instructions in a document or web page that the system reads and follows, contrary to your intent
Typing too quickly
quiz.fb: It is materially more dangerous in agentic systems, where the system can act on the injected instruction rather than merely respond.

quiz.q: When several critical processes depend on a single AI vendor, the organisation has created:
opts: A regulatory requirement
An efficient procurement arrangement
A cost advantage only
A single point of failure across operations
quiz.fb: Concentration is the under-considered vendor risk — a position you would not accept in any other supplier relationship.

quiz.q: After an AI incident, the most important learning question is usually:
opts: Why did detection take as long as it did?
How much did it cost?
Which vendor was responsible?
Who authorised the system?
quiz.fb: Errors will occur. Speed of detection is the variable you control, and it determines the scale of the consequence.

quiz.q: The WEF's position on organisations that attempt to eliminate all AI risk is that they will likely:
opts: Reduce costs significantly
Fall behind in the competitive race
Achieve superior compliance outcomes
Improve staff morale
quiz.fb: The correct posture is controlled experimentation — small, bounded, well-governed initiatives with real stopping criteria.

management.title: Implementation: From Pilot to Production
objectives: Manage an AI initiative through its four lifecycle stages
Design a pilot that produces a decision rather than an impression
Understand why organisations get stuck in pilot purgatory and how to avoid it
Apply stage gates and stopping criteria
Manage the transition from pilot to production
Establish the monitoring that keeps a live system trustworthy

sections.html:
The WEF's implementation guidance frames the AI lifecycle in four stages, each with distinct management requirements:

  1. Design. Define the problem, the success measure, the data, the human oversight and the failure modes. Most implementation failures are traceable to this stage being rushed.
  2. Development. Build or configure, prepare data, test against the defined measure. Expect this to take longer than estimated — this is where the 80% data effort lands.
  3. Deployment. Integrate into workflow, train users, run in parallel, transition. The technical work is usually the smaller part of this stage.
  4. Monitoring. Continuous, permanent. Performance, drift, usage, incidents, value delivered.

The management error that recurs is treating stage four as optional and stage one as a formality. Both are backwards.

sections.h: Designing a pilot that produces a decision
sections.html:
A pilot exists to answer a question, not to demonstrate enthusiasm. Before starting, write down five things:

  1. The question. "Can this reduce document processing time by at least 30% without increasing errors?" — not "can we use AI here?"
