  2. The baseline. Current performance, measured before anything changes. Without this, no pilot can produce a conclusion.
  3. The threshold. The result that means proceed, and the result that means stop. Agreed in advance, in writing, by the people who will make the decision.
  4. The duration. Long enough for a real signal, short enough to force a decision. Six to twelve weeks suits most cases.
  5. The scope. One team, one process, a defined volume.

A pilot without a pre-agreed stopping threshold cannot fail — which means it also cannot succeed, because no result changes anyone's mind. It becomes an expensive way of postponing a decision.

The most common state for AI in mid-sized organisations is a collection of pilots that neither scale nor stop. The causes are identifiable and each has a remedy:

  • No baseline, so results are contested indefinitely. → Measure before starting.
  • No decision owner for scaling. → Name them at the outset, alongside the threshold.
  • No scaling budget. The pilot was funded; production was not. → Fund the pilot and the scale-up decision together, contingent on the threshold.
  • Pilot conditions were unrepresentative — best data, most enthusiastic team, hand-held support. → Pilot in ordinary conditions, not ideal ones.
  • Integration was never addressed, so the pilot ran alongside the real process rather than inside it. → Require the integration path at design stage.
  • Nobody is willing to stop it. → Make stopping a documented, blameless outcome that appears in reporting as a completed experiment.

Deeper dive: the honest pilot

A pilot run with the best data, the most capable team and vendor engineers on hand tells you what is possible under ideal conditions. Production has ordinary data, ordinary staff and no vendor on site. If you want a pilot that predicts production, degrade the conditions deliberately: use a normal team, normal data quality and normal support. A slightly disappointing honest pilot is far more valuable than an impressive misleading one.

Fund and govern in stages, each with a written decision:

  • Gate 1 — Design approved. Problem, baseline, threshold, data confirmed available, risk tier assigned, owner named. Releases pilot funding.
  • Gate 2 — Pilot result. Measured against threshold. Three outcomes only: proceed, iterate once with a revised threshold, or stop. "Continue as is" is not an outcome.
  • Gate 3 — Production readiness. Integration, training, monitoring, oversight, rollback and incident process all in place. Releases production funding.
  • Gate 4 — Post-implementation review, at six months. Did the value materialise? If not, why, and does the system continue?

Gate 4 is the one organisations skip, and it is the one that builds institutional judgement. Without it you never learn whether your business cases were realistic, and every subsequent case repeats the same optimism.

Six things must be true before a system goes live, and the technical readiness is only one of them:

  1. Integration. It sits inside the workflow, not beside it. Anything requiring staff to leave their normal system will decay.
  2. Training delivered, including how to recognise and challenge bad output.
  3. Oversight defined. Who reviews what, how often, with what authority.
  4. Monitoring live — metric, threshold, named recipient of alerts.
  5. Rollback tested. Can you revert to the previous process, and has anyone actually tried?
  6. Support arranged. Who does a user ask when it behaves oddly, and is that person real and available?

Run in parallel where the stakes justify it: the new system operates alongside the existing process, outputs are compared, and you transition only when confidence is evidenced rather than assumed. It costs more for a period and it is the single most reliable protection against a bad go-live.

Four things, reviewed monthly and reported quarterly:

  • Performance against the metric defined at design. Alert on threshold breach.
  • Usage. Falling usage is the earliest signal that something is wrong — users stop before they complain.
  • Override rate. Rising means declining performance or declining trust; near-zero means oversight has become a formality. Both require investigation.
  • Value. Is the benefit in the business case actually appearing in the operational numbers?

Assign monitoring to a named person with the time to do it. Monitoring that is everyone's responsibility is nobody's, and the first indication of failure will come from a customer rather than from your own systems.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: write the stop condition first
practitioner.text: Before a pilot begins, have the decision-maker write and sign one sentence: "If, after ten weeks, X is not at least Y, we will stop this." It takes two minutes and it changes the character of the entire initiative — because from that point the pilot is an experiment with a defined answer rather than a commitment gathering momentum. It also makes stopping a professional outcome rather than a personal defeat, which is what makes stopping possible at all.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Design the pilot for the use case you have been developing through this programme. Write all five elements — question, baseline, threshold, duration, scope — and name the person who will make the go/no-go decision. Then work through the six production-readiness conditions and identify which your organisation could not currently satisfy. Those gaps are the real work of implementation.

takeaways: The four stages are design, development, deployment and monitoring — design is rushed and monitoring is treated as optional
A pilot needs a question, a baseline, a pre-agreed threshold, a duration and a scope
A pilot without a stopping threshold cannot fail, and therefore cannot succeed
Pilot under ordinary conditions, not ideal ones, if you want it to predict production
Fund the pilot and the scale-up decision together, or you will build things you cannot deploy
Gate 4, the six-month post-implementation review, is what builds institutional judgement about your own business cases
Falling usage is the earliest signal of a failing system — users stop before they complain

quiz.q: A pilot with no pre-agreed stopping threshold is problematic because:
opts: Vendors will not support it
It costs more to run
It cannot fail, and therefore cannot succeed — no result changes anyone's mind
It breaches governance rules
quiz.fb: Without a threshold agreed in writing in advance, the pilot becomes an expensive way of postponing a decision.

quiz.q: To make a pilot predictive of production performance, you should run it with:
opts: The largest possible volume
No measurement, to avoid bias
The best available data, the most capable team and vendor engineers on site
Ordinary data quality, an ordinary team and ordinary support
quiz.fb: A slightly disappointing honest pilot is far more valuable than an impressive misleading one.

quiz.q: Which gate do organisations most commonly skip, at the greatest cost to institutional learning?
opts: The six-month post-implementation review
Pilot result review
Production readiness
Design approval
quiz.fb: Without it you never learn whether your business cases were realistic, and every subsequent case repeats the same optimism.

quiz.q: Declining usage of a deployed AI system should be interpreted as:
opts: A training scheduling problem
The earliest signal that something is wrong — users stop before they complain
Evidence of successful automation
A minor administrative issue
quiz.fb: Usage is a leading indicator. By the time complaints arrive, the system has usually been failing for some time.

quiz.q: At Gate 2, the pilot result review, the permitted outcomes are:
opts: Proceed only
Any outcome the project team prefers
Proceed, iterate once with a revised threshold, or stop
Proceed or continue as is
quiz.fb: 'Continue as is' is not an outcome — it is how pilots become permanent without ever being decided upon.

quiz.q: Running a new system in parallel with the existing process before transition is valuable because:
opts: It shortens the project
Vendors require it
It is cheaper
Outputs can be compared, so transition happens on evidenced confidence rather than assumption
quiz.fb: It costs more for a period and is the single most reliable protection against a bad go-live.

management.title: Leading the Transformation: Your Twelve-Month Plan
management.summary: Bringing it together into something you can act on Monday
objectives: Synthesise the programme into a coherent, sequenced twelve-month plan
Set realistic expectations with your board and your organisation
Understand the specific considerations for organisations in developing markets
Know what to do in the first ninety days
Build the leadership habits that sustain the work beyond the first initiative
Complete your capstone AI strategy

sections.html:
Four independent bodies of research have informed this programme. Their conclusions converge in a way that should shape your plan:

  • Deloitte (550 leaders): outcomes are driven by who decides. Distributed decision rights across technology, finance and strategy lenses outperform concentrated ownership, by very large margins.
  • The World Economic Forum: initiatives fail for organisational reasons — capability, data, foundations, governance, finance and project management — not technical ones.
  • Capgemini (500 CXOs): executives are already using AI in strategic work, quietly and without frameworks; the gains accrue to those who use it to challenge their thinking, and the binding constraint is confidence and governance rather than technology.
  • Enterprise practice: value comes from AI integrated across functions with strategic alignment, data foundations and human–AI collaboration — not from isolated pilots.

The common thread is unambiguous. AI is a management problem that happens to involve technology. Every constraint in the evidence is one a leadership team can act on directly, without any technical capability at all.

Months 1–3: Establish and inventory.

  • Name the executive owner and set the decision-rights table (Module 3)
  • Build the register of AI already in use, and issue the acceptable use policy (Module 9)
  • Provide an approved, safe tool so shadow use has an alternative
  • Run the opportunity sweep across every function (Module 4)
  • Complete the readiness assessment with evidence (Modules 2 and 7)
  • Deliver executive and management AI literacy (Module 8)

Months 4–6: Prove.

  • Select two or three use cases from the high-value, high-feasibility quadrant
  • Build full business cases including baselines and stop conditions (Module 6)
  • Run pilots under ordinary conditions, with thresholds agreed in writing (Module 11)
  • Begin the data foundation work the next wave will require (Module 7)
  • Have the employment conversation with your people before the first deployment (Module 8)

Months 7–9: Decide and scale.

  • Take pilot decisions at Gate 2 — proceed, iterate once, or stop. Stop at least one, publicly and without blame
  • Move the successful case to production against the six readiness conditions
  • Establish monitoring with a named owner
  • Report measured value to the board against baseline, not activity

Months 10–12: Institutionalise.

  • Run the first post-implementation reviews and compare outcome to business case
  • Extend literacy training to the staff groups now affected
  • Refresh the use-case pipeline with what you have learned
  • Set the following year's strategy and budget on evidence rather than enthusiasm

What to tell your board at the outset — because saying it now costs far less than explaining it later:

  • The first year builds capability; it does not transform the business. Expect measurable improvement in two or three processes, not a step change in results.
  • Some initiatives will be stopped. This is the design working, not a failure of management.
  • A meaningful share of the investment goes to foundations that produce no direct return but make everything subsequent possible.
  • Timelines will move. Data work consistently takes longer than estimated — plan for it rather than apologising for it.
  • Efficiency gains require a decision to realise them. Time saved converts to value only if roles change or growth is absorbed.

A leadership team that sets these expectations at the start retains credibility through the inevitable difficulties. One that promises transformation in year one spends year two defending itself.

sections.h: Considerations for organisations in developing markets
sections.html:
Several constraints are more binding in markets such as Nepal, and each has a workable response:

  • Scarce specialist talent, and international competition for it. Response: train existing staff rather than attempting to hire specialists, and partner externally for infrequent technical work with mandatory knowledge transfer.
  • Weaker data foundations, with more paper-based and fragmented records. Response: begin with document and language use cases that need little structured data, while building foundations for the next wave.
  • Cost sensitivity and currency exposure on usage-priced international tools. Response: model usage growth explicitly, negotiate caps, and monitor consumption monthly rather than annually.
  • Regulatory uncertainty. Response: govern to a defensible internal standard rather than waiting for rules, so that when they arrive you are adjusting rather than starting.
  • Language. Model performance in Nepali and other regional languages is weaker than in English. Test on your actual material before committing, not on a vendor's demonstration.

There is also a genuine advantage. Organisations without decades of legacy systems and entrenched process can adopt more quickly than large incumbents, and the absence of a heavy existing technology estate removes a constraint that slows many larger organisations considerably.

sections.h: The first ninety days — five actions
sections.html:
1. Name the owner and widen the table. Ensure the technical, financial, strategic and operational lenses are present in every AI decision. Free, and Deloitte's evidence suggests it is the highest-leverage change available.
  2. Build the register. Two weeks. You cannot govern what you have not inventoried.
  3. Issue the policy and provide an approved tool. Converts invisible shadow use into a managed practice.
  4. Run the opportunity sweep. Four questions to every function head. Generates the pipeline and the ownership.
  5. Use the tools yourself, visibly. Including where they failed. This does more for adoption than any communication programme.

None of the five requires technical capability, significant budget or external assistance. All five can begin this month.

• Ask the three questions of every proposal: which decision does it improve, what happens when it is wrong, what data does it need.
  • Form your own view before consulting the model. Protects the judgement your organisation is paying for.
  • Require baselines. No initiative starts without a measured before.
  • Keep stopping things. An organisation that never stops an initiative is not experimenting; it is accumulating.
  • Keep the register current. Quarterly, permanently.
  • Talk to your people about it honestly. Repeatedly, not once.

The organisations that will do well with AI over the coming decade are not those with the largest budgets or the newest tools. They are those whose leadership teams built the habit of deciding well about it — early, cheaply, and with the whole management table in the room.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: pick one thing and start it this week
practitioner.text: The most common outcome of a programme like this is a thoughtful plan that is never executed, because it requires a strategy day that never gets scheduled. Avoid that: select one of the five ninety-day actions and start it before this week ends. The register is usually the best choice — it requires only emails to function heads, it produces findings that create their own urgency, and it makes every subsequent step concrete.

activity.title: Capstone: your AI strategy
activity.text: Assemble the work from across this programme into a document of no more than six pages for your board or management committee: (1) the one-page strategy from Module 2, (2) your maturity and readiness assessment with evidence, (3) the decision-rights table from Module 3, (4) your top three prioritised use cases from Module 4 with the full business case for the first, (5) your governance structure, policy and register from Module 9, and (6) the twelve-month sequence with named owners and the five ninety-day actions. Then present it. A strategy that stays in a drawer is indistinguishable from no strategy at all.

takeaways: The evidence converges: AI is a management problem that happens to involve technology
Sequence the year as establish and inventory, prove, decide and scale, then institutionalise
Tell the board at the outset that year one builds capability rather than transforming the business
In developing markets, train rather than hire, start with document and language use cases, and test regional-language performance on your own material
The absence of a heavy legacy estate is a genuine adoption advantage
Five ninety-day actions require no technical capability, no budget and no consultant
An organisation that never stops an initiative is not experimenting — it is accumulating
Start one action this week; the register is usually the right choice

quiz.q: The common conclusion across the Deloitte, WEF and Capgemini research is that:
opts: AI is fundamentally a management problem that happens to involve technology
Only large organisations can succeed with AI
Technical sophistication is the primary driver of AI returns
Governance is less important than speed
quiz.fb: Every constraint identified in the evidence is one a leadership team can act on directly, without technical capability.

quiz.q: What should a leadership team tell its board about the first year of an AI programme?
opts: That returns are guaranteed
That it builds capability, delivers measurable improvement in two or three processes, and that some initiatives will be stopped
That it will transform business results
That no investment in foundations is required
quiz.fb: Teams that set honest expectations at the start retain credibility through difficulty; those promising transformation spend year two defending themselves.

quiz.q: For an organisation in a market with weaker data foundations, the recommended starting point is:
opts: Hire an international data science team
Wait until an enterprise data programme is complete
Begin with document and language use cases that need little structured data, while building foundations for the next wave
Avoid AI entirely
quiz.fb: Different use cases have different data requirements. Sequencing matters more than waiting for perfect foundations.

quiz.q: Which first-ninety-days action does Deloitte's evidence suggest is the highest-leverage and costs nothing?
opts: Purchasing an enterprise AI platform
Commissioning a consultancy review
Hiring a chief AI officer
Widening the decision table so technical, financial, strategic and operational lenses are all present
quiz.fb: Outcomes peak when decision rights are distributed among complementary leaders. Widening the table is free.

quiz.q: An organisation that has never stopped an AI initiative is most likely:
opts: Accumulating rather than experimenting
Exceptionally well managed
Following best practice
Under-investing
quiz.fb: If every initiative continues, the stopping criteria are not real and the portfolio is not being managed.

quiz.q: A genuine advantage for organisations in developing markets pursuing AI is:
opts: Lower regulatory standards
The absence of decades of legacy systems and entrenched process, allowing faster adoption
Cheaper international software
Fewer competitors
quiz.fb: A heavy existing technology estate is a constraint that slows many larger incumbents considerably.

agile-developers.title: Why Agile Exists
agile-developers.summary: The problem it was invented to solve — start here if it is all new
objectives: Explain how software was built before agile, and why it often went wrong
Describe what iterative delivery changes about risk
Use the basic vocabulary correctly in a team conversation
Recognise that agile is a family of approaches, not one method
Know what this course will and will not teach you

sections.html:
This course is for software developers, testers, and computing students who are new to agile — or who have been working in an agile team without anyone ever explaining why things are done this way.

It assumes you can write code. It assumes nothing else. Every term is defined when it first appears, and nothing here requires prior experience of Scrum, Kanban or any tool.

By the end you will understand how a sprint works, how to write and size a piece of work, how to keep quality high while moving fast, and how to be a useful member of a team rather than a person who writes code alone. There is a companion course, Agile Methodologies for Managers, covering funding, governance and organisational design. This one is about your daily work.

sections.h: How software used to be built
sections.html:
The traditional approach is called waterfall, because work flows downward through fixed phases and does not come back up:

  1. Requirements. Business analysts write down everything the system must do.
  2. Design. Architects design the whole system from that document.
  3. Implementation. Developers build it.
  4. Testing. Testers check the finished system.
  5. Deployment and maintenance. It goes live and is then supported.

Each phase finishes before the next begins, and each produces a document the next phase depends on. On paper this is orderly and easy to plan. It is still the correct approach for some work — building a bridge, for instance, where changing your mind after pouring concrete is genuinely expensive.

sections.h: Why it often failed for software
sections.html:
Waterfall assumes three things that are usually false in software:

  • That the customer knows what they want at the start. Usually they know roughly, and discover the detail by seeing something.
  • That requirements will not change. Over a two-year project the market changes, competitors ship things, laws change and staff leave.
  • That you can estimate accurately from a document. Software estimates made before any code exists are notoriously unreliable.

The result was a recognisable pattern: a team would work for eighteen months, deliver, and find that the customer no longer wanted what was specified — or never had. All the testing happened at the end, so all the bad news arrived at once, at the point when there was no time or money left to respond.

The core insight

The problem was not that people made mistakes. Mistakes are unavoidable. The problem was how long it took to find out. If you are wrong in week two and discover it in week eighty, you have wasted seventy-eight weeks. If you discover it in week four, you have wasted two.

Agile approaches attack that specific problem. Instead of one long cycle, you run many short ones. Each cycle — typically one to four weeks — contains a little planning, a little design, some building, some testing, and a review with whoever the software is for.

At the end of each cycle you have something that actually works. It does very little at first, but it runs, and someone can look at it and react.

Three things follow from that:

  • Feedback arrives constantly instead of at the end, so being wrong is cheap.
  • Risk is retired early. If the hardest part cannot be made to work, you find out in month one.
  • Priorities can change between cycles without the whole plan collapsing.

Two words you will hear constantly. Iterative means repeating a cycle to improve something. Incremental means delivering it in finished pieces. Agile is normally both: you build a small usable piece, then improve it, then add the next.

sections.h: Agile is a family, not a method
sections.html:
There is no single thing called "agile". It is an umbrella term for approaches sharing a set of values. The ones you will meet:

  • Scrum — fixed-length cycles called sprints, with defined roles and meetings. The most widely used, and Modules 3 and 4 cover it.
  • Kanban — continuous flow with limits on how much work is in progress at once. No sprints. Module 7.
  • Extreme Programming (XP) — a set of technical practices such as test-driven development and pair programming. Modules 8 to 11.
  • Scrumban — a common mix of Scrum's structure and Kanban's flexibility.

Most real teams use a combination and call it Scrum. That is normal and not a failure.

• Sprint / iteration — one fixed-length work cycle, usually two weeks.
  • Backlog — the ordered list of everything the team might build.
  • User story — one small piece of wanted behaviour, written from the user's point of view.
  • Increment — the working software produced by a sprint.
  • Standup — the short daily team meeting.
  • Retrospective — the meeting where the team improves how it works.
  • Definition of done — the shared standard a piece of work must meet before it counts as finished.
  • Velocity — how much a team completes per sprint, used for forecasting.

Each of these gets a full treatment later. For now you only need to recognise them.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask why, not just what
practitioner.text: In your first weeks on an agile team you will be told to do things — attend this meeting, size that story, update this board. The developers who become genuinely good at this are the ones who ask what each practice is for. A standup exists so the team can spot blockers early; if yours has become a status report to a manager, it has stopped doing its job. Knowing the purpose lets you tell the difference between a practice that is working and a ritual that is being performed.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Think of a piece of software you have built or worked on. Write down one assumption about it that turned out to be wrong. Then answer two questions: how long did it take to discover, and what would it have cost to discover in the first two weeks instead? That difference is the entire argument for iterative delivery, and you have just made it with your own example.

takeaways: Waterfall assumes requirements are known upfront and will not change, which is rarely true in software
The real problem was not making mistakes but how long it took to discover them
Short cycles produce working software early, so being wrong becomes cheap
Iterative means repeating to refine; incremental means delivering in finished pieces
Agile is a family of approaches sharing values, not one prescribed method
Most real teams blend frameworks, which is normal rather than a failure
Learn the purpose of each practice, not just the mechanics

quiz.q: In waterfall development, all testing typically happens:
opts: At the end, so problems surface together and late
Continuously throughout each phase of the project
Before implementation begins on the codebase
In parallel with the requirements gathering stage
quiz.fb: Bad news arrives at the point when there is least time and money left to respond to it.

quiz.q: The core problem agile was designed to solve is:
opts: That developers write too much untested code
That it took too long to discover a mistake
That documentation was too expensive to produce
That teams were too large to coordinate well
quiz.fb: Being wrong in week two and finding out in week eighty wastes seventy-eight weeks of effort.

quiz.q: 'Incremental' delivery means:
opts: Repeating a cycle to gradually refine one thing
Increasing team size as the project progresses
Delivering the work in finished, usable pieces
Adding more detail to the requirements document
quiz.fb: Iterative means repeating to refine. Agile is usually both at once, but the two words are not interchangeable.

quiz.q: Which statement about agile approaches is accurate?
opts: Agile is a single method with defined mandatory steps
Scrum and agile are two words for the same thing
Only Scrum qualifies as a genuinely agile approach
It is a family of approaches that share common values
quiz.fb: Scrum, Kanban and XP are all agile. Most teams blend them, which is entirely normal.

quiz.q: Waterfall remains a reasonable choice when:
opts: Requirements are genuinely stable and change is costly
The technology being used is entirely unfamiliar to the team
The customer wants to see progress frequently
The team is inexperienced with iterative delivery
quiz.fb: Building a bridge is the standard example: changing your mind after pouring concrete is genuinely expensive.

agile-developers.title: The Agile Manifesto in Plain Language
agile-developers.summary: What the four values and twelve principles actually mean for your work
objectives: State the four values and explain each in your own words
Avoid the common misreadings that damage teams
Connect the twelve principles to daily developer practice
Recognise when a team is following the words but missing the point
Understand what sustainable pace means and why it is in there

sections.html:
In February 2001, seventeen software practitioners met and wrote a short document setting out what they had each found to work. It is called the Agile Manifesto. It is four value statements and twelve principles, and it is about a page long.

It is worth reading in full at some point — it takes five minutes. Almost everything in this course descends from it.

Each is written as a preference between two things, both of which have value:

  • Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
  • Working software over comprehensive documentation
  • Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
  • Responding to change over following a plan

The authors added a line that is nearly always left out when people quote it: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more."

The misreadings to avoid

"Working software over documentation" does not mean write no documentation. "Responding to change over following a plan" does not mean work without a plan. Teams that read it that way end up with no design records, no onboarding material and no forecast — and then blame agile. The statement is about which one wins when the two genuinely conflict.

sections.h: What each value means at your desk
sections.html:
• Individuals and interactions. If you are stuck, walk over and ask — do not spend two days working around a problem someone could explain in five minutes. A process that stops people talking is a broken process.
  • Working software. Code that runs and is tested is the evidence of progress. A detailed design document for something not yet built proves nothing. This is why teams demonstrate working software rather than presenting slides.
  • Customer collaboration. Talk to whoever the software is for, regularly. A developer who has never seen a user work is guessing.
  • Responding to change. When a requirement changes, that is information, not betrayal. Your job is to make the codebase easy to change, which is what Modules 8 to 11 are about.

The principles expand the values. Grouped by what they ask of you:

About delivery:

  • Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
  • Deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, preferring the shorter timescale.
  • Working software is the primary measure of progress.

About change:

  • Welcome changing requirements, even late in development.
  • Business people and developers must work together daily.

About people:

  • Build projects around motivated individuals; give them the environment and support they need, and trust them.
  • Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient way to convey information within a team.
  • The best architectures, requirements and designs emerge from self-organising teams.
  • Sponsors, developers and users should be able to maintain a constant pace indefinitely.

About quality and improvement:

  • Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility.
  • Simplicity — maximising the work not done — is essential.
  • At regular intervals the team reflects on how to become more effective, then adjusts.

sections.h: Two principles developers should take personally
sections.html:
"Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility." This is the sentence that makes agile a technical discipline rather than a meeting schedule. You can only respond to change quickly if the code is easy to change. Every shortcut you take today reduces tomorrow's agility. This is not a moral argument about craftsmanship — it is a mechanical claim about what makes fast change possible.

"Sustainable pace, indefinitely." Agile explicitly rejects the crunch-and-collapse cycle. The reasoning is practical rather than sentimental: tired developers write defects, and defects cost more to fix than the hours saved. If your team is regularly working weekends to make a sprint, the sprint is being over-committed and the retrospective should say so.

sections.h: Following the words, missing the point
sections.html:
You will meet teams doing all the ceremonies with none of the intent. The signs:

  • The standup is a status report to a manager rather than the team coordinating itself.
  • Retrospectives produce actions that are never done, and nobody mentions it.
  • Scope and deadline are both fixed from outside, so nothing can actually adapt.
  • "Working software" is demonstrated but is not tested and cannot ship.
  • Estimates are treated as commitments and used to apply pressure.

Naming this early in your career is useful. It does not make you cynical — it makes you accurate, and it is the first step toward being someone who improves a team rather than merely complying with it.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the strongest principle to quote
practitioner.text: When you need to argue for time to write tests, refactor a nasty module, or fix the build, quote this one: "Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design enhances agility." It reframes quality work from a developer indulgence into the thing that makes future speed possible. Managers who would dismiss "I want to refactor this" will often accept "this module is why our last three estimates were wrong." Say it in terms of future delivery speed, because that is genuinely what it is.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Read the Agile Manifesto in full — it takes five minutes. Then pick the three principles your current or most recent team follows least well. For each, write one specific thing you could do yourself, without needing anyone's permission, that would move it slightly. Those three actions are within your control regardless of how your team is run.

takeaways: The four values are preferences between two valuable things, not prohibitions
Working software is the primary measure of progress, not documents or slides
A changed requirement is information rather than betrayal
Technical excellence is what makes fast change mechanically possible
Sustainable pace is practical, not sentimental — tired developers write defects
Simplicity, defined as maximising work not done, is an explicit principle
Ceremonies without intent are common; naming that accurately is useful

quiz.q: 'Working software over comprehensive documentation' means that:
opts: Only user-facing documentation has any real value
Working software wins when the two genuinely conflict
Documentation should not be produced by agile teams at all
Documentation is written only after release
quiz.fb: The Manifesto explicitly says there is value in the items on the right. Teams that read it as elimination end up with no onboarding material.

quiz.q: Which principle most directly supports a developer asking for time to refactor?
opts: Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient method
Working software is the primary measure of progress
Technical excellence and good design enhance agility
Business people and developers must work together daily
quiz.fb: It reframes quality work from indulgence into the mechanism that makes future change fast.

quiz.q: The Manifesto's principle of sustainable pace exists mainly because:
opts: Labour regulations in most countries require strict limits on working hours
Long hours reduce the accuracy of story estimates
Sponsors prefer predictable weekly resource costs
Tired developers introduce defects that cost more than the hours saved
quiz.fb: The reasoning is practical rather than sentimental. Regular weekend work means sprints are being over-committed.

quiz.q: A daily standup that has become a status report to a manager has:
opts: Lost its purpose, which is the team coordinating itself
Become more efficient by removing team discussion
Matured into a properly governed management reporting mechanism
Been correctly adapted for distributed working
quiz.fb: Knowing the purpose of each practice lets you tell a working practice from a performed ritual.

quiz.q: The principle 'simplicity — the art of maximising the work not done' asks you to:
opts: Use the simplest programming language available to you
Avoid building things that are not actually needed
Write code as quickly as circumstances permit
Reduce the number of team meetings held
quiz.fb: The cheapest, fastest and most reliable feature is the one you correctly decided not to build.

quiz.q: When a requirement changes late in development, the agile response is to treat it as:
opts: A reason to extend the current deadline
A change request requiring formal approval
Information the team should incorporate
A failure of the original analysis work
quiz.fb: Your job is to keep the codebase easy to change, which is what the technical practices modules are about.

agile-developers.title: Scrum: Roles, Events and Artefacts
agile-developers.summary: The framework you are most likely to be working in
objectives: Name the three roles and describe what each is responsible for
Describe each Scrum event and what it is for
Explain the three artefacts and who owns each
Understand what a sprint goal is and why it matters
Recognise the most common ways Scrum is done badly

sections.html:
Scrum organises work into sprints — fixed-length cycles, usually one to four weeks, most commonly two. Every sprint follows the same rhythm, and the length does not change between sprints. That consistency is deliberate: it makes the team's output measurable and its forecasts meaningful.

The goal of each sprint is a potentially releasable increment — something finished enough that it could ship, whether or not it actually does.

• Product Owner. One person responsible for maximising the value of the product. They own and order the Product Backlog, decide what gets built next, and act as the voice of the customer. When you need to know whether something is in scope, you ask them. Critically, priority is their decision, not the team's and not a manager's.
  • Scrum Master. Serves the team by removing impediments, facilitating the events, and protecting the team from interruption. They are not the team's boss and do not assign work. A good one makes themselves progressively less necessary.
  • Developers. Everyone doing the building — programmers, testers, designers, anyone whose work goes into the increment. The team is self-managing: it decides how to do the work and who does what.

Note what is absent: there is no team lead assigning tasks, and no separate testing department. If your team has these, it is running a hybrid — common, and worth understanding as a deliberate variation rather than assuming the book is wrong.

Sprint Planning — at the start. The Product Owner presents the highest-priority backlog items; the team selects what it believes it can complete; together they agree a sprint goal; the team breaks the items into tasks. Typically two hours per week of sprint length.

Daily Scrum (standup) — every day, 15 minutes, same time and place. Each person covers what they did yesterday, what they will do today, and what is blocking them. It is for the team, to coordinate and surface blockers early — not a report to management. If it regularly runs long, the detailed conversation should move to a smaller group afterwards.

Sprint Review — at the end. The team demonstrates working software to stakeholders and collects feedback. This validates whether the sprint goal was met and lets the backlog be adjusted. It is a working session, not a presentation.

Sprint Retrospective — after the review. The team examines how it worked rather than what it built: what to keep, what to fix, and what specific actions to try next sprint. Module 12 covers this in depth.

Backlog Refinement — continuous rather than a formal event, but universally practised. The team reviews upcoming items, clarifies them, estimates effort, breaks large ones down, and removes or reorders items as priorities change.

• Product Backlog. The ordered list of everything wanted — features, improvements and fixes. Owned by the Product Owner, continuously updated. It is never complete.
  • Sprint Backlog. The items selected for this sprint, plus the tasks needed to complete them, plus the sprint goal. Owned by the developers, and it can be adjusted during the sprint as the team learns — provided the sprint goal remains the focus.
  • Increment. The working, tested output of the sprint, meeting the definition of done.

The most under-used part of Scrum. A sprint goal is a single sentence describing what this sprint is trying to achieve — for example, "a customer can register and log in."

It matters for a practical reason. Without a goal, a sprint is just a list of unrelated tickets, and when the team runs short of time it has no basis for deciding what to drop. With a goal, the decision is easy: anything not serving the goal goes first. It also gives the team something to say at the review beyond "we did these fourteen things."

sections.h: How Scrum is commonly done badly
sections.html:
• Sprints with no goal — a list of tickets with a date attached.
  • The standup as a status meeting where everyone reports to the Scrum Master or a manager.
  • No definition of done, so "finished" means something different to each person.
  • Work carried over every sprint, which usually means items are too large or the team is over-committing.
  • The Product Owner is unavailable, so the team guesses at requirements and builds the wrong thing politely.
  • Retrospective actions are never completed, which teaches the team that the meeting is theatre.
  • Testing pushed to the last two days, recreating waterfall inside a two-week box. This is the most common and most damaging.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: know your sprint goal
practitioner.text: At any point in a sprint you should be able to state the sprint goal in one sentence without looking it up. If you cannot, and nor can your teammates, your team is running sprints without goals — which means it is really running two-week batches of unrelated tickets. Raise it at the next retrospective. It is a small change that immediately improves what the team can decide when time runs short, and it is one of the few improvements a junior developer can propose without stepping on anyone's role.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: For your current or most recent sprint, write down: the sprint goal, who the Product Owner is, what your definition of done says, and how many items were carried over from the previous sprint. If you cannot answer two or more of these, you have found the most useful thing to raise at your next retrospective — and this module gives you the language to raise it constructively.

takeaways: Sprints are fixed-length, most commonly two weeks, and the length does not change between them
The Product Owner decides priority; the Scrum Master serves; the developers self-manage
The Sprint Backlog belongs to the developers and can be adjusted if the goal is kept
The daily standup is for the team to coordinate, not to report to a manager
A sprint goal tells the team what to drop when time runs short
Regular carry-over usually means items are too large or the team over-commits
Pushing all testing to the final days recreates waterfall inside a two-week box

quiz.q: Who decides the order of items in the Product Backlog?
opts: The Scrum Master, who facilitates the process
The development team, by consensus vote
The delivery manager or department head
The Product Owner, who owns product value
quiz.fb: Priority is the Product Owner's decision. When you need to know whether something is in scope, you ask them.

quiz.q: The Sprint Backlog is owned by:
opts: The developers who selected the work
The Scrum Master who tracks progress
The Product Owner who prioritised it
Whoever sponsors the initiative financially
quiz.fb: It can be adjusted during the sprint as the team learns, provided the sprint goal remains the focus.

quiz.q: The primary purpose of the daily standup is:
opts: Allowing management to track sprint progress
The team coordinating and surfacing blockers early
Reporting individual progress to the Scrum Master
Assigning the day's tasks to team members
quiz.fb: If it regularly overruns, move the detailed discussion to a smaller group immediately afterwards.

quiz.q: A sprint goal is valuable mainly because it:
opts: Provides a metric for measuring team velocity
Gives the Product Owner a reporting mechanism
Tells the team what to drop when time runs short
Satisfies a formal requirement of the Scrum framework
quiz.fb: Without one, a sprint is a list of unrelated tickets and the team has no basis for deciding what to sacrifice.

quiz.q: A team completes all coding by day eight and does all testing on days nine and ten. This:
opts: Reduces the risk of defects reaching production
Is an efficient use of specialist tester time
Is standard practice in mature Scrum teams
Recreates waterfall inside a two-week container
quiz.fb: It is the most common and most damaging way Scrum is done badly, because bad news still arrives at the end.

quiz.q: Work being carried over into the next sprint every time usually indicates:
opts: Items are too large, or the team is over-committing
The Product Owner is prioritising incorrectly
The definition of done is unnecessarily strict
The sprint length should be extended to three weeks
quiz.fb: Both causes are fixable, and the retrospective is where the team should be raising it.

agile-developers.title: Your First Sprint
agile-developers.summary: What actually happens, day by day, and how to be useful in it
objectives: Know what to expect in each part of a sprint
Participate usefully in planning, standup and review
Ask for help at the right moment rather than too late
Understand what 'done' means before you start work
Avoid the mistakes new developers most commonly make

sections.html:
The team gathers. The Product Owner explains the highest-priority items. The team asks questions until the work is clear, then decides how much it can take on.

What to do as a newcomer: ask questions, even ones you think are obvious. "What should happen if the user enters nothing here?" is a genuinely useful question and is frequently unanswered. Every ambiguity you surface in planning is one you will not have to guess at on day six.

What to avoid: staying silent because you do not want to look inexperienced. The cost of an unasked question is paid later by the whole team.

Before the meeting ends you should know: the sprint goal, which item you are starting, and what "done" means for it.

In most teams you pull work rather than being assigned it — you take the highest-priority item you are able to do. If you are new, it is entirely reasonable to say "I would like to take this one, but I will need help with the database part."

Before writing any code:

  1. Read the acceptance criteria. If there are none, ask for them (Module 5).
  2. Check the definition of done. Does it require tests? A code review? Documentation?
  3. Look for something similar already in the codebase and follow its patterns.
  4. Say how you plan to approach it in the standup or to one teammate. Thirty seconds here has saved a great many wasted days.

Fifteen minutes, standing, same time each day. Three things: what you did yesterday, what you will do today, what is blocking you.

A good standup contribution is specific and short: "Yesterday I finished the login form validation. Today I am starting the password reset email. I am blocked on the SMTP credentials — Anisha, could I get five minutes after this?"

Two rules that matter more than they appear:

  • Say you are blocked, immediately. The single most common new-developer mistake is being quietly stuck for two days. Nobody is impressed by silent struggle; they are frustrated by discovering it late.
  • Take detail offline. If two people begin debugging in the standup, someone should say "let's take that after."

The two-hour rule

A useful convention for anyone new to a codebase: if you have been stuck on the same problem for two hours with no progress, ask. You have shown you tried, and you have not yet burned a day. Most teams will tell you this is exactly the behaviour they want, and almost nobody does it without being told.

This is where sprints quietly go wrong. Things to watch:

  • Finish things before starting new ones. Three items at 80% is worth nothing at the sprint review; one item done is worth something.
  • Update the board honestly. The board is how the team sees itself. An item sitting in "in progress" for eight days is a signal, and hiding it removes the team's ability to help.
  • Raise slippage early. If by day six you know your item will not be finished, say so on day six. The team can re-plan on day six; it cannot on day ten.
  • Do not silently expand scope. Noticing an unrelated improvement is good; adding it without telling anyone is not. Put it in the backlog.

The team demonstrates what it built to stakeholders. If you built something, you will often be asked to demo it.

How to demo well: show the working software rather than slides, walk through it as a user would, keep it short, and be honest about what is not finished. Say "this handles the main path; error handling is next sprint" rather than avoiding the topic and hoping nobody clicks.

Feedback at a review is about the product, not about you. Stakeholders asking for changes is the process working exactly as intended — it is far cheaper to hear it now than after release.

• Being stuck in silence. The most common and the most costly.
  • Saying "nearly done" for several days running. If it has been nearly done for three days, it is not nearly done.
  • Taking on more than one item at a time to look productive.
  • Skipping tests to finish faster, which fails the definition of done and creates work for someone else.
  • Not asking what "done" means before starting.
  • Treating estimates as promises and then working late to protect them rather than reporting the change.
  • Staying quiet in the retrospective. New team members notice things everyone else has stopped seeing, and that perspective has a short shelf life.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: say the uncomfortable thing on day six
practitioner.text: The most valuable habit you can build in your first year is reporting bad news early. On day six of a ten-day sprint, when you first suspect your item will not be finished, say so. It feels like admitting failure and it is the opposite — it gives the team four days to respond instead of none. Developers who do this reliably become trusted very quickly, because the team learns that when you say something is on track, it is.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: For your next work item, before writing any code, write down four things: what "done" means for it, the acceptance criteria, one thing you are unsure about, and who you will ask. Then set yourself the two-hour rule and actually keep it. At the end of the item, note whether asking earlier would have saved time — it usually would have.

takeaways: Ask the obvious question in planning; unasked questions are paid for later by everyone
Before coding, check acceptance criteria, the definition of done, and existing patterns
Say you are blocked immediately — silent struggle impresses nobody and costs days
Apply the two-hour rule when new to a codebase
Three items at 80% are worth nothing at the review; one finished item is worth something
Raise slippage on day six, when the team can still re-plan
Demo working software honestly, including what is not finished

quiz.q: You have been stuck on the same problem for two hours with no progress. You should:
opts: Raise it at the next scheduled retrospective
Ask for help, having demonstrated a genuine attempt
Continue for the rest of the day before asking
Move on to a different item and return to it later
quiz.fb: You have shown you tried and have not yet burned a day. Most teams explicitly want this behaviour.

quiz.q: On day six of a ten-day sprint you realise your item will not be finished. The right action is:
opts: Wait until day nine when you are certain
Work additional hours to protect the estimate
Tell the team immediately so it can re-plan
Quietly reduce the scope of the item
quiz.fb: The team can re-plan on day six and cannot on day ten. Reporting early is what makes a developer trusted.

quiz.q: Having three items at 80% complete at the sprint review is:
opts: A sign of good parallel working across the team
Better than one finished item, since it shows broad progress
Acceptable if the remaining work is documented
Worth nothing, whereas one finished item is worth something
quiz.fb: Finish work before starting new work. Partial items deliver no value and cannot be demonstrated.

quiz.q: During a sprint review, a stakeholder asks for a significant change. This means:
opts: The process is working exactly as intended
The requirements analysis was done poorly
The team should have demonstrated less
The change must wait for the next release
quiz.fb: Hearing it now is far cheaper than hearing it after release. Feedback is about the product, not about you.

quiz.q: Before starting work on an item, you should first check:
opts: How long similar items took previously
What the definition of done requires
Who else is available to help you
Whether the item can be split further
quiz.fb: Also read the acceptance criteria and look for an existing pattern in the codebase to follow.

quiz.q: Noticing an unrelated improvement while working on an item, you should:
opts: Add it while you are already in that code
Leave it entirely for someone else to find
Put it in the backlog and mention it
Fix it and note it in the commit message
quiz.fb: Silently expanding scope makes your work unpredictable and hides effort from the team's planning.

agile-developers.title: User Stories and Definition of Done
agile-developers.summary: How work gets described, and how you know when it is finished
objectives: Read and write a user story in the standard format
Write acceptance criteria that remove ambiguity
Apply the INVEST qualities to judge whether a story is ready
Split a large story into smaller useful ones
Understand what a definition of done is and why it is shared

sections.html:
A user story is a short description of something a user wants, written from their point of view. The standard format:

As a [type of user]
I want [some capability]
So that [some benefit]

For example: "As a registered customer, I want to reset my password by email, so that I can get back into my account without contacting support."

The format matters less than what it forces. It makes you name who the work is for and why it is worth doing. A ticket saying "add password reset endpoint" tells you what to build but not what problem it solves — which means you cannot make good decisions when the detail turns out to be ambiguous.

The most important part is the third line

The "so that" clause is what lets you push back usefully. If you cannot work out what benefit a story delivers, that is worth raising — sometimes the answer is genuinely valuable and was simply not written down, and sometimes nobody can articulate it, which is a useful discovery before you spend a week building it.

sections.h: A story is a placeholder for a conversation
sections.html:
This is the idea most often missed by people new to agile. A user story is deliberately not a specification. It is short because it is meant to prompt a discussion between the developer and the Product Owner, not to replace one.

Practically, this means: when you pick up a story and something is unclear, that is not a defect in the story. That is the story working as designed. Go and ask.

Acceptance criteria are the specific, checkable conditions that must be true for the story to be accepted. They turn a general intention into something testable.

For the password reset story:

  • A user can request a reset link by entering a registered email address.
  • An unregistered email produces the same confirmation message, revealing nothing.
  • The link expires after one hour.
  • The link can only be used once.
  • The new password must meet the existing password policy.
  • The user is notified by email that their password changed.

Notice that the second and sixth criteria are security requirements a developer might not have thought to ask about. Good acceptance criteria surface exactly this kind of thing before you build.

A common alternative format is Given / When / Then: "Given a registered user, when they request a password reset, then an email containing a one-hour link is sent." Both are fine; use whichever your team uses.

A widely used checklist for judging a story. A good story is:

  • Independent — can be built without waiting for another story where possible.
  • Negotiable — the details can still be discussed; it is not a fixed contract.
  • Valuable — delivers something a user or the business would recognise as worth having.
  • Estimable — the team understands it well enough to size it. If it is not estimable, you need more information or a spike.
  • Small — completable within a single sprint, ideally in a few days.
  • Testable — you can demonstrate objectively that it works.

As a developer, the two you will use most are estimable and testable. If you cannot size it, say so in refinement. If you cannot describe how you would prove it works, the acceptance criteria are not finished.

Large stories are the most common cause of work carrying over between sprints. Useful ways to split:

  • By workflow step. Registration, then email verification, then profile setup — rather than all of onboarding at once.
  • By business rule. Handle the standard case first; discounts, exceptions and edge rules become separate stories.
  • By data variation. Support one file format now, others later.
  • Happy path first. The main success path as one story, error handling as another. Common and effective, provided the error handling is genuinely scheduled.
  • By interface. Get it working via the API, then add the user interface.

The wrong way to split is by technical layer — "build the database table", "build the service", "build the UI". Each piece delivers nothing on its own, cannot be demonstrated, and cannot be tested end to end. If your team splits this way, none of your stories are independently valuable.

The definition of done is a single shared checklist that applies to every story. It is not per-story; acceptance criteria are per-story. The definition of done is the team's standard for what "finished" means.

A typical one:

  • Code written and meets the team's style standards
  • Unit tests written and passing
  • Code reviewed and approved by another developer
  • Integrated into the main branch with the build passing
  • Acceptance criteria verified
  • No known defects of medium severity or above
  • Documentation updated where the change affects it
  • Deployed to a test environment

The reason this exists is that without it, "done" means different things to different people — and the difference is discovered at the sprint review, or in production. A shared definition also protects you: if the definition says tests are required, then taking the time to write them is not you being slow, it is you meeting the team's agreed standard.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask for the acceptance criteria
practitioner.text: If you are handed a story with no acceptance criteria, ask for them before starting. The most effective way is not to complain about the ticket but to write your own understanding and check it: "I am reading this as — reset link valid one hour, single use, same message for unknown emails. Is that right?" This takes two minutes, it almost always surfaces at least one thing you had wrong, and it makes you look thorough rather than obstructive.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Take a feature you have built recently and write it as a user story with the three-line format, then write at least five acceptance criteria for it. Check the story against INVEST. Finally, look at your team's definition of done — if there is not one written down, draft what you think it should be and take it to the next retrospective.

takeaways: A user story names who the work is for and why it is worth doing
The 'so that' clause is what lets you push back on work with no clear benefit
A story is a placeholder for a conversation, not a specification
Acceptance criteria surface security and edge-case requirements before you build
INVEST: independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable
Split by workflow, business rule, data or happy path — never by technical layer
The definition of done is one shared checklist, and it protects you as well as the product

quiz.q: The 'so that' clause in a user story exists to:
opts: Record who requested the feature originally
Provide text for the release notes later
Satisfy the standard user story template format correctly
State the benefit, so decisions can be made sensibly
quiz.fb: If nobody can articulate the benefit, that is a useful discovery before a week is spent building it.

quiz.q: You pick up a story and find part of it ambiguous. This means:
opts: The story is working as designed — go and ask
The story is defective and should be rejected
The Product Owner has not done their job properly
You should make a reasonable assumption and proceed
quiz.fb: A story is deliberately short because it is meant to prompt a conversation, not replace one.

quiz.q: Which is the wrong way to split a large user story?
opts: Splitting by business rule, handling the standard case first
Splitting by technical layer, such as database then UI
Splitting by workflow step in the user journey
Splitting the happy path from error handling
quiz.fb: Each layer delivers nothing alone, cannot be demonstrated, and cannot be tested end to end.

quiz.q: In INVEST, 'estimable' means that:
opts: The work can be completed within one sprint
The story has already been given a point value
The team understands it well enough to size it
The estimate has been approved by the Product Owner
quiz.fb: If a story is not estimable, you need more information or a time-boxed spike to investigate.

quiz.q: The definition of done differs from acceptance criteria in that it:
opts: Is written by the Product Owner for each story
Is reviewed and updated during sprint planning
Only applies to stories involving user interfaces
Is one shared checklist applying to every story
quiz.fb: Acceptance criteria are per-story. The definition of done is the team's standard for what finished means.

quiz.q: A well-written acceptance criterion is primarily:
opts: Specific and objectively checkable
Written in the Given/When/Then format
Short enough to fit on one line
Agreed with the whole team in planning
quiz.fb: Given/When/Then is one valid format among several. What matters is that the condition can be verified.

agile-developers.title: Estimation and Velocity
agile-developers.summary: Story points, planning poker, and what estimates are actually for
objectives: Explain why relative sizing is used instead of hours
Participate in planning poker effectively
Understand what velocity is and how it should be used
Recognise when estimates are being misused as commitments
Know what to do when an estimate turns out to be wrong

sections.h: Why not just estimate in hours?
sections.html:
Humans are consistently poor at estimating absolute duration and considerably better at comparison. You may not know how long it takes to walk to the next town, but you can say with confidence that it is about twice as far as the market.

Story points use this. Instead of "this will take 14 hours", the team says "this is about twice the size of that one." Points are a measure of overall size — combining effort, complexity and uncertainty — and they are relative to the team's own reference stories.

Two consequences worth understanding early:

  • Points are meaningless between teams. One team's 5 has no relationship to another's. Anyone comparing point totals across teams is misusing them.
  • Points do not convert to hours. The moment someone declares "a point is four hours", you have reinvented hour estimation with an extra step.

Most teams size using 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 — the gaps widen as the numbers grow. This is deliberate: it reflects that large things are inherently more uncertain, and it stops unproductive arguments about whether something is a 6 or a 7.

A rough convention:

  • 1–2 — small and well understood; a day or less.
  • 3–5 — a typical story; a few days.
  • 8 — large; consider splitting.
  • 13 or more — too big for a sprint. Split it or run a spike first.

Many teams also use ? for "we do not understand this yet" — which is a genuinely useful answer and should trigger a conversation rather than a guess.

The standard technique, and its design is cleverer than it appears:

  1. The Product Owner explains the story; the team asks questions.
  2. Everyone privately chooses a card.
  3. Everyone reveals at the same time.
  4. If estimates differ widely, the highest and lowest explain their reasoning.
  5. Discuss, then re-vote. Usually two rounds is enough.

The simultaneous reveal exists to prevent anchoring — if the senior developer speaks first, everyone converges on their number and the team learns nothing.

The real value is step four. When one person says 2 and another says 13, they are not disagreeing about arithmetic; they know different things. The person who said 13 may know the module has no tests. The person who said 2 may know a library already handles it. That conversation is the point, and the number produced at the end is a by-product.

Velocity is the number of story points a team completes in a sprint. After a few sprints you have an average, and that average forecasts future work: 120 points of backlog at 20 points per sprint suggests roughly six sprints.

Used properly, velocity is a forecasting tool for the team. Rules that keep it useful:

  • Only count finished items. Partial credit destroys the measurement.
  • Use a rolling average of three to six sprints, not the single last figure.
  • Expect variation. Holidays, incidents and departures all move it.
  • Never compare between teams. The unit is not shared.

The misuse to watch for

If velocity becomes a target — "we need to increase velocity by 20%" — the team will simply estimate more generously. The number rises, delivery does not change, and the organisation has destroyed its own forecasting tool while learning nothing. If this starts happening around you, it is worth naming clearly at a retrospective.

sections.h: When an estimate turns out to be wrong
sections.html:
Estimates are wrong routinely. That is expected and is not a failure. What matters is what you do next.

  1. Say so as soon as you know. Not when the sprint ends.
  2. Say why, specifically. "The legacy module has no tests, so I have had to add them before I can change anything safely" is useful. "It is taking longer" is not.
  3. Do not re-estimate the item mid-sprint. Changing the number to match reality corrupts your velocity history. Leave the estimate and let the sprint outcome reflect what happened.
  4. Take it to the retrospective. If the same category of thing is repeatedly underestimated, that is a pattern worth fixing.

Sometimes you genuinely cannot estimate because you do not know enough. The answer is a spike: a time-boxed piece of investigation — "spend one day finding out whether this library can do what we need" — whose output is knowledge rather than shippable code.

Two rules. The time box is fixed: when the day is up, you stop and report what you found, even if the answer is "still unclear". And the spike's output should let the team estimate the real story afterwards, which is how you know whether it worked.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: speak up when your number is different
practitioner.text: In planning poker, when your estimate is far from everyone else's, resist the urge to quietly change it. If you voted 13 and the team voted 3, you know something they do not — or you have misunderstood something. Both are worth five seconds of everyone's time. New developers routinely fold their estimate to match the group, which removes exactly the information the technique was designed to surface. The number matters far less than the reason behind it.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Take five items your team completed recently and, without looking at the original estimates, size them relative to each other using the Fibonacci scale. Then compare with what was actually estimated and how long each really took. Note which ones you would size differently now, and why — that reasoning is the skill you are building.

takeaways: People estimate comparison far better than absolute duration, which is why points are relative
Story points are meaningless between teams and do not convert to hours
The widening Fibonacci gaps reflect genuine uncertainty in larger items
Simultaneous reveal in planning poker exists to prevent anchoring on a senior voice
The discussion between a 2 and a 13 is the point; the number is a by-product
Velocity used as a target produces estimate inflation and no delivery change
Do not re-estimate mid-sprint — it corrupts the history you forecast from

quiz.q: Story points measure size relative to:
opts: A fixed number of hours agreed by the team
The team's own previous reference stories
An industry standard complexity scale
The Product Owner's assessment of value
quiz.fb: This is why one team's 5 has no relationship to another team's 5, and why comparison across teams is a misuse.

quiz.q: Everyone reveals their planning poker card simultaneously in order to:
opts: Ensure the Scrum Master can record all votes
Make the process feel fair to junior members
Prevent anchoring on the first opinion voiced
Save time during the estimation session
quiz.fb: If the senior developer speaks first, everyone converges on their number and the team learns nothing.

quiz.q: When two team members estimate a story as 2 and 13, the valuable part is:
opts: Averaging the two numbers to reach 7
Asking the Product Owner to decide between the two numbers
Re-reading the acceptance criteria together
Their explanations, since they know different things
quiz.fb: One may know the module has no tests; the other may know a library already handles it. That is the information you want.

quiz.q: Setting a target to increase team velocity by 20% will typically produce:
opts: Estimate inflation with unchanged actual delivery
More accurate sizing of large backlog items
Better forecasting accuracy over several sprints
A genuine improvement in delivery throughput
quiz.fb: The number rises, delivery does not change, and the organisation has destroyed its own forecasting tool.

quiz.q: You discover mid-sprint that your item is much larger than estimated. You should:
opts: Re-estimate the item to reflect the true size
Report it immediately and leave the estimate alone
Complete it in your own time to protect the sprint
Move it to the next sprint without discussion
quiz.fb: Changing the number mid-sprint corrupts the velocity history you forecast from. Report the specific reason instead.

quiz.q: A spike is best described as:
opts: A story that exceeds thirteen story points
An urgent defect requiring immediate attention
A time-boxed investigation producing knowledge
A sudden unplanned increase in workload
quiz.fb: When the time box expires you stop and report, even if the answer is still unclear.

agile-developers.title: Kanban and Flow
agile-developers.summary: The other main approach, and why limiting work makes you faster
objectives: Describe how Kanban differs from Scrum
Explain why work-in-progress limits increase throughput
Read a Kanban board and identify bottlenecks
Understand cycle time and why it is measured
Recognise which kinds of work suit Kanban better

sections.html:
Kanban has no sprints, no fixed roles, and no timeboxes. It has three things:

  1. A visualised workflow — a board with a column for each stage the work passes through.
  2. Work-in-progress (WIP) limits — a maximum number of items allowed in each column.
  3. A focus on flow — reducing the time an item takes to travel from request to done.

Work is pulled continuously. When you finish something, you take the next item. There is no two-week commitment and no sprint boundary.

sections.h: Why limiting work makes you faster
sections.html:
This is the counter-intuitive core of Kanban, and it is worth understanding properly because it will feel wrong at first.

Imagine a team of five with fifteen items in progress. Everyone is busy, so utilisation looks excellent. But each person is switching between three things, every switch costs time to reload context, and items sit half-finished waiting for a review or an answer. Nothing finishes.

Now limit work in progress to five. People finish what they started before taking anything new. When someone is blocked, they cannot simply start something else — so they go and help unblock, or fix the underlying problem.

Starting less work finishes more work. The limit converts individual busyness into team throughput, and the discomfort of an idle moment is exactly what forces the team to fix its bottleneck rather than route around it.

What a WIP limit really does

It makes problems visible immediately. If the "code review" column is permanently at its limit, the team can see that reviews are the bottleneck. Without the limit, work simply piles up there quietly and everyone starts something new instead. A board with no WIP limits is just a to-do list on a wall.

A simple board might have: Backlog, Ready, In Progress, Review, Testing, Done. What to look for:

  • A column consistently at its limit — that is your bottleneck, and it is where improvement should be focused.
  • Items sitting still for days — usually blocked, sometimes forgotten. Either way it should be raised.
  • Work piling up before a stage — the queue indicates the stage after it cannot keep pace.
  • Items moving backwards — usually a quality signal; work is failing review or testing and returning.

A useful team habit is to walk the board right to left in the daily meeting, focusing on getting things finished rather than reporting what each person did. Right-to-left keeps the team's attention on completion.

• Cycle time — how long from starting an item to finishing it.
  • Lead time — how long from the request arriving to it being finished, including waiting in the backlog.

Customers experience lead time. Teams usually control cycle time most directly.

The value of measuring cycle time is that it supports honest forecasting without estimation: if 85% of your items finish within six days, you can tell someone "this will most likely be done within six days" without sizing anything. Many mature Kanban teams stop estimating entirely on this basis.

sections.h: When Kanban fits better than Scrum
sections.html:
• Interrupt-driven work. Support, operations and maintenance teams cannot commit to two weeks of scope, because urgent work arrives daily. Sprint commitment becomes a fiction they fail every cycle.
  • Highly variable item sizes. When work ranges from ten minutes to three weeks, sprint planning has little meaning.
  • Continuous delivery. Teams releasing several times a day gain little from a two-week boundary.
  • Very small teams. Two people may find Scrum's full event set heavier than the coordination it provides.

Many teams end up with Scrumban: sprint planning and retrospectives kept for rhythm and improvement, WIP limits and continuous pull adopted for the daily work. This is extremely common and entirely legitimate.

sections.h: What this means for you daily
sections.html:
• Finish before you start. The strongest single habit in this module.
  • When blocked, do not start something new by default. First try to unblock it, or help someone finish theirs.
  • Keep the board accurate. A board that does not reflect reality is worse than no board, because decisions get made from it.
  • Watch your own work in progress. If you personally have three things open, you are the bottleneck.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: limit yourself to one item
practitioner.text: Whatever your team does, try limiting yourself to one item at a time for two weeks. When you are blocked, resist starting something new — spend that time getting unblocked, reviewing someone's code, or helping finish work already in progress. Most developers find they complete more, not less, and the reason is that finishing has value while starting does not. It is also the easiest way to feel why WIP limits work, rather than just accepting the argument.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: For ten recently completed items, record the date work started and the date it was finished, and calculate cycle time for each. Sort them and find the value below which 85% fall. That number is your team's realistic delivery expectation for a typical item — and it is more useful for answering "when will this be done" than any estimate.

takeaways: Kanban is visualised workflow, WIP limits and a focus on flow — no sprints or fixed roles
Starting less work finishes more work, because switching and queueing dominate
A WIP limit makes bottlenecks visible instead of letting work pile up quietly
A board with no WIP limits is a to-do list on a wall
Walk the board right to left to keep attention on finishing
Cycle time supports forecasting without estimation
Interrupt-driven and highly variable work suits Kanban better than Scrum

quiz.q: Limiting work in progress increases throughput because it:
opts: Allows managers to allocate the work more evenly across people
Shortens the time spent in planning meetings
Forces developers to work at a faster pace
Reduces context switching and exposes bottlenecks
quiz.fb: The discomfort of an idle moment is what forces the team to fix its bottleneck rather than route around it.

quiz.q: A Kanban board without work-in-progress limits is:
opts: Effectively a to-do list on a wall
Still valid, provided cycle time is measured
Suitable only for maintenance work
A correct implementation for small teams
quiz.fb: Without limits, work piles up quietly at the bottleneck and everyone simply starts something new.
