quiz.q: A column that is consistently at its WIP limit indicates:
opts: Items in that column are too large
That stage is the team's bottleneck
The team is working at full capacity
The limit has been set too low
quiz.fb: That is where improvement effort should be focused, and the limit is what made it visible.

quiz.q: The difference between cycle time and lead time is that lead time:
opts: Measures only the active working period
Applies to Scrum teams rather than Kanban
Includes waiting in the backlog before work starts
Is measured in story points rather than in calendar days
quiz.fb: Customers experience lead time; teams most directly control cycle time.

quiz.q: Which kind of team most clearly suits Kanban over Scrum?
opts: A team of eight working on one large feature
A team with a stable two-week release cycle
A team building a new product from scratch
A support team receiving urgent work daily
quiz.fb: Sprint commitment becomes a fiction they fail every cycle for reasons entirely outside their control.

quiz.q: When you are blocked on your current item, the better default is to:
opts: Work on unblocking it or help finish other work
Start the next item to stay productive
Wait until the next standup to raise it
Pick up a small unrelated maintenance task instead
quiz.fb: Finishing has value; starting does not. This is the practical meaning of a WIP limit at the individual level.

agile-developers.title: Extreme Programming: The Technical Practices
agile-developers.summary: The practices that make sustained iteration actually possible
objectives: Explain why technical practices are essential rather than optional
Describe the core XP practices and what each protects against
Understand technical debt and how to talk about it
Apply simple design and refactoring principles
Argue for quality work in terms your team will accept

sections.html:
Scrum and Kanban describe how work flows. Neither says anything about how the software is actually built. This is a genuine gap, and it is the reason many teams find that agile "stopped working" after a year.

Here is the mechanism. Agile promises you can respond to change. Responding to change means modifying existing code. If the code is difficult to modify — untested, tangled, poorly named — then every change is slow and risky, and the team gradually loses the ability to be agile at all. The ceremonies continue; the agility disappears.

Extreme Programming is the framework that addresses this directly. Its practices are what make iteration sustainable over years rather than months.

• Test-driven development. Write a failing test, make it pass, then improve the code. Module 9 covers this in full.
  • Continuous integration. Everyone merges to the shared main branch frequently, and every merge is automatically built and tested. Module 10.
  • Pair programming. Two developers, one task. Module 11.
  • Collective code ownership. Anyone may change any part of the codebase. Nobody owns a module privately.
  • Refactoring. Continuously improving the structure of existing code without changing its behaviour.
  • Simple design. Build the simplest thing that works now; do not build for imagined future requirements.
  • Coding standards. A shared style so any developer can read any file without friction.
  • Sustainable pace. No sustained overtime. Tired developers produce defects.
  • Small releases. Ship frequently in small pieces.

Worth dwelling on because it is culturally difficult. In many organisations one developer "owns" a module, and everyone routes changes through them.

This feels safe and creates two serious problems: that person becomes a bottleneck for every change, and when they leave — or are on holiday — nobody can safely touch that code.

Collective ownership means anyone can change anything, which only works if the supporting practices exist: tests to catch mistakes, code review to spread knowledge, and standards so unfamiliar code is still readable. The practices are not independent; each makes the others safe.

The instinct to build flexibility for imagined future requirements is nearly universal and almost always wrong. The future requirement usually does not arrive, or arrives in a different shape, and meanwhile the abstraction makes every present-day change harder.

A useful ordering for "good enough" design — the code should:

  1. Pass all its tests
  2. Reveal its intent clearly to a reader
  3. Contain no duplication
  4. Use the fewest elements possible

You will hear YAGNI — "you aren't gonna need it". It is not an argument against thinking ahead; it is an argument against building ahead. Design so that the future change is possible; do not implement it today.

Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing what it does. Renaming a variable to something meaningful, extracting a long method into smaller ones, removing duplication.

Two rules matter:

  • You need tests first. Refactoring without tests is not refactoring; it is rewriting and hoping. The tests are what let you verify behaviour did not change.
  • Do it continuously, in small pieces. Leave each piece of code slightly better than you found it. Refactoring saved up for a dedicated "cleanup sprint" never happens, because that sprint is always the one that gets cut.

Technical debt is the accumulated cost of shortcuts taken in code. The metaphor is deliberate: like financial debt, it can be a sensible choice, and like financial debt it accrues interest — every future change in that area costs more.

Two kinds worth distinguishing:

  • Deliberate debt. "We are shipping this without proper error handling to make the demo; we will fix it next sprint." Legitimate, provided it is recorded and actually repaid.
  • Accidental debt. Accumulated through inexperience or inattention, discovered later. Also normal.

How to talk about it so people listen. "This code is ugly" gets nowhere. "Changes in this module take about three times longer than elsewhere because there are no tests, which is why our last three estimates in this area were wrong" gets a hearing — because it is stated as a delivery cost, which is what it is.

sections.h: Why these get cut, and what to do
sections.html:
Under deadline pressure, technical practices are the first thing dropped: tests are skipped, review is waived, refactoring is deferred. This is understandable and it is exactly backwards, because these practices are what make the next deadline achievable.

What you can do as an individual developer:

  • Make tests part of the definition of done, so writing them is meeting the standard rather than a personal choice you must defend each time.
  • Include the quality work in the estimate rather than treating it as extra.
  • Refactor as you go, in small pieces, so it never needs approval.
  • Quantify the cost when you raise it, using delivery language.
  • Bring it to the retrospective with a specific example rather than a general complaint.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: leave it better than you found it
practitioner.text: You will rarely be given permission to refactor. So do not ask for it as a separate activity — make it part of how you work. When you are already changing a file, spend five extra minutes renaming a confusing variable or extracting a long method. It is within the work you were already doing, it needs no approval, and across a team over a year it is the difference between a codebase that decays and one that improves. The large refactoring nobody ever authorises is the one you avoid needing.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Find the file in your codebase that developers most dread changing. Write down specifically why: no tests, unclear naming, too long, too many responsibilities. Then estimate how much longer a typical change there takes compared with a well-maintained area. Bring that comparison to your next retrospective — stated as a delivery cost, not a complaint.

takeaways: Scrum and Kanban say nothing about how software is built, which is a real gap
If code is hard to change, agility disappears while the ceremonies continue
Collective code ownership removes bottlenecks but requires tests, review and standards to be safe
YAGNI argues against building ahead, not against thinking ahead
Refactoring without tests is rewriting and hoping
Technical debt accrues interest — every future change in that area costs more
State quality problems as delivery costs, with numbers, and people listen

quiz.q: Why do technical practices matter to a team's long-term agility?
opts: They are required by the Scrum framework rules
Responding to change means changing code, which must stay easy
They reduce the number of meetings the team is required to hold
They allow more accurate story point estimation
quiz.fb: If code is hard to modify, the ceremonies continue while the actual agility disappears.

quiz.q: Collective code ownership requires which supporting practices to be safe?
opts: Separate branches for each area of the codebase
A dedicated technical lead approving all changes
Tests, code review and shared coding standards
Detailed design documents and architecture reviews
quiz.fb: The XP practices are not independent — each one makes the others safe to apply.

quiz.q: 'YAGNI' argues against:
opts: Writing tests for code that is unlikely to change
Thinking about future requirements at all
Refactoring code that currently works
Building for imagined future requirements today
quiz.fb: Design so the future change is possible; do not implement it now. The imagined requirement usually arrives in a different shape.

quiz.q: Refactoring a module that has no test coverage is:
opts: Rewriting and hoping, rather than refactoring
Safe provided the code is reviewed afterwards
Acceptable if changes are kept small
The standard approach for legacy systems
quiz.fb: Tests are what let you verify that behaviour did not change, which is the definition of refactoring.

quiz.q: The most effective way to raise a technical debt problem is to:
opts: Raise it directly with senior management
State it as a measurable delivery cost
Refuse to make further changes to that area
Describe the code quality issues in detail
quiz.fb: 'Changes here take three times longer because there are no tests' gets a hearing. 'This code is ugly' does not.

quiz.q: Technical practices are usually dropped first under deadline pressure, which is backwards because they:
opts: Are required by the organisation's quality policy
Improve team morale during difficult periods
Are what make the next deadline achievable
Take less time than most developers assume
quiz.fb: Include quality work inside the estimate rather than treating it as an optional extra to be defended.

agile-developers.title: Testing and Test-Driven Development
agile-developers.summary: How to move fast without breaking things
objectives: Describe the main levels of automated testing and what each is for
Explain the test-driven development cycle and why the order matters
Write a test that is useful rather than merely present
Understand the test pyramid and why shape matters
Know how to add tests to code that has none

sections.h: Why developers test their own code now
sections.html:
In waterfall, developers wrote code and a separate testing team checked it afterwards. Agile removes that separation, and the reason is timing rather than trust: if testing happens weeks after the code was written, the feedback arrives too late to be cheap, and the developer has forgotten the context.

The practical target is that a change can be verified in minutes, automatically. That is what makes it safe to release every two weeks, and it is what makes refactoring possible at all.

• Unit tests. Test one small piece — usually a function or class — in isolation. Very fast, typically milliseconds. You should have many.
  • Integration tests. Test that pieces work together, often involving a real database or an external service. Slower, and you need fewer.
  • End-to-end tests. Drive the whole system as a user would. Slowest, most brittle, and the most valuable when they pass. Keep few.
  • Manual and exploratory testing. A human deliberately trying to break things and noticing what automation cannot — that something is confusing, ugly or wrong in a way no assertion captures. Still essential.

The recommended shape: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests.

The reasoning is practical. Unit tests are fast and pinpoint the failure precisely. End-to-end tests are slow and tell you only that something, somewhere, broke. A suite dominated by end-to-end tests takes an hour to run, fails intermittently for environmental reasons, and is eventually ignored — which is worse than having no suite, because the team believes it is protected.

The inverted shape — few unit tests and many end-to-end tests — is common and is called an ice-cream cone. If your build takes forty minutes and fails randomly, this is usually why.

TDD reverses the usual order. Instead of writing code and then testing it, you write the test first. The cycle is called red, green, refactor:

  1. Red. Write a small failing test for behaviour that does not exist yet. Run it and watch it fail — this confirms the test actually tests something.
  2. Green. Write the simplest code that makes it pass. Not elegant code; passing code.
  3. Refactor. Now improve the structure, with the test protecting you.

Then repeat, in cycles of a few minutes each.

Why the order matters. Writing the test first forces you to decide what the code should do before deciding how it will do it, which usually produces a cleaner interface. It guarantees every piece of code has a test, because the test existed first. And watching the test fail proves the test works — a test written afterwards that passes immediately may be testing nothing at all.

If TDD feels slow at first

It is slower for the first few weeks. That is normal and everyone experiences it. What changes is the time you stop spending on debugging, on manual re-checking, and on being afraid to change things. Most developers who persist for a month do not go back — but almost nobody finds it comfortable on day three, so do not conclude anything from that.

• It tests behaviour, not implementation. A test that breaks when you rename a private method is testing the wrong thing and will make refactoring painful.
  • It has a clear name describing what it checks. calculatesDiscountForOrdersOverFiveThousand tells you what broke; test3 does not.
  • It fails for exactly one reason. A test asserting fifteen things tells you little when it fails.
  • It is deterministic. A test that passes sometimes is worse than no test, because it trains the team to ignore failures.
  • It is readable. Tests are also documentation — often the most accurate documentation a codebase has.

A common structure is arrange, act, assert: set up the situation, do the thing, check the result. Keeping tests in that shape makes them easy to scan.

Test coverage measures the percentage of code executed by tests. It is useful for finding untested areas and misleading as a target.

Code can be 100% covered by tests that assert nothing meaningful. Coverage tells you what was run, not what was checked. Treat a low number as a warning and a high number as no guarantee at all.

More useful questions: are the important paths tested? Are the edge cases tested? If I broke this function deliberately, would a test catch it?

sections.h: Adding tests to code that has none
sections.html:
You will inherit untested code. Attempting to test all of it at once never works. What does:

  1. Write a test before every bug fix. Reproduce the bug with a failing test, then fix it. Coverage grows exactly where defects actually occur.
  2. Test what you touch. When changing a function, add tests for it first.
  3. Start with characterisation tests. If you do not know what the code should do, write tests capturing what it currently does. They are your safety net for refactoring, even if some of them document bugs.
  4. Prioritise by risk. Test the payment logic before the admin report nobody runs.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: write the failing test for every bug
practitioner.text: Make this an unbreakable personal habit: before fixing any bug, write a test that reproduces it and watch it fail. It takes a few extra minutes and gives you three things — proof you understood the bug, proof your fix actually works, and permanent protection against it returning. It is also the single easiest way to build coverage in a legacy codebase, because bugs cluster in exactly the areas that most need tests. No permission required.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Take a small function you have written recently and build it again using strict TDD — failing test first, minimum code to pass, then refactor. Notice where it felt unnatural. Then take the next bug you fix and write the failing test first. Compare how confident you feel in each fix.

takeaways: Testing moved to developers because late feedback is expensive feedback
Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests
An inverted pyramid produces slow, flaky builds that teams learn to ignore
Red, green, refactor — writing the test first shapes the interface and proves the test works
Test behaviour rather than implementation, or refactoring becomes painful
A flaky test is worse than no test because it trains the team to ignore failures
Coverage tells you what ran, not what was checked

quiz.q: In test-driven development, you watch the new test fail before writing code because it:
opts: Records the defect in the build history
Makes the subsequent code faster to write correctly
Is required by most testing frameworks
Confirms the test genuinely tests something
quiz.fb: A test written afterwards that passes immediately may be asserting nothing at all.

quiz.q: The test pyramid recommends that a suite contains:
opts: Many unit tests and very few end-to-end tests
Equal numbers of each level of test
Mostly end-to-end tests, since they are realistic
Only integration tests, to balance speed and realism
quiz.fb: An inverted shape produces a forty-minute build that fails randomly and is eventually ignored.

quiz.q: A test that passes sometimes and fails other times is:
opts: Acceptable if the failures are rare
Worse than no test, since it trains people to ignore failures
A normal and expected characteristic of integration testing
Useful for detecting timing-related defects
quiz.fb: Determinism is what makes a suite trustworthy. Once failures are routinely ignored, the suite has stopped working.

quiz.q: A test that breaks when you rename a private method is:
opts: A sign that the refactoring was done wrongly
Evidence of good coverage in that area
Testing implementation rather than behaviour
Correctly detecting a breaking change
quiz.fb: Tests coupled to implementation make refactoring painful, which defeats much of their purpose.

quiz.q: A codebase reports 100% test coverage. This tells you that:
opts: Refactoring can be done entirely safely
The code is unlikely to contain defects
All of the important behaviour has been verified
All code was executed, not that it was checked
quiz.fb: Code can be fully covered by tests that assert nothing meaningful. Treat a low number as a warning and a high number as no guarantee.

quiz.q: The most effective way to add tests to a large untested codebase is to:
opts: Write a failing test before every bug fix
Begin with end-to-end tests covering main journeys
Pause feature work for a dedicated testing sprint
Aim for a fixed coverage percentage each sprint
quiz.fb: Bugs cluster in exactly the areas that most need tests, so coverage grows where it matters most.

agile-developers.title: Continuous Integration and Delivery
agile-developers.summary: Why merging often and releasing small makes everything safer
objectives: Explain what continuous integration is and what it prevents
Understand why long-lived branches cause problems
Describe the stages of a typical build pipeline
Distinguish continuous delivery from continuous deployment
Know your responsibilities when the build breaks

sections.h: The problem: integration used to be an event
sections.html:
Historically, developers worked separately for weeks and then merged everything together near the end. That merge was a distinct, dreaded phase, because everyone had changed overlapping code and the conflicts were enormous. Teams frequently discovered that separately-working pieces did not work together at all — at the worst possible moment.

Continuous integration removes the event by making it constant. Everyone merges to the shared main branch frequently — at least daily — and every merge is automatically built and tested.

The insight is the same as elsewhere in this course: if integrating is painful, do it more often, not less. Small merges are trivial; large merges are dangerous. The pain scales non-linearly with how long you wait.

A branch open for three weeks accumulates conflicts every day someone else changes the same files. Worse, the code on that branch is not being tested against everyone else's changes, so problems are invisible until the merge.

Practical guidance:

  • Keep branches short. Hours or a day or two, not weeks.
  • Pull from main frequently so you are integrating continuously in both directions.
  • Break work into small pieces that can each be merged independently. This connects directly to story splitting in Module 5.
  • Use feature flags for incomplete work: merge the code but keep it switched off. This lets you integrate continuously without releasing half-built features.

A build pipeline runs automatically on every push. A typical sequence:

  1. Build — compile the code; fail fast if it does not.
  2. Unit tests — fast, run on everything.
  3. Static analysis — linting, style, common error patterns, security checks.
  4. Integration tests — slower, may need a database.
  5. Package — produce the deployable artefact.
  6. Deploy to a test environment automatically.
  7. End-to-end tests against that environment.

Stages are ordered fast and cheap first so that most failures are reported within a minute or two. A pipeline where you wait twenty minutes to learn about a syntax error is badly ordered.

• Continuous integration — every change is merged and automatically verified.
  • Continuous delivery — every change that passes is ready to release; the decision to release is a human one.
  • Continuous deployment — every change that passes goes to production automatically, with no human step.

Most organisations should target continuous delivery. Continuous deployment requires very strong automated testing, monitoring and the ability to roll back quickly — and it is not a maturity badge. Plenty of excellent teams deliberately keep a human release decision.

A broken main branch blocks everyone, because nobody can safely merge or release. So it takes priority over whatever you were doing.

The conventions:

  1. If you broke it, you fix it, immediately, before starting anything else.
  2. If it cannot be fixed within a few minutes, revert. Reverting is not an admission of failure; it restores everyone else's ability to work. Fix it properly on a branch afterwards.
  3. Tell the team — do not fix it silently, because others need to know whether main is trustworthy right now.
  4. Never merge on top of a broken build. You will not know whether your change works, and you make the failure harder to diagnose.
  5. Never disable a failing test to make the build pass. If a test is genuinely wrong, fix or delete it deliberately, with the team's knowledge.

The habit that quietly kills a pipeline

Once a team starts tolerating a red build — "it's just that flaky test again" — the pipeline stops providing information. Within a few months nobody looks at it, real failures hide among the noise, and the team is back to discovering problems in production. A build that is allowed to stay red is equivalent to having no build at all, and the transition happens gradually enough that nobody notices.

• Run the tests locally before pushing.
  • Push at least once a day.
  • Watch your build after pushing; do not push and walk away.
  • Keep the pipeline fast — if it becomes slow, that is a team problem worth raising.
  • Treat pipeline configuration as real code: reviewed, version-controlled and understood by more than one person.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: do not push and walk away
practitioner.text: The most common small failure of discipline is pushing at the end of the day and leaving before the pipeline finishes. If it fails, the build is broken overnight and the whole team is blocked at nine the next morning. Wait for your build. If you genuinely have to leave, say so in the team channel so someone else can revert it. This costs you five minutes occasionally and saves the team hours regularly.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Look at your team's pipeline and write down each stage and how long it takes. Identify the slowest stage and whether it could run later or in parallel. Then check your own branch history: how long do your branches typically live before merging? If the answer is more than two days, pick your next piece of work and deliberately split it so you can merge daily.

takeaways: If integrating is painful, do it more often — the pain scales non-linearly with delay
Long-lived branches accumulate conflicts and hide problems until the merge
Feature flags let you merge incomplete work without releasing it
Order pipeline stages fast and cheap first so failures report within a minute or two
Continuous delivery keeps a human release decision; continuous deployment does not
If you break the build, fix it or revert immediately — reverting is not failure
A build allowed to stay red is equivalent to having no build at all

quiz.q: Continuous integration addresses which specific problem?
opts: Teams working in different time zones
Integration being a large, risky, late event
Developers writing code without adequate tests
Releases requiring manual approval steps
quiz.fb: Small merges are trivial and large merges are dangerous, so the answer is to integrate more often rather than less.

quiz.q: You need to merge code for a feature that is not finished. The usual solution is:
opts: Ask the team to pause other merges meanwhile
Keep it on a branch until fully complete
Merge it behind a feature flag, switched off
Merge only the tests and hold back the code
quiz.fb: This lets you integrate continuously without releasing half-built functionality to users.

quiz.q: The difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment is that deployment:
opts: Requires significantly more automated testing
Includes end-to-end tests in the pipeline
Applies only to cloud-hosted applications
Releases to production with no human decision
quiz.fb: Most organisations should target continuous delivery. Keeping a human release decision is not a sign of immaturity.

quiz.q: You break the main build and cannot fix it within a few minutes. You should:
opts: Revert your change to unblock the team
Continue debugging until you find the cause
Ask a senior developer to take over the fix
Disable the failing test and fix it later
quiz.fb: Reverting is not an admission of failure. It restores everyone else's ability to work while you fix it properly on a branch.

quiz.q: Pipeline stages should be ordered so that:
opts: Static analysis runs after deployment
Fast, cheap checks run first and fail early
All stages execute fully in parallel
End-to-end tests always run before unit tests
quiz.fb: Waiting twenty minutes to be told about a syntax error means the pipeline is badly ordered.

quiz.q: A team that routinely tolerates a red build has effectively:
opts: Improved velocity by reducing interruptions
Shifted quality responsibility to testers
Lost the value of having a build at all
Adopted a more pragmatic release process
quiz.fb: Real failures hide among the noise, and the team returns to discovering problems in production.

agile-developers.title: Code Review, Pairing and Working in a Team
agile-developers.summary: How to review well, be reviewed well, and collaborate on code
objectives: Give code review feedback that improves code without damaging relationships
Receive review feedback without defensiveness
Understand pair programming and when it is worth the cost
Communicate effectively in a team, including remotely
Ask for and offer help productively

sections.html:
Code review has four purposes, and most teams only consciously pursue the first:

  1. Catching defects before they reach production.
  2. Spreading knowledge — the reviewer learns that part of the system, which is what makes collective ownership possible.
  3. Maintaining consistency so the codebase reads as though written by one person.
  4. Teaching, in both directions.

Recognising the second and third explains why review should not be concentrated in one senior person: doing so keeps knowledge exactly where it already is.

• Review promptly. A review sitting for two days blocks someone. Aim for within a few hours. This matters more than the depth of any individual comment.
  • Comment on the code, never the person. "This loop runs on every request" — not "you wrote this inefficiently."
  • Distinguish severity. Mark clearly what must change, what you suggest, and what is merely an observation. A common convention is prefixes: blocking, suggestion, nit. Without this, authors treat every comment as mandatory and reviews become exhausting.
  • Ask rather than assert when unsure. "What happens if this is null?" invites explanation; "this will break on null" may simply be wrong.
  • Say what is good. Not politeness — it tells the author which choices to repeat.
  • Do not redesign in review. If the approach is fundamentally wrong, that is a conversation, not a comment thread.
  • Approve when it is good enough. Perfect is not the standard; better than what is there, and meeting the definition of done, is.

• Keep changes small. A 50-line change gets a real review; a 2,000-line change gets approved without being read. This is the single biggest thing you control.
  • Explain the context in the description — what and why, and anything you were unsure about.
  • Review your own change first. You will catch the debug statement you left in.
  • Assume good intent. Written feedback reads more harshly than it was meant, especially across cultures and languages.
  • Respond to every comment, even if only to say you have made the change.
  • Disagree openly when you disagree. "I considered that, but chose this because X" is a perfectly good response. Review is a conversation, not an instruction.

The thing to internalise early

Comments on your code are not criticism of you. Every developer, at every level of experience, has their code reviewed and changed. The developers who improve fastest are the ones who treat review as free expert attention on their work rather than as an examination to be passed. That reframing is worth making deliberately in your first year, because the habit sticks.

Two developers, one task, working together. Traditionally one drives (types) while the other navigates (thinks ahead, spots problems), swapping regularly.

The obvious objection is that it halves output. The evidence is more interesting: pairs produce fewer defects and better designs, and the time saved on debugging and rework often offsets much of the cost. It is not always worth it, but it is worth it more often than the arithmetic suggests.

When pairing is clearly worth it:

  • Complex or high-risk work where a mistake is expensive
  • Onboarding — far faster than documentation for transferring context
  • Unfamiliar parts of the system
  • When one person has been stuck for a while

When it usually is not: routine, well-understood work; tasks one person can finish in twenty minutes; and situations where the pair's working styles genuinely clash.

Practical points: swap the keyboard every twenty to thirty minutes, take breaks, and remember it is more tiring than working alone — three or four hours is a full day of pairing.

• Write things down. Decisions made verbally are lost, and remote or absent colleagues never hear them.
  • Over-communicate when remote. Nobody can see that you are stuck, so say so.
  • Update the board honestly. An item stuck for five days is information the team needs.
  • Be reachable in agreed hours and genuinely unreachable outside them.
  • Assume good intent in writing. Terse messages usually mean the sender was busy, not annoyed.

In teams spanning languages and time zones — common for developers in Nepal working with international clients — written clarity matters more than in a co-located team, and the cost of an ambiguous message is a lost day rather than a lost minute.

Asking well: state what you are trying to do, what you have tried, what happened, and what you expected. This is worth doing even when nobody answers — writing it out solves the problem surprisingly often.

Offering well: ask before taking the keyboard. "Would it help to look at this together?" respects that the person may be close to solving it and learning something in the process. Taking over and fixing it silently is faster today and teaches nothing.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: keep your changes small
practitioner.text: If you improve one thing about how you work with a team, make your pull requests small. A 50-line change gets read line by line and genuinely reviewed. A 1,500-line change gets a quick scroll and an approval, which means it received no review at all — while creating the paperwork that says it did. Small changes get better feedback, merge faster, are easier to revert, and cause fewer conflicts. It is entirely within your control and it improves everything downstream of it.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: On your next three code reviews, tag every comment as blocking, suggestion or nit, and include at least one comment on something done well. Separately, look at your last five pull requests and note their size in lines changed. If any exceeded a few hundred lines, plan how you would have split that work into separately mergeable pieces.

takeaways: Code review spreads knowledge and maintains consistency, not only catches defects
Concentrating review in one senior person keeps knowledge where it already is
Mark comments as blocking, suggestion or nit, or authors treat everything as mandatory
Small pull requests get genuine review; large ones get approved unread
Review comments are free expert attention on your work, not an examination
Pairing is worth it for complex, risky, unfamiliar work and for onboarding
Ask for help by stating goal, attempts, result and expectation — it often solves itself

quiz.q: A 2,000-line pull request typically receives:
opts: More comments than a small change
A thorough review, given its importance
Faster feedback from senior reviewers
An approval without being genuinely read
quiz.fb: It creates the paperwork saying review happened while delivering none of the benefit.

quiz.q: Marking review comments as blocking, suggestion or nit exists because otherwise:
opts: Authors treat every comment as mandatory
The tooling cannot track resolution status
Junior developers ignore important issues
Reviewers spend too long writing feedback
quiz.fb: Without severity signals, reviews become exhausting and authors cannot tell what actually matters.

quiz.q: Concentrating all code review in one senior developer:
opts: Is standard practice in regulated environments
Keeps knowledge exactly where it already is
Ensures the highest possible code quality
Reduces the total time spent reviewing
quiz.fb: Spreading knowledge is one of review's main purposes, and it is what makes collective code ownership possible.

quiz.q: Pair programming is most clearly worth the cost when the work is:
opts: Routine and well understood by both people
Small enough to complete in twenty minutes
Complex, risky, or unfamiliar to one person
Under significant deadline pressure
quiz.fb: It is also very effective for onboarding, transferring context far faster than documentation.

quiz.q: When a colleague asks for help, the better first move is to:
opts: Take the keyboard and fix it quickly
Suggest that they raise it at the next standup
Point them to the relevant documentation
Ask whether they would like to look at it together
quiz.fb: They may be close to solving it and learning something. Taking over is faster today and teaches nothing.

quiz.q: Writing out a help request — goal, attempts, result, expectation — is valuable because it:
opts: Frequently solves the problem while writing it
Demonstrates effort to your manager
Reduces the number of interruptions
Creates a written record for future team members
quiz.fb: It is worth doing even when nobody answers, which is why the practice is worth building as a habit.

agile-developers.title: Retrospectives and Your First 90 Days
agile-developers.summary: How teams improve, and how to become good at this quickly
objectives: Participate usefully in a retrospective
Recognise the failure modes that make retrospectives pointless
Understand psychological safety and your part in it
Plan your own development as an agile practitioner
Know what to do in your first three months on a team

sections.html:
At the end of each sprint the team examines how it worked — not what it built. What went well and should continue, what did not, and what specific changes to try next.

This is the mechanism by which an agile team improves. Without it, a team repeats the same problems indefinitely, running the same ceremonies with the same friction. It is the only event whose subject is the team itself.

1. Set the scene (5 min). Remind everyone this is about improving the system, not assigning blame.
  2. Gather data (15 min). Everyone writes observations — what went well, what did not — usually silently first, so the loudest voice does not anchor everyone.
  3. Generate insight (15 min). Group similar items and discuss the underlying causes rather than the symptoms.
  4. Decide actions (15 min). Choose one or two specific changes, each with a named owner and a date.
  5. Close (5 min). Confirm the actions and check how the retrospective itself felt.

The silent writing step matters more than it looks. Without it, the first person to speak sets the agenda and quieter team members — often including the newest, who see the most — contribute nothing.

• No actions come out. The team discusses, feels better, changes nothing, and gradually stops taking it seriously.
  • Actions are never done. Worse than none, because it teaches the team that the meeting is theatre. Put actions on the board like any other work.
  • Too many actions. Twelve improvements means none. One or two, actually completed, beats a list.
  • It becomes a complaint session. Venting has some value but is not improvement. The facilitator should push toward "what will we do differently?"
  • Only safe topics are raised. If the real problem is a manager's behaviour or an unrealistic deadline and nobody says it, the retrospective is not doing its job.
  • The same items recur every sprint. A clear signal the causes are outside the team's control and need escalating.

Retrospectives only work if people can say uncomfortable things without cost. That condition is called psychological safety, and it is built through observable behaviour rather than assurances.

What you can contribute regardless of seniority:

  • Admit your own mistakes first. "I broke the build on Tuesday and it took me too long to notice" makes it safe for others.
  • Never respond to a disclosure with blame, including with a joke at someone's expense.
  • Support someone raising a difficult point, even briefly. Being the second person to say something is genuinely helpful.
  • Ask the naive question. As a new team member you can ask "why do we do it this way?" in a way that nobody else can, and it frequently exposes something worth changing.

Weeks 1–2 — learn. Get the environment running and make one tiny change end to end, however trivial. Read the definition of done, sit in every ceremony, ask what each is for, find out who to ask about what. Write down everything confusing; you will lose this perspective within a month, and it is valuable while you have it.

Weeks 3–6 — contribute. Take small, well-understood items and finish them properly. Write tests. Apply the two-hour rule. Start reviewing others' code — you will learn the system faster from reading it than from writing it. Ask one question in every planning session.

Weeks 7–12 — improve. Take on something slightly beyond your comfort. Raise one specific observation in a retrospective. Fix one thing that annoys everybody — a slow test, a confusing README, a broken script. Offer to pair with someone on unfamiliar work.

By the end of three months you should be able to take a story from the board and finish it without needing help at every step.

• Finish things. The habit that separates reliable developers from busy ones.
  • Say bad news early. Trust is built on this more than on ability.
  • Keep changes small — stories, commits, pull requests, releases. Small is safer at every level, and it is a single habit that pays out in five places.
  • Write the test. Especially for bugs.
  • Leave code better than you found it.
  • Understand why, not just what. The practices are answers to problems; knowing the problem lets you adapt sensibly when the standard answer does not fit.
  • Read code. More than you write. It is how you learn a system and a language.

None of this requires seniority or permission. All of it is available to you from your first week, and doing it consistently is what makes the difference over a career.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: keep a confusion log
practitioner.text: In your first month, keep a running note of everything that confuses you — a badly named function, a step nobody explained, a document that is out of date, a process whose purpose is unclear. You will lose this perspective permanently within about six weeks, because you will have absorbed the assumptions everyone else made long ago. Before that happens, turn the list into two or three specific improvements and raise them. It is the single most valuable contribution a new team member can make, and only you can make it.

activity.title: Practice
activity.text: Write down one specific thing you would raise at your next retrospective — the actual issue, why it matters, and one concrete action you would propose. Then plan your own first-90-days list: three things to learn, one thing you will fix that annoys everyone, and one person you will ask to pair with. Review it after a month.

takeaways: The retrospective is the only event whose subject is the team itself
Write observations silently first, or the loudest voice sets the agenda
One or two actions with owners and dates beats a list of twelve
Actions that are never done are worse than none — they teach the team it is theatre
Recurring items signal causes outside the team's control that need escalating
Admitting your own mistakes first is how a junior developer builds safety
Small changes at every level — stories, commits, pull requests, releases — is one habit that pays out repeatedly

quiz.q: A retrospective examines:
opts: Whether the sprint goal was met by the team
How the team worked, rather than what it built
The quality of the increment for stakeholders
Individual performance across the sprint
quiz.fb: The sprint review covers what was built. The retrospective is the only event whose subject is the team itself.

quiz.q: Retrospective actions that are agreed but never completed are:
opts: A sign the actions were too ambitious
Best carried forward to the following sprint
Worse than no actions, since they teach it is theatre
Acceptable, provided the discussion itself was useful
quiz.fb: Put retrospective actions on the board and track them like any other work item.

quiz.q: Gathering observations silently before discussion prevents:
opts: The meeting from running over its allotted time box
Duplicate items appearing on the board
Disagreement between team members
The loudest voice anchoring the whole session
quiz.fb: Quieter members — often including the newest, who notice most — otherwise contribute nothing.

quiz.q: The same issue appears in four consecutive retrospectives. This most likely means:
opts: Its causes sit outside the team and need escalating
The issue is not actually important to anyone involved
The team is not trying hard enough to fix it
Retrospectives are being held too frequently
quiz.fb: Recurring items are a signal to raise the problem beyond the team rather than to keep re-discussing it.

quiz.q: As a new team member, the perspective that is most valuable and most perishable is:
opts: Your knowledge of the tools used at a previous employer
What confuses you before you absorb the team's assumptions
Your assessment of individual colleagues' abilities
Your view on which framework the team should use
quiz.fb: You lose it permanently within about six weeks, so capture it and turn it into specific improvements while you can.

quiz.q: Which habit most separates reliable developers from merely busy ones?
opts: Responding quickly to messages and requests
Volunteering for the most difficult stories
Finishing work before starting new work
Keeping detailed records of time spent
quiz.fb: Combined with saying bad news early, it is what makes a developer trusted regardless of experience level.

agile-managers.title: What Agile Actually Is — and What It Is Not
agile-managers.summary: Separating the mindset from the ceremonies, and both from the marketing
objectives: State what the Agile Manifesto actually says, and what it deliberately does not say
Distinguish an agile mindset from agile mechanics, and know why the difference decides outcomes
Recognise the most common misreadings of agile that managers act on
Understand where agile came from and why it spread beyond software
Judge whether your organisation is doing agile or being agile

sections.html:
This programme is written for managers, heads of function, programme and portfolio leads, and executives — people who fund agile work, govern it, staff it and answer for it, but who do not run a daily standup.

It assumes you are experienced. It will not teach you to write a user story or facilitate a retrospective; the companion programme Agile Methodologies for Software Developers does that. This one is about the decisions that sit above the team: which approach fits which work, how to fund it, how to structure teams around it, what to measure, how to govern it, whether to scale it, and how to lead the change without becoming one of the majority of transformations that quietly fail.

It also takes a position: agile is a means, not an end. A great deal of what is sold as agile transformation is ceremony without consequence. The programme is built to help you tell the difference.

In 2001, seventeen software practitioners published the Agile Manifesto. It is four value statements and twelve principles, and its structure is more important than most managers realise. The four values are expressed as preferences, not prohibitions:

  • Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
  • Working software over comprehensive documentation
  • Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
  • Responding to change over following a plan

The authors added a sentence that is almost always dropped when the values are quoted: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more."

The misreading that causes the most damage

"Working software over comprehensive documentation" does not mean no documentation. "Responding to change over following a plan" does not mean no plan. Managers who read the Manifesto as a licence to abandon the right-hand column produce projects with no records, no architecture, no forecast and no accountability — and then conclude that agile does not work. It was a statement about relative weight, and it has been read for twenty years as a statement about elimination.

The single most useful distinction in this programme. Organisations adopt agile at two very different depths:

  • Mechanics — "doing agile." The team holds standups, works in two-week sprints, keeps a backlog and runs retrospectives. The visible practices are present.
  • Mindset — "being agile." Decisions move to the people closest to the work. Plans are treated as forecasts to be revised rather than promises to be defended. Change is treated as information rather than failure. Work is measured by value delivered rather than effort expended.

Mechanics without mindset is the most common outcome of an agile transformation, and it is worse than not starting. The team now attends four additional meetings a week, still receives fixed scope on a fixed date from above, still cannot change anything, and has learned that "agile" is a word management uses when it wants more work in less time. Cynicism follows, and it is durable.

Your practical test as a manager: when the team learns something that invalidates the plan, what happens? If the plan changes, you have the mindset. If the team is asked to catch up, you have the mechanics only.

sections.h: Where it came from, and why it spread
sections.html:
Agile originated in software in the early 2000s as a response to a specific failure: large sequential projects that specified everything in advance, built for a year or more, and delivered something the customer no longer wanted. The core insight was not about software. It was about the cost of being wrong for a long time without finding out.

That is why it spread. Organisations in manufacturing, education, healthcare, financial services and government have adopted agile approaches, seeking to become quicker, more responsive and more flexible in fast-moving and complex environments. The Project Management Institute, working with the Agile Alliance, published the Agile Practice Guide specifically for practitioners moving from traditional environments — a signal that agile had become mainstream rather than fringe.

The World Economic Forum has gone further, applying the concept to public policy itself. Its 2018 white paper Agile Governance argues that as traditional policy development lags behind the pace of technological change, governance must become more iterative, more experimental and more collaborative with non-government actors. If the idea now applies to lawmaking, it is not merely a software fashion.

Five claims you will hear that are not true, and that you should be prepared to correct:

  • It is not faster by default. It shortens the time to feedback, not necessarily the time to completion. A project may take just as long and simply be wrong less often.
  • It is not cheaper by default. It changes when money is spent and what you get for it. It is not a cost-reduction programme, and presenting it as one sets a trap you will fall into at the first budget review.
  • It is not a substitute for planning. Research comparing agile and traditional projects has found no difference in the amount of upfront planning; agile projects that plan substantially during execution end up planning more in total.
  • It is not undisciplined. Done properly it demands more discipline than a stage-gated approach, because there is no long quiet period in which problems can hide.
  • It is not universally applicable. This is the most important, and Module 2 gives you the evidence. There are conditions under which agile outperforms and conditions under which it does not.

sections.h: The vocabulary you need to be precise about
sections.html:
• Iterative — repeating a cycle to refine the same thing. Incremental — delivering finished pieces one at a time. Agile is usually both; they are not synonyms.
  • Predictive (waterfall) — scope fixed early, time and cost estimated from it.
  • Adaptive — time and cost fixed, scope varies. This inversion is the heart of the model.
  • Hybrid — a deliberate combination of predictive and adaptive elements in one initiative. Very common and entirely legitimate.
  • Framework — Scrum, Kanban, XP, SAFe. A structure, not a methodology in the older sense.
  • Business agility — the whole organisation's ability to sense and respond, extending beyond delivery teams to finance, HR, marketing and operations.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask what happens when the plan is wrong
practitioner.text: When you want to know how agile an organisation genuinely is, do not count its ceremonies. Ask one question of a team: "The last time you discovered something that meant the plan was wrong — what happened?" The answer tells you everything. Teams in genuinely adaptive organisations describe a conversation, a re-prioritisation and a changed forecast. Teams in ceremonial organisations describe overtime. The ceremonies are identical in both cases, which is why counting them tells you nothing.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Write down the four Manifesto values, then, for each, note honestly what your organisation actually rewards when the two sides conflict. Where the right-hand item wins in practice, name the mechanism that makes it win — a contract clause, a reporting requirement, an approval gate, a bonus scheme. Those mechanisms, not the team's habits, are what you will need to change.

takeaways: The Manifesto states preferences, not prohibitions — the right-hand column still has value
Mechanics without mindset is worse than not starting, because it produces durable cynicism
The diagnostic question is what happens when the team learns the plan is wrong
Agile shortens time to feedback rather than time to completion
Agile projects do not plan less; those planning during execution plan more overall
Adaptive approaches fix time and cost and let scope vary — the inversion of predictive work
The approach is not universally applicable, and Module 2 sets out the conditions

quiz.q: The Agile Manifesto values 'working software over comprehensive documentation'. This means that:
opts: Documentation still has value but carries less weight in a conflict
Documentation should be eliminated entirely from all agile projects
Documentation is the responsibility of a separate team
Documentation is produced only after the software ships
quiz.fb: The Manifesto explicitly states there is value in the items on the right. Reading it as elimination produces projects with no records and no accountability.

quiz.q: An organisation runs standups, sprints and retrospectives, but scope and deadlines are still fixed from above. This is best described as:
opts: A mature agile implementation at scale
Mechanics without mindset, which tends to produce cynicism
Normal early-stage adoption that tends to resolve itself over time
A hybrid approach combining agile and predictive
quiz.fb: The team gains meetings without gaining the ability to adapt, and learns that agile is a word used to request more work.

quiz.q: Research comparing upfront planning in agile and traditional projects has found that:
opts: Traditional projects skip planning more often than agile
Agile projects consistently plan far less than traditional ones
There is no difference in mean upfront planning between them
Planning has no measurable effect on either type
quiz.fb: And where substantial planning happens during execution, agile projects end up doing more planning overall, not less.

quiz.q: In an adaptive approach, which variables are typically fixed and which varies?
opts: Scope is fixed; time and cost are estimated from it
All three are fixed at the start of the work
Cost is fixed; scope and time both vary freely
Time and cost are fixed; scope is allowed to vary
quiz.fb: This inversion of the predictive model is the structural heart of adaptive delivery, and it drives the funding questions in Module 7.

quiz.q: 'Iterative' and 'incremental' describe:
opts: Repeating a cycle to refine, versus delivering finished pieces
The same practice under two different names
Planning styles used only in scaled frameworks
Two competing schools of thought within the broader agile community
quiz.fb: Agile approaches are usually both at once, but the terms are not interchangeable and precision matters in governance discussions.

quiz.q: The World Economic Forum's 2018 work on agile governance argues that:
opts: Public sector agility requires new legislation first
Policy-making must become more iterative as technology outpaces it
Agile methods are fundamentally unsuitable for regulated environments
Governments should adopt Scrum for internal projects
quiz.fb: Traditional policy development lags the pace of innovation, prompting more experimental and collaborative governance approaches.

agile-managers.title: When Agile Works — and When It Does Not
agile-managers.summary: The empirical evidence, including the conditions under which it underperforms
objectives: Understand what large-sample research actually shows about agile and project success
Identify the project conditions that favour or disfavour adaptive approaches
Apply a suitability assessment before committing to an approach
Recognise when a hybrid approach is the correct answer
Avoid the two opposite errors of universal adoption and blanket rejection

sections.h: The evidence base, and why it is thin
sections.html:
Agile is advocated across the professional and academic literature as a superior approach, but empirical evidence substantiating the claim has been notably sparse. Most of what managers are shown is vendor case studies and consultancy surveys with obvious selection effects.

A 2025 study published in the Engineering Management Journal by Serrador and Zadeh is among the more useful correctives. The authors analysed 1,002 projects across multiple industries and countries, of which roughly 935 reported incorporating some form of agile or iterative component. Their headline result supports the general claim — a higher proportion of agile or iterative usage is associated with higher ratings for stakeholder success and overall project success — but the conditional findings are the reason to read it.

The study found agile methods more successful than traditional methods particularly under these conditions:

  • Experienced teams. A significant proportion of experienced members improves outcomes materially.
  • Smaller teams. Benefits diminish as team size grows.
  • Medium to low stakeholder engagement. Counter-intuitive, and discussed below.
  • Unclear goals. Where the objective is genuinely uncertain at the outset, adaptive approaches earn their cost.
  • Medium to high complexity. The harder the problem, the more valuable frequent feedback becomes.

The same study found the effectiveness of agile methods limited in:

  • Low-complexity projects with clear goals. If you know exactly what is needed and it is not difficult, the overhead of iteration buys little.
  • Large teams. Coordination costs rise faster than the benefit.
  • High stakeholder engagement. Where stakeholders are already deeply involved, agile's feedback machinery adds less that was not already present.
  • Inexperienced teams. Self-organisation assumes judgement the team may not yet have.

The finding that should temper the sales pitch

The authors conclude that these results challenge assumptions about agile's universal applicability, and emphasise the benefit of carefully evaluating project-specific factors before implementation. They also note, in fairness, that teams appear to benefit from adopting agile methods even where the project does not fit the ideal use case — which is why they regard the growth of agile as justified. Both halves of that finding matter.

This deserves separate treatment because it is the condition managers most often get wrong, and it is directly relevant to organisations building capability from a standing start.

Agile frameworks deliberately remove structure: no detailed upfront specification, no assigned tasks, no supervisor allocating work. That absence is productive for a team with the judgement to fill it and destructive for a team without. An inexperienced team given autonomy and no guidance does not self-organise; it stalls, or it builds the wrong thing confidently.

The managerial implication is not to withhold agile from junior teams. It is to supply the structure the framework removed, through a strong technical lead, explicit engineering standards, a definition of done that is actually enforced, and closer coaching than a mature team requires. The teams that fail are the ones given the autonomy without the scaffolding.

Various assessment models exist to determine likely fit or gaps for agile approaches, scoring project and organisational factors to indicate alignment or risk. A workable short version — rate each 1 to 5:

  1. Requirement uncertainty. How likely is it that what is needed will change? High favours adaptive.
  2. Feedback availability. Can we show something to a real user or customer every few weeks? If not, iteration loses much of its value.
  3. Team experience. Have these people delivered this kind of work before?
  4. Team size and dedication. Small and dedicated, or large and fragmented across other work?
  5. Cost of change late. High cost of late change favours more upfront definition.
  6. Organisational tolerance. Can funding, governance and contracts actually accommodate varying scope?

Item 6 is the one that fails most often, and it fails at the organisation's level rather than the team's. A team can be perfectly suited to adaptive delivery inside an organisation that cannot fund it, govern it or contract for it. Modules 7 and 9 address this directly.

sections.h: Hybrid is normal, not a compromise
sections.html:
It is not necessary to use a single approach for an entire initiative, and combining predictive, iterative, incremental and adaptive elements produces a hybrid approach that is often the correct answer rather than a failure of nerve.

Common and defensible patterns:

  • Agile development, predictive rollout. Iterative build followed by a sequenced deployment — standard where regulatory approval, physical logistics or training gate the release.
  • Predictive front end, agile delivery. Architecture, procurement or regulatory groundwork settled first, then adaptive build.
  • Agile core, predictive dependencies. The team works adaptively while integrating with vendors and functions that cannot.

Presenting hybrid honestly matters politically. Teams that describe a hybrid approach as "agile" invite the criticism that they are not doing it properly; teams that name it as a deliberate hybrid, with reasons, are much harder to argue with.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: run the suitability filter before the kickoff
practitioner.text: Before committing an initiative to an approach, score it on the six factors with the sponsor, the delivery lead and someone from finance in the room. It takes forty minutes. The value is rarely the score — it is that the disagreements surface immediately. When the delivery lead rates requirement uncertainty at 5 and the sponsor rates it at 1, you have found the argument you were otherwise going to have in month seven, at far greater cost.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take two current initiatives — ideally one you believe suits agile and one you suspect does not. Score both across the six suitability factors. For the weaker fit, decide specifically what you would do: run it predictively, run a hybrid with named boundaries, or fix the organisational constraint that is causing the low score. Write the reasoning down; it is the argument you will need at the next steering meeting.

takeaways: A 1,002-project study associates higher agile usage with higher stakeholder and overall success
Agile outperforms with experienced teams, smaller teams, unclear goals and higher complexity
Its benefits are limited in low-complexity work with clear goals, large teams and inexperienced teams
Teams still appear to benefit even outside the ideal use case, which justifies the general growth
Inexperienced teams need the structure the framework removed, not less guidance
Organisational tolerance for varying scope is the suitability factor that most often fails
Hybrid approaches are legitimate; name them honestly rather than calling them agile

quiz.q: The Serrador and Zadeh study of 1,002 projects found agile methods to be MOST effective in projects with:
opts: Low complexity with clearly specified and stable requirements
Large teams and highly engaged stakeholders
Experienced teams, smaller size and unclear goals
Fixed budgets and externally mandated deadlines
quiz.fb: The same study found benefits limited in low-complexity work with clear goals, large teams, or high stakeholder engagement.

quiz.q: Why do inexperienced teams often struggle with agile approaches?
opts: They lack the tools required by most frameworks
Agile frameworks explicitly exclude junior practitioners from team roles
They are usually assigned to lower-priority initiatives
Frameworks remove structure they do not yet have judgement to replace
quiz.fb: The answer is to supply the removed structure through technical leadership and an enforced definition of done, not to withhold agile.

quiz.q: Which suitability factor most often fails at the organisational rather than the team level?
opts: Whether funding, governance and contracts can accommodate varying scope
Whether feedback can be gathered every few weeks
Whether the team has delivered similar work before
Whether the requirements are likely to change materially during delivery
quiz.fb: A team can be perfectly suited to adaptive delivery inside an organisation that cannot fund it, govern it or contract for it.

quiz.q: An initiative uses iterative development followed by a sequenced regulatory rollout. This should be described as:
opts: A failed agile implementation needing correction
A deliberate hybrid approach, named and justified
An immature stage on the way to full agility
A predictive project with agile terminology applied
quiz.fb: Naming a hybrid honestly, with reasons, is far more defensible than describing it as agile and inviting the charge of doing it badly.

quiz.q: The study's finding on stakeholder engagement was that agile benefits were greater with:
opts: Consistently high stakeholder engagement
Engagement limited to the sponsor alone
Medium to low stakeholder engagement
No stakeholder engagement whatsoever
quiz.fb: Where stakeholders are already deeply involved, agile's feedback machinery adds less that was not already present.

quiz.q: What did the authors conclude about agile's universal applicability?
opts: It should be restricted to software development only
It applies equally well across all project types
Universal adoption remains fully justified despite the mixed empirical results
Their findings challenge that assumption and favour case-by-case evaluation
quiz.fb: They nonetheless note teams benefit even outside the ideal use case, so the growth of agile is justified. Both halves matter.

agile-managers.title: Choosing an Approach: Scrum, Kanban, XP and Hybrids
agile-managers.summary: What each framework is actually for, and how to select between them
objectives: Describe what Scrum, Kanban and XP each optimise for
Match a framework to the characteristics of the work and the team
Understand when combining frameworks is appropriate
Recognise the failure modes specific to each approach
Make and defend a framework selection decision

sections.html:
Scrum organises work into short fixed cycles called sprints, usually one to four weeks, each ending in a potentially releasable increment. It is the most widely adopted framework and the one most managers will encounter first.

Three roles. The Product Owner maximises product value by managing and prioritising the backlog, acting as the voice of the customer. The Scrum Master serves the team by removing impediments and upholding the process. The Development Team builds the increment and is self-managing.

Five events. Sprint Planning selects work and sets a goal; the Daily Scrum is a short alignment meeting; the Sprint Review demonstrates the increment to stakeholders and gathers feedback; the Sprint Retrospective examines how the team worked; and the Sprint itself contains the others. Backlog refinement is a continuous activity widely adopted alongside these.

Three artefacts. The Product Backlog is the prioritised list of everything wanted. The Sprint Backlog is the subset selected for this sprint, and it belongs to the team. The Increment is the working output.

Scrum suits work that can be sliced into two-week chunks, teams that benefit from rhythm, and situations where a regular demonstration to stakeholders is valuable. Its failure mode is the sprint becoming a treadmill — the cadence is kept, the goal is not, and the retrospective becomes a ritual with no consequences.

Kanban has no sprints, no fixed roles and no timeboxes. It has a visualised workflow, explicit work-in-progress limits, and a focus on reducing the time an item takes to travel from request to done.

The central mechanism is the WIP limit, and it is genuinely counter-intuitive to most managers: constraining how many items may be in progress at once increases throughput. Starting less work finishes more work, because context switching and queueing are the dominant costs in knowledge work.

Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably and cannot be batched into sprints — support, operations, maintenance, small change requests, and any team that is interrupt-driven. It also suits teams whose work items vary enormously in size, where sprint commitment is meaningless.

Its failure mode is a board with no limits, which is simply a visible to-do list. If the WIP limits are absent or routinely ignored, the team is not doing Kanban.

XP is the framework concerned with how the work is done technically rather than how it is organised. Its practices include test-driven development, pair programming, continuous integration, collective code ownership, refactoring and a sustainable pace.

XP matters to managers for a reason that is easy to miss. Scrum and Kanban describe how work flows; neither says anything about engineering quality. A team can run flawless Scrum and produce software that becomes unmaintainable within two years. The technical practices are what make sustained iteration possible, and they are the first thing dropped under delivery pressure.

XP suits technically demanding products where quality and frequent release matter. Its failure mode is that its practices are seen as optional developer preferences and cut when a deadline approaches — which is precisely when they are load-bearing.

Selection is a strategic decision based on context, objectives, people and agile maturity, and there is no one-size-fits-all answer. What works for a technology start-up may be wholly inappropriate for a large industrial organisation. Factors to weigh:

  • Team size. Small teams work well with Scrum or XP; large efforts may require a scaling framework (Module 10).
  • Nature of the product. Highly technical products where quality and frequent delivery matter benefit from XP; products with continuous, varied inbound change suit Kanban.
  • Company culture. Hierarchical organisations resistant to change may need a progressive, educational approach before attempting complex frameworks.
  • Level of uncertainty. The more volatile the environment, the more a lightweight iterative approach is warranted.
  • Team maturity. Not all teams are ready to self-organise or apply advanced practices.

Then define the purpose. Speeding time to market, improving business–technology collaboration, raising technical quality and building a customer-centric culture are different goals that point to different answers. If the aim is continuous delivery without blockage, Kanban fits. If the aim is a cohesive team producing iterative deliverables, Scrum is a strong start. If engineering practices are the weakness, XP is the answer.

Combination is common and often better than purity:

  • Scrumban. Scrum's structure with Kanban's flexibility. Useful for teams that need regular delivery but cannot commit to fixed sprint scope — a very common situation in organisations with significant operational load.
  • Scrum plus XP. Scrum's product and team management with XP's technical rigour. Arguably the strongest default for a software product team, and the combination most often missing when quality problems appear.
  • Kanban plus Design Thinking. Suited to discovery phases where the problem itself is still being defined.

You will rarely choose a framework in the abstract. What you will decide is:

  1. Whether this team gets to choose its own. Usually it should. Imposed frameworks are complied with rather than used.
  2. Whether consistency across teams is worth the cost. There is real value in a common language for governance and mobility, and real cost in forcing a support team into sprints.
  3. Whether the technical practices are in place. This is the decision most managers neglect and the one with the longest-lasting consequences.
  4. What you will do when the framework and a deadline conflict. Decide before it happens, because in the moment you will decide badly.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the interrupt test
practitioner.text: If you are unsure whether a team should run Scrum or Kanban, count its interruptions. Ask the team to log, for two weeks, every piece of unplanned work that arrives and must be handled within days. If unplanned work regularly exceeds roughly a quarter of capacity, sprint commitment is a fiction and the team will fail its sprint goal every cycle for reasons outside its control. Put that team on Kanban with WIP limits and stop asking it to commit to two weeks of scope it does not control.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: For one team you are responsible for, work through the five selection factors and state which framework you would choose and why. Then answer the fourth manager's decision explicitly: write down what you will do when the framework and a deadline conflict, and share it with the team before it happens. Finally, check whether the technical practices in Module 3's XP section are present — and if not, note what it would take to establish them.

takeaways: Scrum provides cadence and commitment; its failure mode is a treadmill with no goal
Kanban limits work in progress; starting less work finishes more work
A board without WIP limits is a visible to-do list, not Kanban
XP governs technical quality, which neither Scrum nor Kanban addresses at all
A team can run flawless Scrum and still produce unmaintainable software
Selection depends on team size, product nature, culture, uncertainty and maturity
Scrumban and Scrum-plus-XP are common and often better than framework purity

quiz.q: Limiting work in progress in a Kanban system typically results in:
opts: Higher throughput, because queueing and switching costs fall
Longer cycle times overall but noticeably more predictable delivery
No measurable change to delivery performance
Lower throughput, since fewer items are being worked
quiz.fb: Starting less work finishes more work. Context switching and queueing are the dominant costs in knowledge work.

quiz.q: Which framework addresses engineering quality practices directly?
opts: Scrum, through its sprint review event
Extreme Programming, through its technical practices
Kanban, through its work-in-progress limits
All three address engineering quality to a broadly similar degree
quiz.fb: Scrum and Kanban describe how work flows. Neither says anything about whether the code will be maintainable in two years.

quiz.q: A team is interrupted by unplanned urgent work exceeding a quarter of its capacity. The better fit is:
opts: Extreme Programming, to raise the team's technical quality
Scrum, to impose discipline on the interruptions
Kanban, since sprint commitment would be fiction
A scaling framework to coordinate the demand
quiz.fb: That team will miss its sprint goal every cycle for reasons outside its control, which destroys the meaning of commitment.

quiz.q: In Scrum, who owns the Sprint Backlog?
opts: The Scrum Master, who protects the process
The Product Owner, who prioritises all of the work
The sponsor funding the initiative
The development team that selected the work
quiz.fb: It can be adjusted during the sprint as new learning arises, provided the sprint goal remains the focus.

quiz.q: 'Scrumban' is best described as:
opts: Scrum's structure combined with Kanban's flexibility
A certification level above Scrum Master
Scrum applied to more than one team at once
Kanban operated with fixed two-week planning cycles throughout
quiz.fb: Useful for teams needing regular delivery that cannot commit to fixed sprint scope — common where operational load is significant.

quiz.q: The framework decision managers most often neglect is:
opts: Which agile certifications the Scrum Master currently holds
Whether the technical practices are actually in place
How long the sprint should be
Which tool the team uses to track work
quiz.fb: It is the decision with the longest-lasting consequences, and the practices are first to be cut under delivery pressure.

agile-managers.title: The Manager's New Role
agile-managers.summary: From coordinator to servant leader, and what that actually requires
objectives: Understand what servant leadership means in operational terms
Know what happens to the traditional project manager role
Identify which of your current activities to stop, keep and start
Remove organisational impediments as a primary function
Delegate decisions without abdicating accountability

sections.html:
Many managers are accustomed to sitting at the centre of coordination — tracking progress, resolving dependencies and representing the team's status to the rest of the organisation. That model worked when projects were decomposed into siloed functions and information flowed through a single point.

In high-change work there is more complexity than one person can hold. Cross-functional teams coordinate their own work and collaborate with stakeholders directly. The centre of coordination becomes a bottleneck, and the manager's value has to come from somewhere else.

The Agile Practice Guide puts the reframing in a single sentence worth remembering: the value of project managers is not in their position, but in their ability to make everyone else better.

Servant leadership is the practice of leading through service to the team — understanding and addressing the needs and development of team members to enable the highest possible performance. It is often described in soft terms; it is better understood as a sequence of concrete priorities.

Servant leaders approach the work in this order:

  1. Purpose. Work with the team to define the why, so people can engage and coalesce around the goal. The team optimises at the level of the initiative, not the individual.
  2. People. Once purpose is established, create an environment in which everyone can succeed, and ask each member to contribute across the work rather than only within their speciality.
  3. Process. Do not aim to follow a perfect agile process. Look for results, and let the process serve them.
