  • But conditionally. It performs best with experienced teams, smaller teams, higher complexity and unclear goals; its benefits are limited with large teams, inexperienced teams, low complexity and clear goals.
  • The constraint is usually organisational. Funding, governance, contracts and structure block adaptive delivery far more often than team capability does.
  • Hybrid is legitimate. Combining predictive and adaptive elements is common and frequently correct.
  • Transformation is change management. The base rate for change initiatives applies, and the failure modes are organisational rather than methodological.

The through-line: almost every constraint identified in this programme is one a manager controls. None requires a framework purchase, and most require no budget at all.

Months 1–3: assess and decide.

  • Run the suitability filter on your current portfolio (Module 2); classify each initiative as adaptive, predictive or hybrid
  • Map dependencies and hand-offs for two weeks (Modules 5 and 10)
  • Write the decision-rights map and circulate it (Module 4)
  • Audit your metrics and stop reporting activity data upward (Module 8)
  • Assess readiness honestly and be willing to defer (Module 11)

Months 4–6: change one system mechanism.

  • Convert one initiative to incremental funding with real stop points (Module 7)
  • Replace one governance artefact with a demonstration (Module 9)
  • Start the impediment list and report its age (Module 4)
  • Make one structural change: dedicate members, or remove one hand-off (Module 5)
  • Begin three-point forecasting from actual throughput (Module 6)

Months 7–9: extend and measure.

  • Extend to a second team, chosen for willingness rather than importance
  • Renegotiate one contract's scope-change clause (Module 7)
  • Publish the five-number measurement set (Module 8)
  • Review honestly, including what has not worked (Module 11)

Months 10–12: consolidate.

  • Compare claimed benefits to observed outcomes across the portfolio
  • Decide on scaling only if the dependency map justifies it (Module 10)
  • Retire internal policies whose purpose has passed (Module 9)
  • Set next year's approach on evidence rather than enthusiasm

• Year one builds capability. Expect measurable improvement in cycle time and predictability on two or three initiatives, not a step change in business results.
  • There will be a performance dip before improvement. Say so now.
  • Some initiatives will be stopped. That is the funding model working, not a failure.
  • The organisation will have to change, not only the teams. Name which mechanism you will change first.
  • This is not a cost programme. Say it explicitly and early, because someone will assume otherwise and the assumption is very hard to correct later.

sections.h: Considerations for Nepal and comparable markets
sections.html:
• Team experience is the binding constraint. Evidence is clear that agile underperforms with inexperienced teams. In a market with a young technology workforce and high attrition, this matters more than framework selection. Invest in technical leadership and enforced standards before adopting more ceremony.
  • Outsourced and client-driven work often arrives with fixed scope and price. The contracting module is therefore more important here than in markets with more product work. Capped time-and-materials and fixed-price-per-increment are the realistic negotiating positions.
  • Time-zone overlap with international clients is a structural constraint, not a communication problem. Negotiate it explicitly at contract stage.
  • Hierarchy is a genuine cultural factor. Teams accustomed to deference will not self-organise because they have been told to. Servant leadership requires visible, repeated demonstration before it is believed.
  • Attrition erodes accumulated practice. Document decisions and reasoning, or each departure resets the team.
  • The advantage: smaller organisations have less legacy governance to dismantle. A twenty-person company can change its funding model in a meeting. That is not available to an enterprise.

• Ask what happened when the plan was wrong. The diagnostic from Module 1, useful indefinitely.
  • Report ranges, never single dates.
  • Track impediment age and treat it as a measure of your own performance.
  • Protect team-level metrics from evaluation. Say it repeatedly; teams assume otherwise.
  • Keep stopping things. A portfolio in which nothing is ever cancelled is not being managed.
  • Change one system mechanism a year. Structure outlasts enthusiasm.
  • Say the uncomfortable number first. Credibility compounds, and it is the only asset that lets you use ranges and stop criteria at all.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: pick the system change first
practitioner.text: The instinct is to start with the teams, because that is visible and feels like progress. Start instead with one organisational mechanism — the funding model for a single initiative, or the contents of the monthly report. It is slower, less visible and far more durable, because team practices decay back toward what the surrounding system rewards. Change the system and team behaviour follows without being managed. Change only the teams and you will be managing it forever.

activity.title: Capstone: your adoption plan
activity.text: Write a plan of no more than five pages for your executive team: (1) the named problem this addresses and the measure that will move; (2) your portfolio classified as adaptive, predictive or hybrid with reasoning; (3) the one organisational mechanism you will change in the first six months; (4) your decision-rights map; (5) the five-number measurement set and what you will stop reporting; and (6) the readiness assessment, including what would make you recommend deferring. Then present it, and keep the deferral option genuinely open.

takeaways: Agile outperforms conditionally, and the conditions are knowable in advance
The binding constraint is usually organisational rather than team capability
Almost every constraint in this programme is one a manager controls without budget
Change one system mechanism in the first six months or the change is read as optional
Tell the board that year one builds capability and that there will be a dip
In markets with young workforces, team experience matters more than framework selection
Team practices decay back toward whatever the surrounding system rewards

quiz.q: The evidence in this programme suggests the most common constraint on adaptive delivery is:
opts: The particular delivery framework the organisation selected
Insufficient tooling and automation investment
Organisational funding, governance and contracting
The technical skill of the delivery teams
quiz.fb: Almost every constraint identified is one a manager controls, and most require no budget at all.

quiz.q: When beginning an adoption, the more durable starting point is to change:
opts: Team-level practices, since the results appear more quickly
The project management tooling used across teams
The job titles and reporting lines within delivery
One organisational mechanism such as funding or reporting
quiz.fb: Team practices decay back toward whatever the surrounding system rewards. Change the system and behaviour follows.

quiz.q: For organisations in markets with a young technology workforce, the priority should be:
opts: Technical leadership and enforced standards before more ceremony
Outsourcing delivery until internal capability matures
Selecting the most widely certified framework that is available
Adopting a scaling framework early for consistency
quiz.fb: The evidence is clear that agile underperforms with inexperienced teams, and structure must replace what the framework removes.

quiz.q: What should a manager tell the board about year one?
opts: It will reduce delivery costs across the portfolio
It builds capability and will include a performance dip
It requires no change to existing governance
It will deliver measurable business results within two quarters
quiz.fb: Stating that this is not a cost programme, explicitly and early, is also necessary, because someone will assume otherwise.

quiz.q: A portfolio in which no initiative is ever cancelled indicates that:
opts: Business cases are being prepared rigorously
Teams are consistently meeting their commitments
The portfolio is not actually being managed
Prioritisation at intake is working effectively
quiz.fb: Incremental funding only creates control if the stop option is genuinely exercised from time to time.

quiz.q: A structural advantage smaller organisations hold over large enterprises is that they:
opts: Attract more experienced agile practitioners
Face lower client expectations on delivery dates
Require fewer cross-team dependencies by nature
Have less legacy governance to dismantle
quiz.fb: A twenty-person company can change its funding model in a single meeting. That option is not available to an enterprise.
